                "id": "australia-news/2026/jan/31/australia-heatwave-bom-weather-forecast-hot-temperature-eighth-day-cool-change",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "australia-news",
                "sectionName": "Australia news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T01:17:20Z",
                "webTitle": "Heatwave across Australia\u2019s south-east continues for eighth day ahead of a welcome cool change",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/jan/31/australia-heatwave-bom-weather-forecast-hot-temperature-eighth-day-cool-change",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/australia-news/2026/jan/31/australia-heatwave-bom-weather-forecast-hot-temperature-eighth-day-cool-change",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Heatwave across Australia\u2019s south-east continues for eighth day ahead of a welcome cool change",
                    "standfirst": "
The BoM forecasts parts of inland NSW will exceed 45C on Saturday, with Thargomindah in Queensland to reach 46C, Mildura 45C and Canberra 41C
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast
",
                    "trailText": "The BoM forecasts parts of inland NSW will exceed 45C on Saturday, with Thargomindah in Queensland to reach 46C, Mildura 45C and Canberra 41C",
                    "byline": "Caitlin Cassidy",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
A cool change this weekend is expected to bring an end to eight consecutive days of blistering temperatures above 40C in Australia\u2019s south-east.
 
But before it does, the heat continued on Saturday. Heatwave warnings remained in place for parts of every state and territory excluding Tasmania, with Canberra forecast to reach a top of 41C and parts of inland New South Wales, including Broken Hill, expected to climb higher than 45C.
 
 
 Related: \u2018Air conditioners are struggling\u2019: parts of NSW, Queensland and Victoria swelter as heat records tumble 
 
  
Maximums peaked around 50C on Friday across the northern parts of South Australia and western NSW, including 49.8C at Marree and 50C at Andamooka near Roxby Downs \u2013 both record temperatures. It was the seventh day the temperature was above 46C in Marree.
 
Ceduna climbed above 49C this week, while temperatures rose above 48C in Port Augusta, Port Pirie and Tarcoola.
 
Top temperatures forecast for Saturday included 49C at Ivanhoe in western NSW, 48C at Wilcannia and 47C at Cobar. Mildura in Victoria was forecast to reach 45C, while further north, Thargomindah in Queensland was expected to reach 46C.
 
Sign up: AU Breaking News email
 
Dean Narramore, a senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, said inland parts of south-eastern Australia had suffered through record heat all week, with Saturday marking the final day of temperatures in the mid to high 40s.
 
He said widespread rain and storms across tropical north Australia due to a monsoon low would bring cooler air to parts of Victoria and South Australia on Saturday, sweeping through the remainder of the country\u2019s south-east on Sunday. Temperatures could tumble by as much as 15C.
 
\u201cThrough inland areas, heat will really be the big story once again, where we see another day of temperatures in the mid to high 40s through south-western parts of Queensland,\u201d he said.
 
\u201cAnother very hot day is on the way on Saturday in northern South Australia, but it\u2019ll be much cooler through southern South Australia thanks to those fresh and gusty south to south-easterly winds, with temperatures in the high 20s to low 30s.\u201d
 
In NSW, Narramore said temperatures would once again soar in the mid to high 40s in the west, with cooler conditions expected on the coast and thunderstorms in the south-east.
 
Temperatures were expected to reach the mid 40s in Victoria\u2019s north-west for the final day, with cooler conditions continuing along southern parts of the state.
 
Two fires in Victoria were not yet under control on Saturday, including at Carlisle River in the Otways and the Walwa bushfire on the NSW border. Both were at a watch and act level, with communities slowly returning to the area.
 
On Sunday, Sydney was expected to reach a top of 29C, with showers and thunderstorms possible, while Canberra was forecast to drop down to 31C and Melbourne to reach a maximum of 19C with a few showers. Brisbane was forecast to reach 33C, while Adelaide was expected to reach 25C.
 
Australia is experiencing its second major heatwave for January, off the back of another earlier in the month, which analysts said was made five times more likely due to global heating.
 
The climate crisis has increased the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including heatwaves and bushfires.
 
Hotter than average days and nights were expected to continue until April for much of the country, according to the latest long-range forecast. Sea surface temperatures would remain warmer than average globally, including around Australia.
  ",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/senate-funding-deal-partial-shutdown-looms",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T00:47:09Z",
                "webTitle": "US Senate approves deal to fund government and discuss ICE restrictions",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/senate-funding-deal-partial-shutdown-looms",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/senate-funding-deal-partial-shutdown-looms",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "US Senate approves deal to fund government and discuss ICE restrictions",
                    "standfirst": "
Partial shutdown of government still expected to begin after midnight Friday, lasting at least through weekend
",
                    "trailText": "Partial shutdown of government still expected to begin after midnight Friday, lasting at least through weekend",
                    "byline": "Chris Stein in Washington and Lauren Gambino in Los Angeles",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
The US Senate approved a major government funding package on Friday, after the killings of two US citizens by federal agents in Minneapolis upended spending talks and gave the out-of-power party rare leverage over Donald Trump\u2019s mass deportation campaign.
 
In a 71-29 tally, the Senate overcame opposition from a handful of Republicans to rally behind a deal the president struck with Democrats, an unusual display of bipartisanship as tensions rise nationally over the presence of Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE) agents in US cities.
 
The package still needs approval by the House of Representatives, which is out of session and not scheduled to return until Monday, meaning a partial shutdown of the federal government was expected to begin when funding lapses at midnight Friday.
 
If the House approves the measure swiftly, the impact of the funding lapse is likely to be minimal as most federal employees don\u2019t work over the weekend, and Trump has pledged to sign the package into law as soon as it reaches his desk.
 
The deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both US citizens shot dead in Minneapolis amid a surge of immigration enforcement agents, prompted Senate Democrats to block passage of a measure funding the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE. That jeopardized a broader legislative package intended to continue funding through September for a slew of government departments.
 
The Senate\u2019s top Democrat, Chuck Schumer, outlined a series of reforms to federal agents he wants codified in the DHS\u2019s funding measure, including the requirement that officers wear body cameras, abide by a code of conduct and cease wearing masks and conducting \u201croving patrols\u201d aimed at people they suspect of being illegally in the United States.
 
 
 Related: Anti-ICE protests being held across US as organizers urge national strike 
 
  
\u201cIf our colleagues are not willing to enact real change \u2013 real, strong change \u2013 they should not expect Democratic votes,\u201d Schumer said, following the Friday evening vote. \u201cWe have only a few days to deliver real progress for the American people; the eyes of the nation are watching.\u201d
 
The Senate approved the package after it rejected a series of amendments, including one offered by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont that sought to repeal the $75bn in additional funding for ICE provided by Trump\u2019s so-called \u201cbig, beautiful bill\u201d and transfer it to Medicaid. The amendment failed, but in a sign of the shifting politics, the proposal earned two Republican votes.
 
\u201cWe don\u2019t need a domestic army in America to terrorize people; we need to guarantee healthcare to all Americans,\u201d Sanders said. Republicans argued it was an attempt to \u201cdefund\u201d the agency and give healthcare to undocumented immigrants.
 
While the package easily cleared the 60-vote threshold needed to pass in the Senate, many Democrats stuck to their pledge not to approve any additional funding for DHS without clear restrictions on the way ICE agents operate.
 
\u201cI meant what I said: I refuse to fund an agency that lets federal agents kill US citizens with impunity,\u201d Arizona senator Ruben Gallego said on Friday. \u201cWe need real reform and accountability on paper.\u201d
 
Schumer\u2019s office announced on Thursday evening that a deal had been reached with Republicans to quickly pass through the Senate five spending bills that had bipartisan agreement and would continue the operations of departments including defense, labor, and health and human services through September. Funding for the DHS would be addressed with a stopgap measure lasting two weeks, which would allow time for negotiations over the Democrats\u2019s demands for reforms to immigration enforcement.
 
\u201cThis is a pretty somber moment that we are in,\u201d said senator Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the appropriations committee who led negotiations on the spending bill. \u201cI very seriously doubt the White House would have agreed to renegotiate constraints on DHS, if not for the national outcry from the American people.\u201d
 
The bill next goes to the House for approval.
 
\u201cThe earliest floor action we could have is Monday, so we could inevitably be in a short shutdown situation,\u201d the Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, told USA Today. \u201cBut the House is going to do its job. We want to get the government funded, as does the president.\u201d
 
The agreement had been expected to be put to a vote by the Senate on Thursday evening, but Republican Lindsey Graham reportedly held up the process of passing it unanimously, demanding the removal of a provision undoing the ability of lawmakers to sue the government if their phone call records were obtained by the FBI as part of its investigation into Trump\u2019s 2020 election meddling.
 
An earlier version of the spending bill passed by the House last week repeals that law.
 
The agreement represents an opportunity for Democrats to impose guardrails on Trump\u2019s mass deportation campaign, which began immediately after he took office a year ago and has seen masked federal agents fan out to major cities nationwide.
 
The result has been hundreds of thousands of arrests and deportations, but also killings by ICE agents, detentions of US citizens, and complaints from local leaders and advocacy groups of brutal tactics by officers and violations of rights.
 
\u201cWe\u2019re going to have to evaluate what the real opportunity is to get dramatic change at the Department of Homeland Security. It needs to be bold, it needs to be meaningful, and it needs to be transformative,\u201d the Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said on Friday.
 
But it has come together too late to prevent several federal government departments from closing their doors or curtailing services over the weekend and perhaps on Monday, the first business day when the shutdown will be in effect.
 
Its reception in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives remains uncertain. The chamber had passed both the DHS bill and the five spending bills last week, with seven Democrats joining with the GOP to advance the latter despite calls that it be held up over Good\u2019s killing.
 
However, several rightwing lawmakers have demanded that if the measures return to the chamber, they be coupled with legislation conservatives have demanded such as the Save Act, which would impose identification requirements to vote that critics say would disenfranchise swaths of Americans.
 
\u201cEVERY SINGLE APPROPRIATIONS BILL THAT IS VOTED OUT OF THE HOUSE MUST HAVE THE SAVE ACT ATTACHED,\u201d the Florida congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna said Friday.
 
Their opposition could complicate passage of the spending measures, since Republicans control the chamber with 218 seats to the Democrats\u2019 213. Jeffries warned that Republicans will be blamed if their infighting prevents passage of the spending bills.
 
\u201cThe demands being made by far-right extremists in the House Republican conference are going nowhere, and if, for whatever reason, Speaker Johnson bends the knee to the far right, then Republicans are going to shut the government down,\u201d he said.
 
Even if negotiations stall over restrictions on the administration\u2019s immigration crackdown and DHS spending lapses, it is unlikely to halt ICE\u2019s deportation operations. The agency received $75bn from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year that it could use, and the Trump administration could also mandate that its employees continue working during a shutdown.
",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-minnesota-protest-charges",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T00:07:12Z",
                "webTitle": "Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon released after arrest over Minnesota church protest",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-minnesota-protest-charges",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-minnesota-protest-charges",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon released after arrest over Minnesota church protest",
                    "standfirst": "
Lemon and three others charged with civil rights crimes, says DoJ, as White House celebrates arrest on social media
",
                    "trailText": "Lemon and three others charged with civil rights crimes, DoJ says, as White House celebrates arrest on social media",
                    "byline": "Sam Levine, Jeremy Barr and Anna Betts in New York",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Don Lemon, the former CNN anchor, was released on Friday after being arrested late on Thursday on charges that he violated federal law during a protest at a church in Minnesota earlier this month.
 
Outside a federal courthouse in downtown Los Angeles after his release, Lemon vowed not to be silenced, saying: \u201cI have spent my entire career covering the news. I will not stop now.\u201d
 
\u201cThe first amendment to the US Constitution protects that work for me and countless other journalists who do what I do. I stand with all of them, and I will not be silenced. I look forward to my day in court.\u201d
 
The justice department charged Lemon and three others with civil rights crimes, saying they interfered with the exercise of religious freedom at a place of worship and conspired to do so.
 
Abbe Lowell, a lawyer for Lemon, said Lemon was \u201ctaken into custody by federal agents last night in Los Angeles, where he was covering the Grammy awards\u201d.
 
\u201cDon has been a journalist for 30 years, and his constitutionally protected work in Minneapolis was no different than what he has always done,\u201d Lowell said. \u201cThe first amendment exists to protect journalists whose role it is to shine light on the truth and hold those in power accountable.
 
\u201cInstead of investigating the federal agents who killed two peaceful Minnesota protesters, the Trump justice department is devoting its time, attention and resources to this arrest, and that is the real indictment of wrongdoing in this case,\u201d Lowell added. \u201cThis unprecedented attack on the first amendment and transparent attempt to distract attention from the many crises facing this administration will not stand. Don will fight these charges vigorously and thoroughly in court.\u201d
 
 
 Related: Who is Don Lemon, the ex-CNN anchor arrested over a Minnesota church protest? 
 
  
One of the charges against Lemon also alleges that he violated the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (Face) Act, which penalizes people who go beyond peaceful protest to threaten, obstruct or injure someone who is trying to access a reproductive health clinic or \u201cplace of religious worship\u201d.
 
The Face Act is traditionally used to protect abortion providers and clinics from violence. However, when Trump retook power last year, administration officials said they would largely stop enforcing the law against anti-abortion activists, and pardoned several people who\u2019d been convicted under it. In September, the administration filed Face Act charges against pro-Palestinian activists who had protested at a synagogue. The lawsuit marked the first time that the US government had ever used the Face Act to protect houses of worship.
 
 The White House celebrated Lemon\u2019s arrest with a post on X. \u201cWhen life gives you Lemons,\u201d the White House account\u2019s official post said, accompanied by a chain emoji.
 
Georgia Fort, an independent journalist, was also arrested, according to Pam Bondi, the US attorney general. Fort posted a video on Facebook claiming federal agents were at her door. \u201cAs a member of the press, I filmed the church protest a few weeks ago, and now I\u2019m being arrested for that,\u201d she said. \u201cIt\u2019s hard to understand how we have constitutional rights when you can just be arrested for being a member of the press.\u201d
 
Lemon\u2019s arrest sparked outrage from former colleagues, first amendment advocates and members of Congress.
 
\u201cThis is outrageous and cannot stand. The First Amendment is under attack in America!\u201d Lemon\u2019s former CNN colleague Jim Acosta wrote in a post on X.
 
CNN also condemned the arrest. A network spokesperson said: \u201cThe FBI\u2019s arrest of our former CNN colleague Don Lemon raises profoundly concerning questions about press freedom and the first amendment. The Department of Justice already failed twice to get an arrest warrant for Don and several other journalists in Minnesota, where a chief judge of the Minnesota federal district court found there was \u2018no evidence\u2019 that there was any criminal behavior involved in their work.\u201d
 
The spokesperson added: \u201cThe first amendment in the United States protects journalists who bear witness to news and events as they unfold, ensuring they can report freely in the public interest, and the DoJ\u2019s attempts to violate those rights is unacceptable. We will be following this case closely.\u201d
 
On Friday afternoon, the Human Rights Campaign, Stand Up for America and other local groups showed up at the courthouse to support Lemon. Also at the courthouse, Jane Fonda, an actor and longtime activist, spoke with reporters, saying she was present on behalf of the Committee for the First Amendment, a coalition of about 3,000 people from the entertainment industry organized to protect constitutional rights.
 
\u201cThey arrested the wrong Don,\u201d Fonda said, in a thinly veiled reference to Trump. She called Lemon\u2019s arrest by the president\u2019s administration \u201cone page more out of an authoritarian playbook\u201d.
 
\u201cDon Lemon is a professional journalist,\u201d she said. \u201cHe and his producer were doing their job, nothing more, nothing less. And he\u2019s been arrested, and they\u2019ll make up all kinds of defamatory things to say about him.\u201d
 
She added: \u201cWe can\u2019t fall for it. We have to speak up.\u201d
 
The top Democrats in Congress, Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, also condemned Lemon\u2019s arrest.
 
\u201cLet\u2019s be very clear \u2013 this arrest is not just about one journalist in one incident. The arrest is a dark message to journalists everywhere: if you dare criticize this administration, watch your back,\u201d Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, said on the Senate floor.
 
\u201cThat is not democracy. That is a police state and that is pure authoritarian bile. Democracy will suffer if the government chokes our civil liberties. Under this administration, the Department of Justice has all too often become the Department of Vengeance. Don Lemon should be released at once and the frivolous charges against him dropped.\u201d
 
The arrest comes as last week a federal magistrate judge took the unusual step of declining to sign off on an arrest warrant for Lemon, a decision that reportedly enraged Bondi.
 
\u201cWe\u2019re going to pursue this to the ends of the Earth,\u201d Harmeet Dhillon, who heads the department\u2019s civil rights division, said during an interview with Megyn Kelly on Friday.
 
In a video posted on his online show\u2019s YouTube channel, Lemon attended a protest in which demonstrators disrupted a church service. In an interview with Lemon, a demonstrator described the action as a clandestine operation in which they disrupt \u201cbusiness as usual\u201d at a surprise location. Three demonstrators have already been arrested in connection with the protest on charges of conspiring to interfere with the civil rights of others.
 
After the magistrate judge rejected charges against Lemon, Lowell said the department should drop its effort against his client.
 
\u201cShould the Department of Justice continue with a stunning and troubling effort to silence and punish a journalist for doing his job, Don will call out their latest attack on the rule of law and fight any charges vigorously and thoroughly in court,\u201d he said.
 
Lemon left CNN in 2023 after a 17-year career at the network. As the host of the network\u2019s 10pm hour for several years, his star rose as a frequent critic of Trump during his first administration, memorably branding him a racist. His exit from the network was abrupt, and came only a few months after he had switched to become co-host of the network\u2019s morning show.
 
Carter Sherman contributed reporting

                "id": "film/commentisfree/2026/jan/31/melania-film-donald-trump-documentary-cinema-sydney-australia",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "film",
                "sectionName": "Film",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T00:06:12Z",
                "webTitle": "I endured the Melania film so you don\u2019t have to \u2013 my only regret is not buying popcorn so one of my senses was entertained | Caitlin Cassidy",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/commentisfree/2026/jan/31/melania-film-donald-trump-documentary-cinema-sydney-australia",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/film/commentisfree/2026/jan/31/melania-film-donald-trump-documentary-cinema-sydney-australia",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "I endured the Melania film so you don\u2019t have to \u2013 my only regret is not buying popcorn so one of my senses was entertained",
                    "standfirst": "
\u2018Everyone wants to know,\u2019 Melania says at the beginning of the two-hour extravaganza \u2013 but do we?
",
                    "trailText": "\u2018Everyone wants to know,\u2019 Melania says at the beginning of the two-hour extravaganza \u2013 but do we?",
                    "byline": "Caitlin Cassidy",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
It\u2019s Friday afternoon at Hoyts on Sydney\u2019s northern beaches, and the atmosphere is horrific. I am here to see Amazon\u2019s $75m \u201cdocumentary\u201d on Melania Trump, which has already been condemned as a flop ahead of its release.
 
When I arrive, I panic for a second that I have the time wrong. There are no Melania posters anywhere and the screening is tucked into the back bottom corner of the large movie theatre, like the weird leftover table at a wedding.
 
Eventually, just eight people arrive. The cinema has a capacity of about 150 people. There\u2019s a couple, an elderly lady, a few middle-aged men and me. We all sit in the back for some reason.
 
 
 Related: Melania review \u2013 Trump film is a gilded trash remake of The Zone of Interest  
 
  
I wonder if the terrible showing is because it\u2019s a weird time of day to watch a movie. But of the five evening screenings of Melania taking place on its opening day at cinemas across Sydney, none have sold more than 16 tickets. One has sold just six.
 
Earlier viewings that were slated for 11am in Australia were pulled at the last minute due to a miscommunication over Amazon MGM Studios\u2019 worldwide embargo, preventing any screenings from going ahead before 4pm AEST.
 
This means I am one of less than 100 people in the city of Sydney, population 5.5 million people, to see Melania\u2019s debut. Who are my peers? Maga fans willing to pay $26.75, or just journalists forced to endure the 1-hour-and-48-minute running time so the general public doesn\u2019t have to?
 
The film, which documents the 20 days preceding Donald Trump\u2019s return to power in January 2025, was screened at the White House on Saturday and had its official premiere at Washington\u2019s Kennedy Center \u2013 which the president has renamed the Trump-Kennedy Center in a legally disputed move \u2013 on Thursday, before its release in 27 countries.
 
The timing for its release could\u2019ve been better, coming off the back of the second killing of a civilian by ICE in less than a month, but is there ever good timing with the Trump administration?
 
A spoiler of sorts: I am not a big fan of Melania Trump. I have laughed about her weird, oversized hats and periodically indulged in conspiracy theories that she has been replaced by a lookalike.
 
As celebrities go, she is extremely far down my list of People I Would Like to See a Documentary About.
 
Of course, liking a famous person isn\u2019t a prerequisite for watching a documentary about them. I enjoyed Tiger King despite not enjoying the man commonly known as Tiger King.
 
Yet Melania has been directed by the disgraced film-maker Brett Ratner, marking his first feature in 12 years after being accused of sexual misconduct by multiple women in 2017 (which he has denied).
 
It would be hard to view this as anything other than a propaganda exercise: the president\u2019s Battleship Potemkin.
    
When the film begins, I immediately regret not buying popcorn so at least one of my senses would be entertained. In what feels excruciatingly slow, the first 10 minutes are just her using various modes of transport. Getting ushered into a black car. Boarding a plane. Wishing staff \u201cHappy New Year\u201d in monotone.
 
Then there is her first voiceover.
 
\u201cEveryone wants to know, so here it is, 20 days in my life, family, business, philanthropy and becoming first lady of the United States again.\u201d
 
The next segment of the film is Melania trying on outfits. Then she is looking at the menu for the inauguration dinner. Then she is with an interior designer, discussing nightstands and cabinets for the White House.
 
 
 Related: Eggs, hats and unfettered ambition: what we learned about Melania Trump from her documentary 
 
  
This could be the ultimate trad wife film, I ponder, except that Melania doesn\u2019t actually do anything domestic \u2013 other people do it for her while she instructs them.
 
Some of the weirdest moments are her interactions with the president. In one scene, she is on the phone to Trump as he excitedly discusses how many electoral college votes he won. \u201cThat\u2019s a good one,\u201d she says robotically, then \u201cbye, congrats\u201d.
 
In another scene, they briefly discuss their son, Baron. \u201cI love him, he has an incredible mind,\u201d she says poetically.
 
At this point, I have been to the toilet twice, clutched my face and whispered \u201coh my God\u201d when I\u2019ve checked the time and it has barely passed.
 
The final half is of the inauguration itself. \u201cThat\u2019s the hat,\u201d someone in the cinema remarks when her bizarre outfit is revealed.
 
The most animated she gets is when YMCA comes on at their final ball. There is a look of pure delight on her face. Otherwise she looks either robotic or furious.

                    "bodyText": "It\u2019s Friday afternoon at Hoyts on Sydney\u2019s northern beaches, and the atmosphere is horrific. I am here to see Amazon\u2019s $75m \u201cdocumentary\u201d on Melania Trump, which has already been condemned as a flop ahead of its release. When I arrive, I panic for a second that I have the time wrong. There are no Melania posters anywhere and the screening is tucked into the back bottom corner of the large movie theatre, like the weird leftover table at a wedding. Eventually, just eight people arrive. The cinema has a capacity of about 150 people. There\u2019s a couple, an elderly lady, a few middle-aged men and me. We all sit in the back for some reason. I wonder if the terrible showing is because it\u2019s a weird time of day to watch a movie. But of the five evening screenings of Melania taking place on its opening day at cinemas across Sydney, none have sold more than 16 tickets. One has sold just six. Earlier viewings that were slated for 11am in Australia were pulled at the last minute due to a miscommunication over Amazon MGM Studios\u2019 worldwide embargo, preventing any screenings from going ahead before 4pm AEST. This means I am one of less than 100 people in the city of Sydney, population 5.5 million people, to see Melania\u2019s debut. Who are my peers? Maga fans willing to pay $26.75, or just journalists forced to endure the 1-hour-and-48-minute running time so the general public doesn\u2019t have to? The film, which documents the 20 days preceding Donald Trump\u2019s return to power in January 2025, was screened at the White House on Saturday and had its official premiere at Washington\u2019s Kennedy Center \u2013 which the president has renamed the Trump-Kennedy Center in a legally disputed move \u2013 on Thursday, before its release in 27 countries. The timing for its release could\u2019ve been better, coming off the back of the second killing of a civilian by ICE in less than a month, but is there ever good timing with the Trump administration? A spoiler of sorts: I am not a big fan of Melania Trump. I have laughed about her weird, oversized hats and periodically indulged in conspiracy theories that she has been replaced by a lookalike. As celebrities go, she is extremely far down my list of People I Would Like to See a Documentary About. Of course, liking a famous person isn\u2019t a prerequisite for watching a documentary about them. I enjoyed Tiger King despite not enjoying the man commonly known as Tiger King. Yet Melania has been directed by the disgraced film-maker Brett Ratner, marking his first feature in 12 years after being accused of sexual misconduct by multiple women in 2017 (which he has denied). It would be hard to view this as anything other than a propaganda exercise: the president\u2019s Battleship Potemkin. When the film begins, I immediately regret not buying popcorn so at least one of my senses would be entertained. In what feels excruciatingly slow, the first 10 minutes are just her using various modes of transport. Getting ushered into a black car. Boarding a plane. Wishing staff \u201cHappy New Year\u201d in monotone. Then there is her first voiceover. \u201cEveryone wants to know, so here it is, 20 days in my life, family, business, philanthropy and becoming first lady of the United States again.\u201d The next segment of the film is Melania trying on outfits. Then she is looking at the menu for the inauguration dinner. Then she is with an interior designer, discussing nightstands and cabinets for the White House. This could be the ultimate trad wife film, I ponder, except that Melania doesn\u2019t actually do anything domestic \u2013 other people do it for her while she instructs them. Some of the weirdest moments are her interactions with the president. In one scene, she is on the phone to Trump as he excitedly discusses how many electoral college votes he won. \u201cThat\u2019s a good one,\u201d she says robotically, then \u201cbye, congrats\u201d. In another scene, they briefly discuss their son, Baron. \u201cI love him, he has an incredible mind,\u201d she says poetically. At this point, I have been to the toilet twice, clutched my face and whispered \u201coh my God\u201d when I\u2019ve checked the time and it has barely passed. The final half is of the inauguration itself. \u201cThat\u2019s the hat,\u201d someone in the cinema remarks when her bizarre outfit is revealed. The most animated she gets is when YMCA comes on at their final ball. There is a look of pure delight on her face. Otherwise she looks either robotic or furious. As I emerge from the cinema, I have the strange feeling that I have not only learned nothing but lost brain cells. \u201cWhat did you think?\u201d I ask the elderly lady. \u201cI loved it, wow!\u201d she cries. I pin down the only two people who didn\u2019t see the movie alone. The couple tell me they\u2019re a fan of Trump, and of Melania, but they found the experience too much like a \u201cPR vehicle\u201d. \u201cIt\u2019s not as insightful as I thought it would be,\u201d one says. \u201cI\u2019ve loved Melania for 15 years \u2026 and I feel like it was made to make Trump look better,\u201d the other says. \u201cAs much as it was for her, it was for him.\u201d Isn\u2019t everything.",

            {
                "id": "commentisfree/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-arrest-first-amendment-journalism",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "commentisfree",
                "sectionName": "Opinion",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T00:05:35Z",
                "webTitle": "The arrest of Don Lemon is blatant censorship. And he is not the only one | Seth Stern",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-arrest-first-amendment-journalism",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/commentisfree/2026/jan/30/don-lemon-arrest-first-amendment-journalism",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "The arrest of Don Lemon is blatant censorship. And he is not the only one",
                    "standfirst": "
Thursday\u2019s arrests of Lemon and independent journalist Georgia Fort demonstrate the administration\u2019s lawless crusade against routine journalism
",
                    "trailText": "Thursday\u2019s arrests of Lemon and independent journalist Georgia Fort demonstrate the administration\u2019s lawless crusade against routine journalism",
                    "byline": "Seth Stern",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Two federal courts reviewed the government\u2019s evidence against journalist Don Lemon and declined to approve his arrest last week. But nevertheless, the attorney general, Pam Bondi, persisted, desperate to please her authoritarian boss no matter what the constitution and law say or what her ethical obligations as an attorney require.
 
Thursday\u2019s arrests of Lemon and Georgia Fort, an independent journalist \u2013 like the recent raid on Hannah Natanson, the Washington Post reporter \u2013 demonstrate the administration\u2019s lawless crusade against routine journalism. In normal times the expectation is that even when a journalist\u2019s conduct might technically fit the legal elements of a crime \u2013 jaywalking to get footage of a protest, for example \u2013 prosecutors will exercise their discretion and judgment to not apply the law in a manner that chills the free press.
 
Those assumptions are inverted now. Even when journalists\u2019 conduct is plainly non-criminal, prosecutors will work overtime to figure out some way to harass them, no matter how frivolous. Discouraging journalists from doing their job is not a side-effect they seek to avoid \u2013 it\u2019s the whole point. There is no telling what nonsensical legal theories the administration may advance if it decides to make an example of a reporter it doesn\u2019t like. The law and constitution are only marginally relevant \u2013 the only real rule is don\u2019t piss off Trump.
 
The two federal laws under which Lemon and Fort are reportedly charged are entirely inapplicable. One punishes conspiracies to stop people from exercising constitutional rights. The journalists, of course, didn\u2019t conspire with anyone to do anything nefarious. They simply documented news. It\u2019s ironic that Lemon and Fort are accused of exactly what the Trump administration actually did \u2013 intimidating those who exercise core constitutional freedoms, like documenting news. In fact the very next section of the criminal code prohibits deprivation of constitutional rights \u201cunder color of law\u201d, ie, by the government. Maybe the officials involved in Lemon and Fort\u2019s arrests should think about lawyering up.
 
The other law being wielded against the journalists similarly requires an intent to interfere with religious worship (or access to reproductive health clinics), not the lawful documentation of news events by journalists who neither plan protests nor participate in them. Journalists follow the news \u2013 they don\u2019t decide where it happens. Protesters in Minneapolis chose to demonstrate at the church because the pastor was a higher-up with ICE \u2013 one of the federal agencies terrorizing their city and murdering their neighbors \u2013 not because some journalists told them to.
  
 
 
For those of us who have been monitoring press freedom abuses at the local level, it\u2019s all too familiar
 
 
  
These recent developments are unprecedented at the federal level \u2013 never before has an attorney general personally involved herself in pursuing vindictive criminal charges against journalists the administration doesn\u2019t like, who merely covered a protest. But for those of us who have been monitoring press freedom abuses at the local level (my employer, Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF) operates the US Press Freedom Tracker database), it\u2019s all too familiar.
 
When Natanson was raided, we pointed to the 2023 raid of the Marion County Record in rural Kansas on sham allegations that reporters broke identity theft laws, as well as the raid the same year of the Florida journalist Tim Burke\u2019s home newsroom over nonsensical computer crime charges for publishing news he found online.
 
This time, the first case that came to mind was that of the North Carolina journalists Matilda Bliss and Veronica Coit of the Asheville Blade. It\u2019s a small, self-proclaimed leftist news co-op with which local officials have long feuded.
 
On Christmas night of 2021, Bliss and Coit went to a public park to document a homeless encampment sweep. Their filming of the obviously newsworthy event was routine, except that the park closed at 10pm, and police chose to conduct the encampment sweep after that time. They were arrested, charged and convicted, to the dismay of press freedom advocates everywhere \u2013 after all, they didn\u2019t decide where and when news would take place.
 
The cases against Lemon and Fort may be even weaker given the legal elements of the laws under which they were charged. But they underscore the same absurdity. What if police had shot someone at the encampment sweep (an even more realistic possibility at protests in Minneapolis)? Would reporters be expected to not report the news due to a curfew?
 
When an outlet like the Blade is targeted it\u2019s easy to assume that more mainstream reporters with larger audiences have nothing to worry about. Obviously, that\u2019s not so. We shouldn\u2019t give the Trump administration too much credit for creativity \u2013 their playbooks have been tested outside of the national headlines in places like Asheville.
 
The Blade is not the only example. Before Trump\u2019s administration sought to charge Lemon and Fort under a conspiracy law, nonsensically connecting dots between their first amendment-protected conduct and alleged crimes by protesters, prosecutors in Atlanta tried (and failed) to convict people who had merely distributed pamphlets or held press conferences for \u201cconspiring\u201d with other activists opposing the \u201cCop City\u201d police training facility who allegedly committed real crimes. Trump\u2019s federal prosecutors tried something similar last year by indicting the Texas activist Daniel \u201cDes\u201d Sanchez for conspiring to conceal evidence by transporting anarchist literature after a protest attended by his wife where someone else allegedly shot a police officer.
 
Once again, what starts on the fringes at the local level previews what\u2019s to come in the national news headlines. If local authorities like those who targeted Biss and Coit in furtherance of their own petty grudges don\u2019t like what they\u2019re seeing from the Trump administration, they need to take a good look in the mirror. And journalists need to be the ones to hold that mirror up to their censorial faces. Reporters are often reluctant to make themselves the story, but they\u2019re not the ones doing that, the government is.
 
Of course these days being seen as navel-gazing isn\u2019t the only thing journalists may be afraid of. It\u2019s understandable \u2013 no one wants to be arrested. But the Trump administration\u2019s unconstitutional prosecutions have repeatedly failed in court because judges and juries don\u2019t find them credible (unfortunately, the judges who rule against the administration have largely declined to sanction or hold in contempt attorneys who disregard the law \u2013 hopefully that\u2019ll change in Lemon and Fort\u2019s cases). We\u2019ve already seen in Minneapolis that public pressure makes a difference, even with this administration. Fighting back has a far better track record than self-censorship and capitulation, which only invites more attacks.
 
     
  • Seth Stern is the director of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation and a first amendment lawyer
    •

                "fields": {
                    "headline": "One in seven food delivery businesses in England are \u2018dark kitchens\u2019, study shows",
                    "standfirst": "
University researchers say growth of the hidden fast food industry may pose risks to public health
",
                    "trailText": "University researchers say growth of the hidden fast food industry may pose risks to public health",
                    "byline": "Sarah Marsh Consumer affairs correspondent",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
One in seven food businesses on major delivery platforms, including Deliveroo and Just Eat, is now a \u201cdark kitchen\u201d, a university study shows.
 
The findings, which shine a light on the scale of the hidden takeaway industry, found that 15% of all online food retailers in England were dark kitchens.
 
Also known as \u201ccloud\u201d, \u201cghost\u201d or \u201cvirtual\u201d kitchens, they are delivery-only with no customer-facing storefront.
 
Despite rapid growth, they have \u2013 until now \u2013 lacked a clear and consistent definition, creating challenges for regulators, local authorities, food safety officers, industry stakeholders and consumers.
 
Dr Lucie Nield, co-lead investigator from the University of Sheffield, said: \u201cPeople deserve greater transparency about the food they are ordering online, and these businesses must be held to the appropriate regulatory standards. 
 
\u201cWithout this, dark kitchens risk falling through the gap, with potential consequences for public health, particularly by encouraging increased use of online takeaways, greater availability and therefore greater consumption of high fat, salt or sugar food.
 
\u201cDark kitchens have previously been poorly defined and under-researched, making their impacts difficult to fully understand. 
 
\u201cAdopting a shared definition is essential for clearer communication, more effective regulation and inspection and for driving public health agendas.\u201d
    
The study, which was commissioned by the National Institute for Health and Care Research, brought together multiple university teams to establish the first industry-wide framework for defining and identifying dark kitchens.
 
Researchers worked with academics, public health professionals, local authorities, national governing bodies, industry workers and consumers to ensure the definition reflected how the businesses operated.
 
The final wording was: \u201cTechnology-enabled commercial kitchen(s) operating primarily for delivery, to fulfil remote, on-demand, consumer online orders of food for immediate consumption.\u201d
 
The academics also examined the scale of dark kitchens on major delivery apps. 
 
Using data-scraping methods across platforms such as Uber Eats and Deliveroo, they identified clusters of food brands operating from the same postcode, a key indicator of delivery-only hubs. 
 
The study also cross-referenced locations using tools such as Google Maps, highlighting how difficult these businesses can be for consumers and regulators to spot.
 
Although dark kitchen models offer commercial advantages, including lower operating costs and flexible locations, the research highlighted potential implications for public health.
 
Unlike traditional takeaways, which can be regulated by local authorities using spatial planning policy, dark kitchens are far less visible. 
 
Management zones around schools, which are designed to limit the density of takeaways and support healthier food environments, do not apply to dark kitchens and may be undermined by their activities.
 
Researchers also raised concerns around food safety and transparency, particularly for customers with allergies or dietary sensitivities. Because multiple businesses can operate from the same kitchen space, consumers may not always be aware of shared preparation environments or potential allergen cross-contamination.
 
A survey in 2023 found that 40% of participants bought a takeaway at least weekly, commonly via delivery apps and mainly as a treat or for convenience. 
 
Awareness of dark kitchens was low, with only a quarter having heard of them and just 9% knowingly using one. However, after reading a working definition, more than half said they would consider buying from a dark kitchen, though most wanted this to be made explicit.
 
The new industry-wide definition is aimed at bringing delivery-only hubs under stricter planning and public health oversight with clearer regulation, inspection processes and consumer understanding.

                "id": "food/2026/jan/31/new-type-of-bordeaux-wine-to-gain-official-status-as-result-of-climate-pressure",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "food",
                "sectionName": "Food",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-31T00:01:42Z",
                "webTitle": "New type of Bordeaux wine to gain official status as result of climate pressure",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/jan/31/new-type-of-bordeaux-wine-to-gain-official-status-as-result-of-climate-pressure",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/food/2026/jan/31/new-type-of-bordeaux-wine-to-gain-official-status-as-result-of-climate-pressure",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "New type of Bordeaux wine to gain official status as result of climate pressure",
                    "standfirst": "
Exclusive: Formal validation for claret reflects hotter conditions, falling consumption and shift towards chillable reds
",
                    "trailText": "Exclusive: Formal validation for claret reflects hotter conditions, falling consumption and shift towards chillable reds",
                    "byline": "Tom\u00e9 Morrissy-Swan",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Bordeaux\u2019s wine industry has historically adapted to consumer habits. In the 1970s the region leaned towards white, but by the 2000s was famed for powerful oak-aged reds. 
 
Now it\u2019s turning to a much older form of red with a name familiar to anglophones: claret. With origins in the 12th century, when it was first shipped to Britain, claret was soon our favoured wine, an unofficial byword for bordeaux red, which in recent decades has become increasingly full-bodied.
 
The Bordeaux protected designation of origin has now formally validated bordeaux claret, linking it to the existing Bordeaux appellation. Yet the bottles, available from the 2025 vintage, will differ from what many in Britain consider claret \u2013 lighter, less tannic and lower in alcohol.
 
 
 Related: French winemakers \u2018battle for survival\u2019 as minister prepares for crisis talks 
 
  
Bordeaux has been greatly affected by climate breakdown. Some impacts have been a \u201cpositive challenge\u201d, said St\u00e9phanie Sinoquet, the managing director of the Bordeaux growers\u2019 association, with producers turning to untraditional, heat-resistant grape varieties. Warmer conditions were allowing grapes to reach a \u201cbetter and more consistent ripeness\u201d.
 
Consequently, ever-rising alcohol levels were of concern \u2013 15% is now common. For Jean-Raymond Clarenc, the director of the Bordeaux branch of the Grands Chais de France, the new classification is a \u201cstrategic response to these environmental shifts. By opting for shorter macerations and a profile that values freshness over power, we can produce balanced, elegant wines even in warmer vintages. It\u2019s a way of turning a climatic challenge into an oenological opportunity.\u201d
 
Wine consumption habits are changing for several reasons. Warmer weather means drinkers are seeking lighter, fruitier bottles \u2013 in France as well as Britain, consumption of red wine is falling. Lighter, chillable reds have become de rigueur \u2013 bordeaux claret is designed to be consumed at 8-12C, experts told the Guardian. \u201cFresher and fruitier styles are perceived as more relaxed and inclusive,\u201d said Sinoquet, adding they were more versatile and easier to drink outside meals.
 
While lighter claret (and the even lighter clairet, a dark ros\u00e9) never fully disappeared, Bordeaux producers turned to powerful reds that earned international acclaim and appealed to wealthy collectors, and their prices soared. \u201cClassic bordeaux reds will continue to offer the structured, age-worthy styles,\u201d said Sinoquet.
 
Many cited bordeaux\u2019s spiralling prices as a reason for its struggles. \u201cA 50-year boom is over, vineyards are being abandoned, we\u2019ve even ripped out a few plots ourselves,\u201d said Tony Laithwaite, the founder of the wine retailer Laithwaites. He cited collapsing demand in key markets including China, sales in France dropping and a swing towards white wine. \u201cBordeaux\u2019s posh and pricey image just doesn\u2019t fit any more, in these times of straitened circumstances for everyone.\u201d
 
For Jonathan Kleeman, a sommelier and wine consultant, millennials are less likely to collect expensive wines than previous generations, preferring wines that are ready to drink. \u201cThe new category is going to be interesting,\u201d Kleeman said. \u201cIt actually harks back to the old days. Bordeaux didn\u2019t used to be the big wines they are today. It\u2019s actually bringing an old English term back.\u201d
 
Could it confuse drinkers? \u201cNot really, these wines are aimed at younger generations who don\u2019t really use the word \u2018claret\u2019,\u201d he said. Kleeman cited other old wines now fashionable again, from p\u00e9tillant naturel or \u201cpet-nat\u201d, a traditional form of sparkling wine, to the use of amphorae, ceramic storing vessels popular with natural wine producers. \u201cIt could be a very good move, and people \u2018in the know\u2019 might like the irony of calling it \u2018claret\u2019.\u201d
 
Today, Burgundy is widely considered the world\u2019s most expensive wine region. Will claret be more in line with its pinot noir reds? \u201cI don\u2019t think so,\u201d said sommelier Tom Claxton. \u201cI think the similarities will be a lighter body, but I\u2019d expect these to be more playful or \u2018fun\u2019 wines.\u201d

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/atlanta-fbi-boss-reportedly-ousted-fulton-county",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:34:40Z",
                "webTitle": "Atlanta FBI boss reportedly ousted after questioning DoJ\u2019s renewed interest in 2020 election",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/atlanta-fbi-boss-reportedly-ousted-fulton-county",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/atlanta-fbi-boss-reportedly-ousted-fulton-county",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Atlanta FBI boss reportedly ousted after questioning DoJ\u2019s renewed interest in 2020 election",
                    "standfirst": "
Paul W Brown reportedly voiced concerns about the FBI\u2019s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in Fulton county
",
                    "trailText": "Paul W Brown reportedly voiced concerns about the FBI\u2019s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in Fulton county",
                    "byline": "Sara Braun",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
The special agent in charge of the FBI\u2019s Atlanta field office was reportedly removed from his post after questioning the Trump administration\u2019s renewed interest in investigating the role of Fulton county, Georgia, in the 2020 election.
 
The agent, Paul W Brown, had expressed concerns around the unsubstantiated allegations of voter fraud in Fulton county, which have been perpetuated by Donald Trump since he was defeated by Joe Biden in the 2020 election, according to an MS NOW report on Friday. Citing sources, MS NOW also reported that Brown refused to carry out searches and seizures of records connected to the election that Trump lost four years before winning a second presidency in 2024.
 
News of Brown\u2019s ouster came after the justice department on Thursday executed a search warrant and seized records from the Fulton county elections office in the Atlanta area. Authorities seized 700 boxes related to 2020 election results in the county, which Biden won.
 
 
 Related: Democrats express alarm at Tulsi Gabbard\u2019s presence at FBI elections office raid 
 
  
Trump\u2019s national intelligence director, Tulsi Gabbard, was also seen at the county\u2019s election office that day, drawing concern from Democratic lawmakers about partisan overreach.
 
Brown was replaced the week before the service of the search warrant at the elections office, as first reported by the Associated Press. The personnel decision was not publicized by the FBI, and the AP said the reason for Brown\u2019s removal was not immediately clear.
 
Robb Pitts, the Fulton county board of commissioners chair, spoke out against the Trump administration\u2019s decision to raid the office, arguing that it was unjustified political retribution. Pitts also reaffirmed that, despite the search warrant, the county had nothing to hide.
 
\u201cFulton county elections are fair and lawful, and the outcome of the 2020 election will not change,\u201d he said. \u201cPeriod.\u201d
 
The Guardian has reached out to the FBI for comment.
 
Election integrity experts have said that the 2020 presidential race was the most secure to date. And dozens of legal challenges brought by Trump\u2019s allies that sought to challenge his defeat in that election failed.
 
Nonetheless, Trump continues to falsely claim that the 2020 election was rigged against him in favor of Biden.
 
Trump has not questioned the integrity of the 2024 presidential race, which he won against Vice-President Kamala Harris after Biden dropped his re-election campaign late in the contest.
",

            {
                "id": "football/2026/jan/30/premier-league-news-michael-carrick-manchester-united-newcastle-eddie-howe-the-talk",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "football",
                "sectionName": "Football",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:33:16Z",
                "webTitle": "Premier League news: Carrick vows United will not ease up; Isak saga is behind us, says Howe",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jan/30/premier-league-news-michael-carrick-manchester-united-newcastle-eddie-howe-the-talk",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/football/2026/jan/30/premier-league-news-michael-carrick-manchester-united-newcastle-eddie-howe-the-talk",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Premier League news: Carrick vows United will not ease up; Isak saga is behind us, says Howe",
                    "standfirst": "
News from Friday\u2019s press conferences, including Everton, Tottenham, Manchester City and West Ham
",
                    "trailText": "News from Friday\u2019s press conferences, including Chelsea, Tottenham, Manchester City and West Ham",
                    "byline": "Guardian sport",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Taking Fulham lightly would be \u2018bang out of order\u2019
  
Michael Carrick says Manchester United would be \u201cbang out of order\u201d if they take Fulham for granted on Sunday afterimpressive wins against Manchester City and Arsenal. Those victories have lifted United to fourth, on 38 points, four points ahead of Fulham, and Carrick warned there would be no change of approach when Marco Silva\u2019s side arrive at Old Trafford.
 
\u201cTough game, tough challenge,\u201d said United\u2019s interim manager. \u201cMarco has got Fulham into a really good team. Just because we are at home, taking anything for granted is bang out of order so it might be a case it\u2019s the same flow of the game as the last two weeks. No shame in that, we will deal with the game in front of us and do whatever it takes to come out on top.\u201d
 
Joshua Zirkzee, who has returned to training after injury, has been linked with a transfer before Monday\u2019s deadline. \u201cI think Josh has just been trying to work to get fit and get back around the group and it\u2019s been great to have him back training yesterday,\u201d said Carrick. \u201cThat\u2019s literally as far as it goes for me and for Josh. I\u2019m looking forward to working with him. Nothing else needs to be said.\u201d
 
Carrick did confirm Patrick Dorgu will be unavailable for a prolonged period due to the muscle problem he sustained at Arsenal. \u201cHe\u2019s disappointed, he\u2019s had such a big couple of weeks,\u201d said Carrick. \u201cWe weren\u2019t sure whether it was a little bit of cramp or something more serious and at the moment it looks a little bit more on the serious, so it\u2019ll be a few weeks for that. How many, we\u2019ll have to wait and see.\u201d Jamie Jackson
 
No bad blood over Isak wrangle, says Howe
  
Eddie Howe is not expecting to welcome any new faces to his Newcastle squad before the transfer window closes on Monday night but travels to Liverpool on Saturday buoyed up by a fine away performance at the Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain. 
 
That 1-1 draw on Wednesday night secured Newcastle a two-legged European playoff against Qarabag. It entails a long trek to Baku but Howe believes his team\u2019s recent struggles on the road should be consigned to the past. \u201cIt was a high-level, elite, game in Paris,\u201d he said. \u201cMy players showed their quality; we\u2019ve proved how good we are away from home. We should have no fears now.\u201d
 
More immediately, Newcastle are seeking a first Premier League win at Liverpool since 1994, with Howe maintaining the bad blood provoked by Alexander Isak\u2019s protracted \u00a3125m transfer to the Merseyside club last summer is forgotten. \u201cWe\u2019ve moved on,\u201d he said. \u201cWhat happened is irrelevant now. We\u2019re not looking back, we\u2019re looking forward. There\u2019s certainly nothing (animosity behind the scenes) on our side.\u201d
 
While Isak is sidelined by a broken leg, Newcastle\u2019s captain, Bruno Guimar\u00e3es, faces a fitness test on his ankle injury. Although Joelinton will be absent, Guimar\u00e3es\u2019s midfield sidekick appears weeks rather than months away from a return.\u201cJoe flew to Barcelona for an injection into his groin,\u201d said Newcastle\u2019s manager. \u201cAnd the specialist feels his return could be quite quick, we\u2019re looking at weeks not months.\u201d
 
The full-back Tino Livramentois pencilled in to recover from hamstring trouble in time for a return in early March. Louise Taylor
 
Fair to judge me on this season, says Slot
  
Arne Slot has said it is fair to judge him on a troubled second season at Liverpool and not his title-winning debut, with online abuse \u201cpart of the job\u201d of being a manager in 2026.
 
Slot has received fierce criticism on social media, a lot of it personal, and it reignited when his team\u2019s 13-game unbeaten run ended at Bournemouth last Saturday. Even comfortable passage into the last 16 of the Champions League for a second successive season on Wednesday, courtesy of a 6-0 rout of Qarabag, did not spare Slot criticism, specifically in regards to one post-match comment. 
 
A reminder that Liverpool exited the Europa League quarter-finals against Atalanta two years ago, before sailing through the Champions League group two years running, landed Slot in trouble with the keyboard warriors.
 
Rather than feeling entitled to more respect for winning Liverpool\u2019s 20th league championship last year, the Dutchman accepts that he should be judged on the merits of the current campaign. Liverpool are sixth, 14 points behind leaders Arsenal, before facing Newcastle at Anfield on Saturday. 
 
\u201cMaybe that has changed for managers, that even if you have won something there is still room for criticism, which to a certain extent is normal because we are in a new season and I was the first to say to the players: \u2018We have to forget last season\u2019,\u201d said Slot. \u201cSo it is fair that people judge me on this season and not on last season.\u201d
 
\u201cIt is the part of the job, part of the thing we are living in,\u201d Slot added. \u201cWhat I meant [about the Europa League comment] was that season Liverpool ended up third in the league and we are currently sixth, so I didn\u2019t want to make the point that was a poor season. 
 
\u201cI only said we have achieved so much at this club but sometimes we also have to enjoy a moment like this. We cannot take those things for granted. For all the other things that are being said, that is what you have to accept if you are a manager that is not winning enough games.\u201d
 
Slot\u2019s options are stretched for the visit of Newcastle on Saturday, though Ibrahima Konat\u00e9 should return from compassionate leave and Curtis Jones is available after illness. But the head coach insists he is happy with the size of Liverpool\u2019s squad and the club\u2019s business model. \u201cEveryone talks about \u00a3450m [being spent] but we had to recoup \u00a3300m [since 2024],\u201d he said. \u201cThat\u2019s our model and I am not frustrated about that. Maybe I am little bit frustrated that too many people don\u2019t notice what our model is. That\u2019s the model I stepped in to and I even embrace it. It\u2019s a good model to have for any club.
 
\u201cWe were able to achieve a lot of good things since this ownership is here with this model of sustainability. So we sold for \u00a3300m and bought \u00a3450m. But \u00a3250m we haven\u2019t used yet \u2013 Alexander Isak, Jeremie Frimpong only a little bit and Giovanni Leoni not at all. That is the reality.\u201d Andy Hunter
 
Fulham sign Bobb for \u00a327m
  
Fulham have completed the signing of winger Oscar Bobb from Manchester City on a five-year deal. The 22-year-old Norway international has moved to Craven Cottage in what is understood to be a \u00a327m deal.
 
Meanwhile, Pep Guardiola missed media duties before his side\u2019s trip to Tottenham for personal reasons on Friday. The Manchester City manager was due to hold a lunchtime press conference to preview Sunday\u2019s Premier League game but the club later confirmed the assistant Pep Lijnders would take his place.
 
It comes after Guardiola gave a speech in support of Palestinian children at a charity concert in his home city of Barcelona on Thursday. The club said Guardiola was not present due to a personal reason. The Spaniard was expected to be back for training on Saturday. PA Media
   
Frank convinced Spurs owners \u2018super committed\u2019
  
Thomas Frank talked up the \u201cbig commitment\u201d of Tottenham\u2019s owners despite a quiet January and insisted transfers were not as easy as Football Manager after they missed out on Antoine Semenyo. Spurs will face Semenyo on Sunday when Manchester City visit and Frank revealed the former Bournemouth attacker had been a big target for this winter transfer window before he decided to join Guardiola\u2019s title-chasing side.
 
With only days of the window left, Tottenham have signed Conor Gallagher from Atl\u00e9tico Madrid and the teenage Brazilian left-back Souza, but sold last season\u2019s leading scorer Brennan Johnson and lost Mohammed Kudus, Richarlison, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ben Davies and Lucas Bergvall to serious injuries in January.
 
It led Frank to acknowledge his current squad of players to choose from was weaker than at the start of this month, but he rejected any notion that the majority owners ENIC \u2013 run by the Lewis family Trust \u2013 were not committed to this project with Spurs down in 14th in the Premier League table.
 
Before a daunting run of fixtures in February, which begins with the visit of City, Frank said: \u201cI think we lost, I can\u2019t remember, six or seven players inside three weeks in January? That\u2019s crazy. There were definitely too many, so yeah of course [the squad] it\u2019s weaker than we started the first of January.
 
\u201cI can promise that the Lewis family is super committed to this project. They want to do everything and I would go against my rule, hopefully only once, that there\u2019s no doubt it\u2019s clear that the club wants to sign Semenyo. They did everything. I think that\u2019s a clear signal.
 
Frank revealed a late call would be made on Micky van de Ven after he missed the impressive midweek victory at Eintracht Frankfurt with a \u201cminor\u201d injury, but Spurs could still be without eight players despite Pedro Porro and Richarlison being primed for a return at the end of February. PA Media
 
Nuno believes Traor\u00e9 can boost survival drive
  
Nuno Esp\u00edrito Santo believes he can get the best out of Adama Traor\u00e9 and that the \u201cunique\u201d winger can boost West Ham\u2019s efforts to beat the drop after the manager was reunited with Traor\u00e9, having coached him at Wolves, rescuing the 30-year-old from a disappointing season at Fulham.
 
\u201cI\u2019ve worked with him for many years, and I know him well,\u201d said Nuno. \u201cHe\u2019s unique \u2013 there aren\u2019t many players with his ability one-on-one, or with his pace. He\u2019s going to give us many things that we need. He possesses great threat, and he has great energy, not only on the pitch, but in the dressing room and at the training ground too. He\u2019s a special person to have around. It\u2019s not up to me to judge what\u2019s happened to him before. I\u2019m just happy to have him here.\u201d
 
The Hammers briefly closed the gap to 17th-placed Nottingham Forest to two points last weekend after beating Sunderland, but Forest responded a day later by winning at Brentford to leave Nuno\u2019s side five adrift of safety going into Saturday\u2019s trip to Chelsea. \u201cWe just have to focus on ourselves, and ignore what our opponents are doing,\u201d Nuno added. \u201cWe have to try to compete well, play well, achieve results and keep going. We can\u2019t focus on what the other teams are doing, because we can\u2019t control that.\u201d PA Media
 
Rosenior reinforcements \u2018must be right\u2019
  
Liam Rosenior said Chelsea are ready to move in the final days of the transfer window if the right players are available. The Blues are in the market for a central defender and have been optimistic that a deal for a long-term target could be reached before the end of January.
 
A long-term injury to Levi Colwill which is likely to see him miss the whole season has left Chelsea short of options in the position, but it is understood no emergency cover is likely to be sanctioned with the club preferring to stick with their recruitment plans from before the England defender\u2019s injury.
 
The deadline for deals is on Monday night and Rosenior confirmed that the sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Lawrence Stewart are actively working on strengthening the team and are ready to back their head coach. \u201cThe guys are working hard to stay on top of things in terms of information on what\u2019s out there, who\u2019s interested in our players,\u201d said Rosenior. \u201cIt\u2019s about being prepared for any development.
 
\u201cMy job along with the guys is to make the squad in every area as strong as it can possibly be. Certain players come up that you don\u2019t expect to come up, and then can strengthen you. Whether that\u2019s a striker or a wide player or a defender. If we see something, I know the guys are willing to do it. I don\u2019t want to bring in players for the sake of bringing in players. There\u2019s a possibility it could be busy, a possibility it could be quiet.\u201d PA Media

                    "bodyText": "Taking Fulham lightly would be \u2018bang out of order\u2019 Michael Carrick says Manchester United would be \u201cbang out of order\u201d if they take Fulham for granted on Sunday afterimpressive wins against Manchester City and Arsenal. Those victories have lifted United to fourth, on 38 points, four points ahead of Fulham, and Carrick warned there would be no change of approach when Marco Silva\u2019s side arrive at Old Trafford. \u201cTough game, tough challenge,\u201d said United\u2019s interim manager. \u201cMarco has got Fulham into a really good team. Just because we are at home, taking anything for granted is bang out of order so it might be a case it\u2019s the same flow of the game as the last two weeks. No shame in that, we will deal with the game in front of us and do whatever it takes to come out on top.\u201d Joshua Zirkzee, who has returned to training after injury, has been linked with a transfer before Monday\u2019s deadline. \u201cI think Josh has just been trying to work to get fit and get back around the group and it\u2019s been great to have him back training yesterday,\u201d said Carrick. \u201cThat\u2019s literally as far as it goes for me and for Josh. I\u2019m looking forward to working with him. Nothing else needs to be said.\u201d Carrick did confirm Patrick Dorgu will be unavailable for a prolonged period due to the muscle problem he sustained at Arsenal. \u201cHe\u2019s disappointed, he\u2019s had such a big couple of weeks,\u201d said Carrick. \u201cWe weren\u2019t sure whether it was a little bit of cramp or something more serious and at the moment it looks a little bit more on the serious, so it\u2019ll be a few weeks for that. How many, we\u2019ll have to wait and see.\u201d Jamie Jackson No bad blood over Isak wrangle, says Howe Eddie Howe is not expecting to welcome any new faces to his Newcastle squad before the transfer window closes on Monday night but travels to Liverpool on Saturday buoyed up by a fine away performance at the Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain. That 1-1 draw on Wednesday night secured Newcastle a two-legged European playoff against Qarabag. It entails a long trek to Baku but Howe believes his team\u2019s recent struggles on the road should be consigned to the past. \u201cIt was a high-level, elite, game in Paris,\u201d he said. \u201cMy players showed their quality; we\u2019ve proved how good we are away from home. We should have no fears now.\u201d More immediately, Newcastle are seeking a first Premier League win at Liverpool since 1994, with Howe maintaining the bad blood provoked by Alexander Isak\u2019s protracted \u00a3125m transfer to the Merseyside club last summer is forgotten. \u201cWe\u2019ve moved on,\u201d he said. \u201cWhat happened is irrelevant now. We\u2019re not looking back, we\u2019re looking forward. There\u2019s certainly nothing (animosity behind the scenes) on our side.\u201d While Isak is sidelined by a broken leg, Newcastle\u2019s captain, Bruno Guimar\u00e3es, faces a fitness test on his ankle injury. Although Joelinton will be absent, Guimar\u00e3es\u2019s midfield sidekick appears weeks rather than months away from a return.\u201cJoe flew to Barcelona for an injection into his groin,\u201d said Newcastle\u2019s manager. \u201cAnd the specialist feels his return could be quite quick, we\u2019re looking at weeks not months.\u201d The full-back Tino Livramentois pencilled in to recover from hamstring trouble in time for a return in early March. Louise Taylor Fair to judge me on this season, says Slot Arne Slot has said it is fair to judge him on a troubled second season at Liverpool and not his title-winning debut, with online abuse \u201cpart of the job\u201d of being a manager in 2026. Slot has received fierce criticism on social media, a lot of it personal, and it reignited when his team\u2019s 13-game unbeaten run ended at Bournemouth last Saturday. Even comfortable passage into the last 16 of the Champions League for a second successive season on Wednesday, courtesy of a 6-0 rout of Qarabag, did not spare Slot criticism, specifically in regards to one post-match comment. A reminder that Liverpool exited the Europa League quarter-finals against Atalanta two years ago, before sailing through the Champions League group two years running, landed Slot in trouble with the keyboard warriors. Rather than feeling entitled to more respect for winning Liverpool\u2019s 20th league championship last year, the Dutchman accepts that he should be judged on the merits of the current campaign. Liverpool are sixth, 14 points behind leaders Arsenal, before facing Newcastle at Anfield on Saturday. \u201cMaybe that has changed for managers, that even if you have won something there is still room for criticism, which to a certain extent is normal because we are in a new season and I was the first to say to the players: \u2018We have to forget last season\u2019,\u201d said Slot. \u201cSo it is fair that people judge me on this season and not on last season.\u201d \u201cIt is the part of the job, part of the thing we are living in,\u201d Slot added. \u201cWhat I meant [about the Europa League comment] was that season Liverpool ended up third in the league and we are currently sixth, so I didn\u2019t want to make the point that was a poor season. \u201cI only said we have achieved so much at this club but sometimes we also have to enjoy a moment like this. We cannot take those things for granted. For all the other things that are being said, that is what you have to accept if you are a manager that is not winning enough games.\u201d Slot\u2019s options are stretched for the visit of Newcastle on Saturday, though Ibrahima Konat\u00e9 should return from compassionate leave and Curtis Jones is available after illness. But the head coach insists he is happy with the size of Liverpool\u2019s squad and the club\u2019s business model. \u201cEveryone talks about \u00a3450m [being spent] but we had to recoup \u00a3300m [since 2024],\u201d he said. \u201cThat\u2019s our model and I am not frustrated about that. Maybe I am little bit frustrated that too many people don\u2019t notice what our model is. That\u2019s the model I stepped in to and I even embrace it. It\u2019s a good model to have for any club. \u201cWe were able to achieve a lot of good things since this ownership is here with this model of sustainability. So we sold for \u00a3300m and bought \u00a3450m. But \u00a3250m we haven\u2019t used yet \u2013 Alexander Isak, Jeremie Frimpong only a little bit and Giovanni Leoni not at all. That is the reality.\u201d Andy Hunter Fulham sign Bobb for \u00a327m Fulham have completed the signing of winger Oscar Bobb from Manchester City on a five-year deal. The 22-year-old Norway international has moved to Craven Cottage in what is understood to be a \u00a327m deal. Meanwhile, Pep Guardiola missed media duties before his side\u2019s trip to Tottenham for personal reasons on Friday. The Manchester City manager was due to hold a lunchtime press conference to preview Sunday\u2019s Premier League game but the club later confirmed the assistant Pep Lijnders would take his place. It comes after Guardiola gave a speech in support of Palestinian children at a charity concert in his home city of Barcelona on Thursday. The club said Guardiola was not present due to a personal reason. The Spaniard was expected to be back for training on Saturday.                 "id": "football/2026/jan/30/jack-grealish-everton-injury-rest-of-season-david-moyes-manchester-city",
