                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:30:38Z",
                "webTitle": "David Moyes resigned to being without Jack Grealish for rest of Everton\u2019s season",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jan/30/jack-grealish-everton-injury-rest-of-season-david-moyes-manchester-city",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/football/2026/jan/30/jack-grealish-everton-injury-rest-of-season-david-moyes-manchester-city",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "David Moyes resigned to being without Jack Grealish for rest of Everton\u2019s season",
                    "standfirst": "
  • Club will continue to pay wages and manage his recovery
  • Grealish loan from Manchester City has \u00a350m buy option
",
                    "trailText": "Surgery on a fractured foot means Jack Grealish is unlikely to play for Everton again this season, ending his outside shot at England\u2019s World Cup squad",
                    "byline": "Andy Hunter",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Everton will continue to pay Jack Grealish\u2019s wages and manage his recovery from a fractured foot despite being resigned to losing the on-loan forward for the rest of the season.
 
Grealish\u2019s season and outside hopes of making England\u2019s World Cup squad are effectively over with the 30-year-old expected to undergo surgery on the injury. A final decision will be taken in conjunction with his parent club, Manchester City, but under the terms of last summer\u2019s loan move \u2013 which will cost Everton in the region of \u00a312m \u2013 there is no option to cut the deal short.
 
\u201cThese situations [whether to operate] would normally be taken over by the parent club. I think that at the moment we\u2019re going to probably control most of Jack\u2019s situation.\u201d said David Moyes. Asked whether Grealish could return to City early, the Everton managed replied: \u201cNo. And you wouldn\u2019t for the money.\u201d
 
Grealish has been revitalised at Everton following a difficult period at City, producing six Premier League assists, but the finances required for a permanent transfer mean he might have played his final game for the club.
 
Everton have an option to buy Grealish for \u00a350m this summer, when he will have only 12 months remaining on his City contract, but Moyes insisted it was \u201cfar too early\u201d for a long-term decision. He wants to add to his squad before Monday\u2019s transfer deadline with a right back and striker on his wish-list. Moyes admitted the club have been trying to sign a new right-back for over a year without success, and while he wants to improve the squad in this window, Everton\u2019s owners, The Friedkin Group, may prefer to wait until the summer.
 
\u201cI think the club have got a little bit of that,\u201d said Moyes on waiting for the summer window. \u201cI would like to improve, I don\u2019t want to miss any opportunity where I can improve Everton. I get it that we\u2019ve got to remember we are just out of financial problems, so if anybody is out there thinking we are going to spend \u00a340m on somebody then we are not in that place at the moment.
 
\u201cThat\u2019s not to say we couldn\u2019t do it in the summer, but I don\u2019t think we are really in that place yet. But if I have my way, I think we need to. And obviously losing Jack Grealish as well is a big blow to us regarding limiting our attacking options.\u201d
 
Everton could replace Grealish with Chelsea\u2019s Tyrique George. The left winger is available on loan and has attracted interest from several Premier League and European clubs.

                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/new-epstein-files-howard-lutnick-island",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:26:21Z",
                "webTitle": "Trump commerce secretary Howard Lutnick arranged to visit Epstein island, files show",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/new-epstein-files-howard-lutnick-island",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/new-epstein-files-howard-lutnick-island",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Trump commerce secretary Howard Lutnick arranged to visit Epstein island, files show",
                    "standfirst": "
Newly released documents reveal Lutnick sent email to \u2018Jeff\u2019 and floated plan for \u2018Sunday evening for dinner\u2019
",
                    "trailText": "Newly released documents reveal Lutnick sent email to \u2018Jeff\u2019 and floated plan for \u2018Sunday evening for dinner\u2019",
                    "byline": "Anna Betts",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Howard Lutnick, currently serving as Trump\u2019s US secretary of commerce, arranged to visit Jeffrey Epstein\u2019s island in 2012, according to Epstein-related files released by the Department of Justice on Friday.
 
According to the newly released documents, on 20 November 2012, Epstein\u2019s longtime assistant emailed Lutnick saying that \u201cJeffrey Epstein understands you will be down in St Thomas some over the holidays\u201d and that \u201cJeffrey requested I please pass along some phone numbers to you so the two of you can possibly get together.\u201d
 
On 19 December 2012, Lutnick sent an email to \u201cJeff\u201d telling him that that he and several others, including his wife, children and some friends and their children, were visiting the Caribbean and were on Lutnick\u2019s boat.
 
\u201cWe are landing in St Thomas early Saturday afternoon and planning to head over to St Bart\u2019s/Anguilla on Monday at some point\u201d Lutnick wrote. \u201cWhere are you located (what is exact location for my captain)?? Does Sunday evening for dinner sound good?\u201d
 
An individual whose name is redacted replied: \u201cBelow from Jeffrey: come sat or sunday lunch? little st james on the map, behind christmans cove.\u201d
 
The documents appear to suggest that a meeting took place, as on 24 December, Epstein emailed his assistant with the subject line: \u201cplease forward to howard lutnik\u201d.
 
The email body reads: \u201cnice seeing you, read #2 dot three.\u201d The assistant responds \u201cWill do!\u201d and then forwards the message to Lutnick.
 
On Friday, the New York Times reached Lutnick by phone and Lutnick said he could not comment about the island visit because he had not seen the latest tranche of Epstein documents.
 
\u201cI spent zero time with him,\u201d Lutnick said before ending the call.
 
Also among the newly released tranche of files related to Epstein are documents suggesting Lutnick invited Epstein to a fundraiser for Hilary Clinton in 2015.
 
The document includes an email dated 3 November 2015 in which Epstein\u2019s longtime assistant forwarded him an email from Lutnick, the former CEO of the financial firm Cantor Fitzgerald, with an invitation to a \u201cvery =ntimate [sic] fundraising event\u201d for Hillary Clinton on 11 November.
 
Per the document, Epstein\u2019s assistant forwarded the invitation email to Epstein that same day.
 
It is unclear whether Epstein attended the event.
 
At the time, the New York Post reported on a fundraiser that month held at Lutnick\u2019s home, which the paper described as being \u201cnext door to Jeffrey Epstein\u2019s house\u201d. It is not clear if it was the same event.
 
These new documents come after Lutnick acknowledged in a podcast interview with the New York Post\u2019s Miranda Devine that Epstein was his neighbor, and recounted that in 2005 Epstein invited Lutnick and his wife into his home, and gave them a tour.
 
\u201cBig living room, and then across from it is double doors, I assume it\u2019s the dining room, and he opens the doors and there\u2019s a massage table in the middle of the room, and candles all around and stuff,\u201d Lutnick said. \u201cI say to him, \u2018Massage table in the middle of your house? How often you have a massage?\u2019 And he says, \u2018Every day.\u2019 And then he like gets, like, weirdly close to me and he says, \u2018And the right kind of massage.\u2019
 
\u201cNow, my wife is standing here, so she looks at me and I look at her and we say, \u2018I\u2019m sorry, we have to go,\u2019\u201d Lutnick continued. \u201cAnd we left, and in the six or eight steps it takes to get from his house to my house, my wife and I decided that I will never be in the room with that disgusting person ever again. So I was never in the room with him socially, for business, or even philanthropy. If that guy was there, I wasn\u2019t going, cause he\u2019s gross.\u201d
 
The commerce department did not immediately respond to a comment request from the Guardian regarding the 2015 email.
 
Cantor declined to comment about the 2015 fundraiser to the Guardian.
",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-detains-kids-minnesota-liam-ramos-school",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:24:14Z",
                "webTitle": "ICE detains two more students from Liam Ramos\u2019s school, officials say",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-detains-kids-minnesota-liam-ramos-school",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-detains-kids-minnesota-liam-ramos-school",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "ICE detains two more students from Liam Ramos\u2019s school, officials say",
                    "standfirst": "
The brothers\u2019 mother was taken by ICE and Minnesota educators were forced to bring the children to her
",
                    "trailText": "The brothers\u2019 mother was taken by ICE and Minnesota educators were forced to bring the children to her",
                    "byline": "Sam Levin",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has taken custody of two children who attend the same Minnesota elementary school as Liam Ramos, the detained five-year-old, according to school officials.
 
The superintendent of the school district in Columbia Heights, a Minneapolis suburb, told the Guardian that two brothers, in second and fifth grades, were detained with their mother on Thursday. The mother has a pending asylum case and the family has since been transported to a Texas detention facility, the school official said.
 
Their detention comes amid growing outrage over the government\u2019s continued holding of Liam, a pre-schooler, who is at the same Texas facility with his father and was reported this week to be in a \u201cdepressed\u201d state.
 
The mother of the two boys was first taken into custody during a court appointment for her ongoing immigration case on Thursday, said Zena Stenvik, the superintendent. The mother called school leaders from detention asking that they bring her children to her at the Whipple federal building, a local facility where immigration officers have been holding people arrested during the Trump administration\u2019s aggressive immigration operation in the region.
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested over Minnesota church protest 
 
  
The mother told the school there was no other family to take care of her sons, leaving her no choice but to have her boys detained with her, Stenvik said.
 
\u201cIt was awful. It was heartbreaking for everybody,\u201d the superintendent said. \u201cThis isn\u2019t something we are prepared or trained for. We\u2019ve dedicated our lives to protecting and educating children.\u201d
 
Stenvik said she and Jason Kuhlman, the boy\u2019s principal at Valley View elementary school, made a plan to have trusted school officials be by the boys\u2019 side to comfort and take care of them as they escorted them into the detention center to be reunited with their mother.
 
\u201c[For ICE] to put us in a position like that, I don\u2019t have words \u2026 the frustration, the anger, it\u2019s overwhelming,\u201d Kuhlman told Minnesota Public Radio. \u201c[The boys] were very quiet and \u2026 stoic until we walked through the doors of the Whipple building, and then the older one started to get upset and rightfully so. He\u2019s a fifth-grader, so I guarantee he knows what\u2019s going on \u2026 I think the fear started setting in.\u201d
 
The family has not been publicly identified and the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Friday.
 
A school nurse held both of the boys\u2019 hands as they walked into the facility, said Stenvik. Kuhlman had the family\u2019s immigration paperwork on him and asked officials if the mother and her children could be released with the school leaders, but agents refused, the superintendent said: \u201cIt was very, very traumatic for the children and adults alike.\u201d
 
Leslee Sherk, principal of Columbia academy, another school in the district, also accompanied the boys to the facility and told Minnesota Public Radio they appeared in shock: \u201cIt\u2019s a lot of people in there with guns and weapons and formality and security and masks \u2026 It is not a place for kids. It\u2019s scary.\u201d
 
The boys and their mother have since been transferred to the family immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas, the superintendent said. Joaquin Castro, a Texas Democratic congressman, visited Liam and his father at the facility this week and said he was concerned about the boy\u2019s mental state.
 
There are now five students enrolled in the Columbia Heights school district who are detained in Dilley, Stenvik said.
 
Liam and his father were taken into custody last week as they came home from school. DHS has said agents weren\u2019t targeting Liam and alleged that his mother refused to take him. But school officials, some who rushed to the scene of the arrests, have said it appeared agents were trying to use the boy as \u201cbait\u201d to get his family members to open their front door so agents could potentially detain others.
 
Liam\u2019s family has an active asylum case and had entered the US at an authorized port of entry, lawyers have said.
 
Minneapolis immigrants\u2019 rights lawyers have been fighting in court to stop ICE from rapidly transferring detained people out of state, which they say takes them out of the court jurisdiction in Minnesota, making it harder for families to access their lawyers and fight their cases.
 
In another case last week, immigration agents detained a two-year-old girl and her father in Minneapolis and quickly transported them to Texas despite a judge\u2019s order to keep them in state, lawyers said. The government has since returned the girl to Minnesota, allowing her to be reunited with her mother, following a federal judge\u2019s order.
 
\u201cThis will have long-lasting negative impacts on our children, not just for those who are horrifically detained, but those who are living in fear, those who are not leaving their homes and are now learning online, and those who are driving to school and being stopped,\u201d Stenvik said. \u201cWe are not crime-ridden here. Our students and their families are not criminals \u2026 Our families deserve to go back to living in a peaceful way.\u201d

                "id": "tv-and-radio/2026/jan/30/under-salt-marsh-review-jonathan-pryce-sky-atlantic-now",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "tv-and-radio",
                "sectionName": "Television & radio",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T22:05:39Z",
                "webTitle": "Under Salt Marsh review \u2013 Rafe Spall\u2019s thrilling Welsh crime drama is clever, gripping TV",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/jan/30/under-salt-marsh-review-jonathan-pryce-sky-atlantic-now",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/tv-and-radio/2026/jan/30/under-salt-marsh-review-jonathan-pryce-sky-atlantic-now",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Under Salt Marsh review \u2013 Rafe Spall\u2019s thrilling Welsh crime drama is clever, gripping TV",
                    "standfirst": "
This carefully plotted tale of the investigation into a small boy\u2019s death is a compelling, psychologically astute watch \u2013 which constantly pulls the rug out from under you
",
                    "trailText": "This carefully plotted tale of the investigation into a small boy\u2019s death is a compelling, psychologically astute watch \u2013 which constantly pulls the rug out from under you",
                    "byline": "Lucy Mangan",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
By \u2019eck \u2013 it\u2019s grim out west. Such is the overriding impression wrought by Under Salt Marsh, a six-part crime drama set in the fictional Welsh town of Morfa Halen. As the title suggests, the town sits alongside the treacherously boggy lands, under lowering skies and just, but only just, above rising sea levels. The latter is threatening to make the defences the inhabitants are struggling to build obsolete. A huge storm is thought to be approaching and emergency evacuation warnings readied. Think of the place as a conservation area for the pathetic fallacy. There is a lot of actual and metaphorical gloom about. Much of it is attached to local primary school teacher Jackie Ellis (Kelly Reilly). Already bowed under the weight of her nine-year-old niece Nessa\u2019s (Amara Atwal) disappearance three years ago, she finds the body of one of her pupils, Cefin, as she walks home across the marshes one night. The child has apparently drowned in a drainage ditch.
 
When detective Eric Bull (Rafe Spall), who was also involved in Nessa\u2019s case, arrives to investigate the boy\u2019s death, it becomes clear from his and Jackie\u2019s immediate hostility that they have a fraught history \u2013 although its precise nature differs slightly from the one audiences have come to expect. It\u2019s a series that is good at subverting expectations at every turn \u2013 not least in its delicate evocation of grief and the manifold ways a landscape can affect its people. Morfa Halen\u2019s townsfolk are hardy and self-reliant, qualities born of their environment and isolation. But the drama poses the question of whether such independence serves a person or a community equally well under more extreme circumstances \u2013 be they meteorological or emotional \u2013 or whether a community can implode under the strain.
 
Creator Claire Oakley parcels out her plot carefully \u2013 possibly a little too slowly, unless your appetite for brooding shots of liminal flatlands and distant mountains is inexhaustible \u2013 and clues, questions and suspects accrue. A missing pair of blue wellies, a partial handprint in the mud and a saltwater/freshwater differential suggest the boy did not die in the ditch but was moved there from elsewhere. This in turn suggests another party\u2019s involvement and the possibility that it could also shed light on Nessa\u2019s fate.
 
The local landlady\u2019s unstable son Osian (Julian Lewis Jones) has much to say about his belief that the town is being poisoned and an alibi for the night of Cefin\u2019s death. A new lead comes in the form of the discovery, via a box of schoolwork and other mementoes that Jackie has kept, in which both Nessa and Cefin drew a picture of what looks like an astronaut before they went missing. But Cefin\u2019s best friend James (Osian Emlyn) tells them it is of \u201cthe bee man\u201d. This leads them to the people who \u201clive in unison with the Earth\u201d on nearby Spider Island. Kieran (Nigel James Bradley), their resident apiarist, was interviewed as a possible suspect in Nessa\u2019s disappearance but Jackie\u2019s knowledge of her home town and its inhabitants\u2019 histories reveal a truth more painful to Cefin\u2019s father than the arrest of his son\u2019s killer would have been. Another great strength of Under Salt Marsh is its teasing out of the inevitable connections, crosscurrents and secrets that bind a community but can also fracture it under pressure.
 
We also get insight into the personal lives of the two main characters. Bull is unexpectedly recognised by one of the visiting men from the environmental institute, and we realise he too is keeping an important secret. The way the local people treat Jackie indicates some common knowledge of past troubles, and her casual assignations with James\u2019s uncle Dylan (Harry Lawtey) \u2013 whose own alibi for the night of the probable murder is not fully established \u2013 may be becoming less casual than either of them is prepared for.
 
There were only two episodes available for review but, with a little leap of faith, viewers can surely look forward to a compelling, psychologically astute thriller that manages to weave a thoughtful meditation on the ramifications of isolation and suffering round its narrative poles. There is also the background presence of Jonathan Pryce as the dead boy\u2019s grandfather, Solomon. So far, Solomon\u2019s role has been limited to unleashing his sheep at the town hall meeting to show his contempt for the notion of evacuating the place, and later leading people in a shoreline hymn to commemorate his grandson. But you don\u2019t hire Pryce just for this \u2013 Solomon surely has more of a part to play. We will have to wait, maybe slightly impatiently if the pace doesn\u2019t pick up, and see.
 
\u2022 Under Salt Marsh aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now
",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/man-sentenced-false-confession-charlie-kirk-killing",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:52:33Z",
                "webTitle": "Man accused of falsely confessing to killing Charlie Kirk faces up to 15-year sentence",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/man-sentenced-false-confession-charlie-kirk-killing",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/man-sentenced-false-confession-charlie-kirk-killing",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Man accused of falsely confessing to killing Charlie Kirk faces up to 15-year sentence",
                    "standfirst": "
George Zinn, 71, further admitted to possessing child sexual abuse material and pleaded no contest to allegations
",
                    "trailText": "George Zinn, 71, further admitted to possessing child sexual abuse material and pleaded no contest to allegations",
                    "byline": "Ramon Antonio Vargas",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
A man accused of trying to thwart authorities investigating Charlie Kirk\u2019s killing by falsely confessing to the deadly shooting faces up to 15 years in prison after pleading no contest to the allegation \u2013 and separately admitting to possessing child sexual abuse material.
 
The case centering on George Zinn, 71, all but concluded at a court hearing on Thursday in Provo, Utah, about 5 miles away from the college campus where the Turning Point USA executive director was fatally shot on 10 September 2025.
 
Documents filed in Zinn\u2019s case alleged that he began screaming, \u201cI shot him \u2013 now shoot me,\u201d at Utah Valley University immediately after Kirk was killed by a sniper while speaking there. Video of officers at the scene having restrained Zinn circulated widely online, leading some to believe that he was the conservative political activist\u2019s killer.
 
But, after experiencing an unspecified medical episode and being brought to a hospital, Zinn allegedly told officers he was \u201cglad he said he shot the individual so the real suspect could get away\u201d, police documents said. He also purportedly said he had illicit child sexual abuse material on his cellphone, so he was worried about investigators looking at the device.
 
Authorities subsequently charged Zinn with second-degree obstruction of justice as well as various counts of sexual exploitation of minors. The latter counts were connected to more than 20 images depicting child sexual abuse, including of minors believed to be between five and 12 years old \u2013 along with explicit messages sharing the imagery with others.
 
On Thursday, in front of Utah state court judge Thomas Low, Zinn pleaded no contest to a reduced, third-degree obstruction charge related to the events at UVU. Zinn additionally pleaded guilty to two of the sexual exploitation of minors counts.
 
Low sentenced Zinn to up to five years in prison for the obstruction plea. The other plea got Zinn one to 15 years in prison, as Utah news outlets KSL and ABC 4 first reported.
 
It is ultimately up to a state parole board to determine how long Zinn is going to remain imprisoned, Utah\u2019s Salt Lake Tribune wrote.
 
Zinn\u2019s history of criminal charges and convictions in Utah reportedly dates back three decades. Notably, days after the deadly Boston Marathon terrorist bombing in 2013, he was arrested for allegedly asking Salt Lake City, Utah, marathon organizers if they needed help setting up bombs at the finish line.
 
Utah state prosecutors charged Tyler Robinson with aggravated murder in Kirk\u2019s killing, which was one of several prominent instances of political violence in the US in 2025. Prosecutors have said they plan to seek the death penalty against Robinson, who has pleaded not guilty.

                "id": "film/2026/jan/30/once-upon-a-time-in-harlem-documentary-review",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "film",
                "sectionName": "Film",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:47:03Z",
                "webTitle": "Once Upon a Time in Harlem review \u2013 remarkable Harlem Renaissance documentary",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/jan/30/once-upon-a-time-in-harlem-documentary-review",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/film/2026/jan/30/once-upon-a-time-in-harlem-documentary-review",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Once Upon a Time in Harlem review \u2013 remarkable Harlem Renaissance documentary",
                    "standfirst": "
Sundance film festival: a once-in-a-lifetime dinner party from 1972 is transformed into a thrilling and inspiring hang-out movie
",
                    "trailText": "A once-in-a-lifetime dinner party from 1972 is transformed into a thrilling and inspiring hang-out movie",
                    "byline": "Adrian Horton in Park City",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
In August 1972, the experimental film-maker William Greaves convened a once-in-a-lifetime dinner party at Duke Ellington\u2019s townhouse in Harlem. The occasion was a celebration and reconsideration of the Harlem Renaissance, the watershed African American cultural movement of the 1920s. The guest list included its still-living luminaries, some of the 20th century\u2019s most influential \u2013 and still underappreciated \u2013 musicians, performers, artists, writers, historians and political leaders, all in their sunset years. Over four hours and untold glasses of wine, talk wheeled freely from vivid recollections to consternation, lively anecdotes to contemplations of ongoing struggle. Greaves, by then niche renowned for his innovatively meta documentary Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One, lightly directed the conversation but otherwise let the energy flow. He considered it the most important footage he ever recorded.
 
 
 Related: Seized review \u2013 captivating documentary goes inside a shocking newspaper raid 
 
  
You could probably release that remarkable footage in full, completely unedited and unstructured, and still have a good documentary; every piece is now, 50 years later \u2013 the same distance to us as the Harlem Renaissance was to them \u2013 a bridge to a time no living person can remember, each face and gesture informed by decades of aftermath no straightforward nonfiction film on the period could capture. But Once Upon a Time in Harlem, directed by Greaves\u2019s son David, who was one of four cameramen that day, manages to seamlessly clip and contextualize the party into 100 mesmerizing minutes. It\u2019s both a sublime hang-out of a film and a celebration of individual achievements, a fascinating map of a long-ago scene and a referendum on legacy.
 
That this sumptuous footage, allowed room to breathe, exists at all feels like a miracle; that it takes shape here as a coherent, inventive yet straightforwardly informative film is an intergenerational feat. The footage was originally shot but not used for his 1974 film From These Roots, but William Greaves always intended to shape it \u2013 fly-on-the-wall observations and direct interviews \u2013 into a Harlem Renaissance retrospective, but fell ill before he could complete it; when he died in 2014, at the age of 87, it passed to his widow Louise, who continued work until her own death in 2023, at the age of 90. Now David, along with his daughter Liani Greaves as producer, serve as stewards of William\u2019s archive, supplemented by grants and community funding.
 
They smartly stay out of the way, merely adding nametags and archival photographs as footnotes to the discussions at hand. The structure of the film, which premiered at the Sundance film festival, follows the arc of the party; tentative, polite greetings and warm memories eventually give way to impassioned discussions, even arguments \u2013 should they still use the loaded word \u201cnegro\u201d even though it was demeaning, or convert to \u201cAfro-American\u201d? \u2013 as well as tipsy crosstalk, all within a relaxed atmosphere of hard-won camaraderie. Occasionally, the Greaveses include welcome clips of William lightly prompting conversation to the more tentative guests on, say, the revolution that was jazz music. \u201cIt would be considered a revolution in relation to other music,\u201d says the painter Aaron Douglas. \u201cIt was not a revolution to us\u201d
 
I am tempted, at this point, to just keep quoting extensively from the many subjects, whose personal histories, stories and inside jokes need no summary. Among them: the musicians Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle, whose 1921 musical Shuffle Along was one of the first all-Black Broadway shows; the historians Nathan Huggins and John Henrik Clarke; the poets Arna Bontemps and Frank Horne (uncle of Lena Horne); the actors Leigh Whipper and Irvin C Miller; the photographer James Van Der Zee; the librarians Regina Anderson and Jean Blackwell Hutson; the society page editor Gerri Major and Ida Mae Cullen, the widow of poet Countee Cullen. They speak of departed friends and figures \u2013 some long gone, such as the controversial Pan-Africanist Marcus Garvey, and some, such as the poet Langston Hughes, only a few years past. Some, like the 96-year-old Whipper, had parents who were enslaved, their inclination toward the arts a very expression of liberation.
 
To watch them grapple, in real time, with what happened then and what it means now (the participants being somewhere between their 60s and Whipper\u2019s 96 years old, they are amusingly consternated by the ignorance of the youths), is a faultless, captivating experience. The Harlem Renaissance, says Major, was the first time Black people were recognized as creative people. According to Bontemps, it was a \u201cprism\u201d of the Black experience from all time. Schuyler viewed it as not a renaissance at all but an \u201cawakening\u201d. Whatever the view, it eventually looped back to concerns of ongoingness \u2013 whether the cultural flourishing died on the vine or carried forward into the fraught present. \u201cThe Harlem Renaissance isn\u2019t dead,\u201d Huggins argues, \u201cbecause the Harlem Renaissance lives with everybody.\u201d Fifty years later, every person at the party now gone, Once Upon a Time in Harlem keeps that flame alight.
 
     
  • Once Upon a Time in Harlem is screening at the Sundance film festival and is seeking distribution
    •

                "id": "technology/2026/jan/30/elon-musk-epstein-files-island-visits",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "technology",
                "sectionName": "Technology",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:19:06Z",
                "webTitle": "Elon Musk had more extensive ties to Epstein than previously known, emails show",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jan/30/elon-musk-epstein-files-island-visits",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/technology/2026/jan/30/elon-musk-epstein-files-island-visits",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Elon Musk had more extensive ties to Epstein than previously known, emails show",
                    "standfirst": "
Newly released files from DoJ show the pair making plans in 2012 and 2013 for the Tesla CEO to visit Epstein\u2019s island
",
                    "trailText": "Newly released files from DoJ show the pair making plans in 2012 and 2013 for the Tesla CEO to visit Epstein\u2019s island",
                    "byline": "Nick Robins-Early",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Elon Musk had more extensive \u2013 and more friendly \u2013 communications with the financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein than previously publicly known, according to documents released on Friday by the Department of Justice. Emails in the files appear to show the two cordially messaging each other on two separate occasions to make plans for Musk to visit Epstein\u2019s island.
 
The documents include Musk and Epstein emailing in both 2012 and 2013 to determine when Musk should make the trip to Little St James. Neither exchanges appear to have resulted in Musk visiting the island, due to logistical issues.
 
\u201cWill be in the BVI/St Bart\u2019s area over the holidays. Is there a good time to visit?\u201d Musk states on 13 December 2013.
 
\u201cany day 1st - 8th . play it by ear if you want. always space for you,\u201d Epstein replies.
 
Musk then sends several emails relaying his schedule, and the two settle on 2 January as a date for the visit. The email exchange ends with Epstein telling Musk that he would need to remain in New York and sending his regrets that they could not meet.
 
\u201cBad news- Unfortunately , my schedule will keep me in New York . I was really looking forward to finally spending some time together with just fun as the agenda. so i am very disappointed. Hopefully we can schedule another time in the near future,\u201d Epstein wrote.
 
 
 Related: US justice department releases more than 3 million new pages of Epstein files 
 
  
In November 2012, Epstein sent Musk an email asking \u201chow many people will you be for the heli to island\u201d.
 
\u201cProbably just Talulah and me. What day/night will be the wildest party on your island?\u201d Musk replied, in an apparent reference to his former wife Talulah Riley.
 
Musk followed up with an email on 25 December in response to another Epstein message that encouraged him to visit and offered use of his helicopter.
 
\u201cDo you have any parties planned? I\u2019ve been working to the edge of sanity this year and so, once my kids head home after Christmas, I really want to hit the party scene in St Barts or elsewhere and let loose. The invitation is much appreciated, but a peaceful island experience is the opposite of what I\u2019m looking for,\u201d Musk wrote.
 
\u201cUnderstood , I will see you on st Barth, the ratio on my island might make Talilah uncomfortable,\u201d Epstein responded.

\u201cRatio is not a problem for Talulah,\u201d Musk said.
 
On 2 January 2013, Musk sent Epstein an email suggesting that the visit wouldn\u2019t take place saying: \u201cLogistics won\u2019t work this time around.\u201d
 
Musk has been harshly critical of those linked to Epstein, but the newly released emails appear to contradict his own longstanding denial of any ties of his own. The Tesla CEO told Vanity Fair in 2019 that Epstein was \u201cobviously a creep\u201d and claimed that Epstein \u201ctried repeatedly to get me to visit his island. I declined.\u201d The emails between the two moguls come years after Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor in Florida. Authorities later arrested Epstein in 2019 on federal sex-trafficking charges.
 
A separate email in the documents shows Epstein\u2019s longtime assistant Lesley Groff appearing to make plans for Epstein to have lunch at SpaceX in 2013, stating: \u201cElon Musk appreciates the invitation to the Ranch but has commitments\u2026 Lunch on Monday Feb.25th at 1pm at Space X is confirmed\u201d. It is unclear whether the lunch took place or whether Musk was in attendance. Yet another series of exchanges from March 2013 features Epstein and Musk emailing back and forth after Epstein sends him congratulations a day after a SpaceX rocket launch.
 
A representative for Musk and his artificial intelligence company, xAI, did not immediately return a request for comment.
 
The newly released emails between Musk and Epstein, who was found dead in his prison cell in 2019 and for years has been the subject of speculation over his connections to some of the world\u2019s most powerful people, are part of a tranche of 3 million documents that the justice department made public on Friday.
 
Musk has faced pressure to address any potential connection to Epstein in the past, including after an earlier justice department release of documents related to the investigation mentioned his name. House Democrats last year released a copy of Epstein\u2019s daily schedule, which showed a calendar entry from 2014 that states \u201cReminder: Elon Musk to island Dec. 6 (is this still happening?)\u201d. No other information was included, and Musk denied making plans for the visit in a post on X.
 
\u201cThis is false,\u201d he wrote in response to a post that mentioned the allegations.
 
Musk has also denied knowing Epstein\u2019s longtime co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell, claiming that a much-circulated photo of the two of them together at an event was because she \u201cphotobombed\u201d him at a Vanity Fair party. Musk stated that he once visited Epstein\u2019s Manhattan apartment \u201cfor about 30 minutes\u201d with his ex-wife Talulah Riley as part of research for a book she was writing, but did not specify an exact date.
 
While he has denied a personal connection to Epstein, Musk has invoked the sex offender\u2019s name to attack others. He claimed during his public falling-out with Donald Trump last year that the president\u2019s name was in the Epstein files. He later appeared to delete his posts on X accusing Trump of ties to Epstein. Musk also insulted fellow tech mogul Bill Gates in May over the Microsoft founder\u2019s relationship with Epstein, lashing out after Gates criticized him for cuts to humanitarian aid.
 
\u201cWho does Bill Gates think he is to make comments about the welfare of children given that he frequented Jeffrey Epstein?\u201d Musk said.

A separate email in the documents shows Epstein\u2019s longtime assistant Lesley Groff appearing to make plans for Epstein to have lunch at SpaceX in 2013, stating: \u201cElon Musk appreciates the invitation to the Ranch but has commitments\u2026 Lunch on Monday Feb.25th at 1pm at Space X is confirmed\u201d. It is unclear whether the lunch took place or whether Musk was in attendance. Yet another series of exchanges from March 2013 features Epstein and Musk emailing back and forth after Epstein sends him congratulations a day after a SpaceX rocket launch. A representative for Musk and his artificial intelligence company, xAI, did not immediately return a request for comment. The newly released emails between Musk and Epstein, who was found dead in his prison cell in 2019 and for years has been the subject of speculation over his connections to some of the world\u2019s most powerful people, are part of a tranche of 3 million documents that the justice department made public on Friday. Musk has faced pressure to address any potential connection to Epstein in the past, including after an earlier justice department release of documents related to the investigation mentioned his name. House Democrats last year released a copy of Epstein\u2019s daily schedule, which showed a calendar entry from 2014 that states \u201cReminder: Elon Musk to island Dec. 6 (is this still happening?)\u201d. No other information was included, and Musk denied making plans for the visit in a post on X. \u201cThis is false,\u201d he wrote in response to a post that mentioned the allegations. Musk has also denied knowing Epstein\u2019s longtime co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell, claiming that a much-circulated photo of the two of them together at an event was because she \u201cphotobombed\u201d him at a Vanity Fair party. Musk stated that he once visited Epstein\u2019s Manhattan apartment \u201cfor about 30 minutes\u201d with his ex-wife Talulah Riley as part of research for a book she was writing, but did not specify an exact date. While he has denied a personal connection to Epstein, Musk has invoked the sex offender\u2019s name to attack others. He claimed during his public falling-out with Donald Trump last year that the president\u2019s name was in the Epstein files. He later appeared to delete his posts on X accusing Trump of ties to Epstein. Musk also insulted fellow tech mogul Bill Gates in May over the Microsoft founder\u2019s relationship with Epstein, lashing out after Gates criticized him for cuts to humanitarian aid. \u201cWho does Bill Gates think he is to make comments about the welfare of children given that he frequented Jeffrey Epstein?\u201d Musk said.",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/andrew-intimate-dinner-with-jeffrey-epstein-after-prison-release-files-suggest",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:09:33Z",
                "webTitle": "Andrew went to intimate dinner with Epstein after his prison release, files suggest",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/andrew-intimate-dinner-with-jeffrey-epstein-after-prison-release-files-suggest",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/andrew-intimate-dinner-with-jeffrey-epstein-after-prison-release-files-suggest",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Andrew went to intimate dinner with Epstein after his prison release, files suggest",
                    "standfirst": "
Famous figures including Woody Allen were invited to party with disgraced financier and Mountbatten-Windsor, documents indicate
",
                    "trailText": "Famous figures including Woody Allen were invited to party with disgraced financier and Mountbatten-Windsor, documents indicate",
                    "byline": "Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor attended an intimate party with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein months after he was released from prison, files suggest.
 
The US justice department released another cache of documents relating to the disgraced financier on Friday.
 
They include emails from the Hollywood publicist Peggy Siegal to several high-profile figures in relation to a \u201clast-minute casual dinner\u201d for Mountbatten-Windsor, who was in New York on an \u201cunofficial private visit\u201d in December 2010.
 
The gathering appears to have taken place at Epstein\u2019s New York home, where Mountbatten-Windsor was staying.
 
Mountbatten-Windsor previously said the purpose of his trip was to sever ties with Epstein, who was jailed for child sexual abuse offences in July 2009. During the visit, Mountbatten-Windsor and Epstein were pictured walking together in Central Park.
 
The former prince said in his disastrous Newsnight interview in 2019 that he chose to meet Epstein in person to end the friendship as he felt breaking the news \u201cover the telephone was the chicken\u2019s way of doing it\u201d.
 
However, newly released emails indicate that Siegal drew up a guest list for what she described as a \u201cvery interesting, fast, fun dinner\u201d involving Mountbatten-Windsor and Epstein.
 
She invited the film director Woody Allen and his wife, Soon-Yi Previn; the political strategist George Stephanopoulos and his wife, the actor Alexandra Wentworth; the journalist Katie Couric and the talkshow host Charlie Rose. It is not clear who ultimately attended, but the emails suggest Wentworth withdrew because her children were sick.
 
In the emails, Siegal told Stephanopoulos: \u201cCome on time and you will have private time with Andrew as he is staying at the house.\u201d
 
Separate emails between Epstein and an account named \u201cThe Duke\u201d on 11 and 12 August 2010 suggest the financier wanted to introduce \u201cA\u201d to a 26-year-old Russian woman, whom he suggested he \u201cmight enjoy having dinner with\u201d.
 
Epstein wrote that the woman would be in London in August 2010. \u201cThe Duke\u201d replied that he would be in Geneva \u201cuntil the morning of the 22nd but would be delighted to see her\u201d and then asked: \u201cWill she be bringing a message from you? Please give her my contact details to get in touch.\u201d
 
The email is signed \u201cA\u201d, with what appears to be an email signature that reads \u201cHRH Duke of York KG\u201d.
 
The person asked Epstein whether there was \u201cany other information you might know about her that might be useful to know?\u201d, to which he replied: \u201cshe 26, russian, clevere beautiful, trustworthy and yes she has your email\u201d.
 
In another email released, Epstein\u2019s accomplice, the British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell, addressed a sender who calls themselves \u201cThe Invisible Man\u201d as \u201cAndrew\u201d, and referred to \u201cSarah and the kids\u201d.
 
An email exchange from August 2002 shows the two accounts talking about organising a weekend together on \u201cthe Island\u201d only for the Invisible Man to decline, with Maxwell suggesting \u201c5 stunning red heads\u201d would be there.
 
Epstein killed himself in prison in 2019 as he faced fresh child sexual abuse charges. Mountbatten-Windsor has withdrawn from royal life and been stripped of his titles over his links to Epstein.
 
In 2022, he paid a reported \u00a312m settlement to Virginia Giuffre. Giuffre, who killed herself last April, claimed she was forced to have sex with Mountbatten-Windsor after being trafficked to him by Epstein. He has always strenuously denied these allegations and made the payment without admitting liability.
 
The files released on Friday also show that Maxwell sent an email to the Invisible Man expressing her condolences on the loss of his grandmother, the queen mother, who died in 2002.
 
It read: \u201cSweat pea \u2013 sorry you had to rush home, and also under such sad circumstances. However much the passing was to be expected in one so old, it does not make it any less sad.
 
\u201cShe was wonderful, and I am happy that I managed to meet her and speak with her. We shall reschedule. Love you. Gx.\u201d
 
A reply the next day from the Invisible Man reads: \u201cGot your message this morning. Sorry to have missed you yesterday I will ring later today to chat. A xxx.\u201d
 
Maxwell is serving a 20-year jail sentence in the US for child sex trafficking.
 
In another email from the same account, the sender asks someone, whose name has been redacted, if they are having more children and labelling them \u201csuper sperm\u201d.
 
The email said: \u201cSorry \u2013 I am in LA on my way to Hawaii. Is it true you are having more children? I shall have to refer to you as super sperm!\u201d
 
The tranche of messages also show Elon Musk had more extensive ties to Epstein than previously known.
 
Emails from 2013 appear to show the two cordially messaging each other to make plans for the entrepreneur to visit Epstein\u2019s island Little St James.
 
It also emerged that Epstein sent thousands of pounds in bank transfers after his release from prison in 2009 to Peter Mandelson\u2019s husband Reinaldo Avila da Silva, according to the emails published by the US Department of Justice.
 
Da Silva emailed Epstein on 7 September 2009, about two months after Epstein was released from prison, asking him to fund an osteopathy course and other expenses.
 
Mandelson said on Friday: \u201cI was never culpable or complicit in his crimes. Like everyone else I learned the actual truth about him after his death.\u201d
 
Da Silva has not yet commented.

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/epstein-files-3-million-new-pages",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:05:24Z",
                "webTitle": "US justice department releases more than 3 million new pages of Epstein files",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/epstein-files-3-million-new-pages",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/epstein-files-3-million-new-pages",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "US justice department releases more than 3 million new pages of Epstein files",
                    "standfirst": "
Batch includes more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images related to disgraced financier, Todd Blanche says
  • Elon Musk had more extensive ties to Epstein than previously known, emails show
  • Epstein files release \u2013 latest updates
",
                    "trailText": "Batch includes more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images related to disgraced financier, Todd Blanche says",
                    "byline": "Joseph Gedeon in Washington",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
The US deputy attorney general, Todd Blanche, said on Friday that the justice department had released more than 3m pages of documents related to its investigation into the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in a long-awaited announcement that appears to represent the bulk of the so-called Epstein files that have dogged Donald Trump politically.
 
In a testy news conference, Blanche said that the release would include more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, which will have \u201cextensive redactions\u201d. He added that the Trump administration had produced roughly 3.5m pages in an effort to comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act. He said that they include large quantities of commercial pornography and images \u201cthat were seized from Epstein\u2019s devices\u201d.
 
\u201cThe department\u2019s collection effort resulted in more than 6m pages being identified as potentially responsive, including Department and FBI emails, interview summaries, images, videos and various other materials collected and generated during the various investigations and prosecutions that the act covered,\u201d Blanche said.
 
While an analysis is still under way, the file release exposed previously unknown financial ties and social connections between Epstein and prominent figures in the US and UK.
 
One back-and-forth email chain between Epstein and Elon Musk in 2012 shows the world\u2019s richest billionaire responding to the question \u201chow many people will you be for the heli[copter] to the island\u201d with \u201cwhat day/night will be the wildest party on =our island?\u201d
 
Documents also reveal that Howard Lutnick, Trump\u2019s commerce secretary, planned a visit to Epstein\u2019s private island in December 2012 with his wife and children for a lunch gathering, despite claiming last year that he and his wife had been so \u201crevolted\u201d by Epstein around 2005 that they decided to \u201cnever be in a room with that disgusting person ever again\u201d.
 
A day after the planned meeting, the emails show Epstein\u2019s assistant forwarded Lutnick a message from Epstein that read: \u201cNice seeing you.\u201d
 
Emails also show Epstein transferred thousands of pounds to the former British ambassador Peter Mandelson\u2019s husband, Reinaldo Avila da Silva, beginning in September 2009, just two months after Epstein\u2019s release from prison for soliciting prostitution from a minor. The payments included \u00a310,000 for osteopathy school fees and anatomical models, followed by monthly transfers of $2,000, with Mandelson himself instructing Epstein in one email to structure the arrangement as a loan \u201cto avoid a gift-tax filing\u201d.
 
Other emails reveal that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, more commonly known as ex-prince Andrew, attended an intimate dinner party at Epstein\u2019s New York home in December 2010 \u2013 during the same visit the former prince claimed was meant to sever ties with the convicted sex offender \u2013 with Peggy Siegal, a publicist, assembling a guest list including Woody Allen and George Stephanopoulos.
 
A group of Epstein survivors released a statement condemning the justice department for naming victims while in some cases redacting the names of the accused.
 
\u201cThis latest release of Jeffrey Epstein files is being sold as transparency, but what it actually does is expose survivors,\u201d the statement reads. \u201cOnce again survivors are having their names and identifying information exposed, while the men who abused us remain hidden and protected. That is outrageous.\u201d
 
Trump promised during the 2024 campaign to release the Epstein files, but after taking office, he spent months downplaying the files\u2019 significance and at times lashing out at Republicans who demanded their release.
 
The files became Trump\u2019s \u201cworst issue by far\u201d, according to the CNN analyst Harry Enten, who noted that while 87% of Republicans approved of his overall job performance in a September NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, only 45% approved of his handling of the Epstein files.
 
Under mounting pressure from both parties, Trump abruptly reversed course in November, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act while dismissing the controversy as a \u201cDemocrat hoax\u201d.
 
A letter from the Department of Justice to Congress on Friday explained that the documents were drawn from primary sources spanning 20 years, including the Florida and New York cases against Epstein, the Ghislaine Maxwell prosecution, investigations into Epstein\u2019s death and multiple FBI investigations. The department has also filed court motions to release additional materials currently covered by protective orders from a civil lawsuit and grand jury materials from a case against corrections officers who worked where Epstein died.
 
Blanche said that what was withheld were personal and medical files, documents depicting death, physical abuse and injury, as well as any depiction of child sexual abuse \u201cthat would jeopardize an active federal investigation\u201d. He shared that the department will submit to the House and Senate judiciary committees a report listing \u201call categories of records released and withheld\u201d.
 
Approximately 200,000 pages were redacted or withheld based on various legal privileges including attorney-client privilege and work-product doctrine, according to the letter to Congress.
 
When asked whether there were new names in the document drop, Blanche said he did not have anything to share.
 
He did say that the release reiterated what \u201cPresident Trump has said for years \u2026 which is detailing his relationship, and lack thereof, with Mr Epstein, and what he thought about Mr Epstein\u201d.
 
The justice department also established an email inbox for victims to report redaction concerns and will allow members of Congress to view unredacted portions under confidentiality agreements. Democratic congressman Ro Khanna, who co-authored the Epstein Files Transparency Act to secure their official release, said the redactions are potentially suspicious.
 
\u201cThe DoJ said it identified over 6m potentially responsive pages but is releasing only about 3.5m after review and redactions,\u201d Khanna said in a statement. \u201cI will be reviewing closely to see if they release what I\u2019ve been pushing for: the FBI 302 victim interview statements, a draft indictment and prosecution memorandum prepared during the 2007 Florida investigation, and hundreds of thousands of emails and files from Epstein\u2019s computers.\u201d
 
Just before the files being released to the public, Blanche told Fox News Digital that \u201cin none of these communications, even when doing his best to disparage President Trump, did Epstein suggest President Trump had done anything criminal or had any inappropriate contact with any of his victims\u201d. Later in his press conference, the deputy attorney general said he wanted to dispel rumors about Trump and the justice department working hand-in-hand on Epstein.
 
\u201cWhat we told our reviewers, is that that was the goal \u2026 there\u2019s this mantra out there that, oh, you know, the Department of Justice is supposed to protect Donald J Trump, and that\u2019s what we were telling that\u2019s not true,\u201d Blanche told reporters. \u201cThat was never the case. We are always concerned about the victims.\u201d
 
The huge document dump follows weeks of delay after the department conceded in a 5 January letter that only 12,285 documents totaling 125,575 pages had been published to date, falling far short of a 19 December deadline mandated by the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The attorney general, Pam Bondi, in the letter, wrote that \u201cmore than 2 million documents potentially responsive to the Act\u201d were under various phases of review at the time.
 
Documents released in prior batches under the act have detailed systemic failures by law enforcement officials to stop Epstein\u2019s abuse and included graphic testimony about the recruitment methods used to ensnare victims.
 
Earlier disclosures under the act included grand jury testimony describing how Maxwell allegedly asked one victim to recruit other girls, telling her \u201cthey have to look young at least\u201d, though the victim refused, saying she \u201cdidn\u2019t want anyone else to go through that\u201d.

                    "body": "
\u2022 The French rugby union player Uini Atonio illustrates Thursday\u2019s Six Nations match in tomorrow\u2019s What\u2019s On supplement (p14); however, after the issue went to press, he announced his retirement. This image is in print only.
 
\u2022 The TV series Great News is no longer on Netflix as we said in an article about comfort TV, but it is on Apple TV (Stop the blues a-callin\u2019!, 10 January, What\u2019s On, p2).
 
\u2022 An article said that 24,000 people \u201cin Tunbridge\u201d had been left without drinking water for two weeks last month; the reference should have been to Tunbridge Wells (Water restored to most homes in Kent and Sussex, 17 January, p22). This error was in print only.
 
\u2022 Other recently amended articles include:
 
Judge blocks Trump officials from detaining refugees in Minnesota
 
As the Taliban continue their war on women and girls, it is clear that appeasement has failed
 
What is Nipah virus? Key things to know about the disease amid cases in India
 
Virginia voters to decide on amendment to protect abortion rights
 
Bari Weiss\u2019s new CBS hires include \u2018germ theory denialist\u2019 doctor
 
Labour risks election wipeout unless it improves Britain\u2019s high streets, study finds
 
Browns to appoint Todd Monken as head coach after slew of candidate withdrawals
 
Editorial complaints and correction requests can be sent to: guardian.readers@theguardian.com.
 
You can also write to: Readers\u2019 editor, Kings Place, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU, or leave a voicemail on +44 (0) 20 3353 4736.

                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T21:00:38Z",
                "webTitle": "Five Great Reads: how Animalia became a global bestseller, hand-me-down recipes, and the genius of Miles Davis",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/jan/31/five-great-reads-how-animalia-became-a-global-bestseller-hand-me-down-recipes-and-the-genius-of-miles-davis",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/australia-news/2026/jan/31/five-great-reads-how-animalia-became-a-global-bestseller-hand-me-down-recipes-and-the-genius-of-miles-davis",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Five Great Reads: how Animalia became a global bestseller, hand-me-down recipes, and the genius of Miles Davis",
                    "standfirst": "
Guardian Australia\u2019s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Imogen Dewey
  • Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here
",
                    "trailText": "Guardian Australia\u2019s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Imogen Dewey",
                    "byline": "Imogen Dewey",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Good morning. Food, books, jazz \u2026 today\u2019s spread of good stories from around the Guardian takes in some reliable ingredients for a pleasant weekend. The two other great reads here (about a post-nuclear ghost town, and the fear of dying alone) may not exactly fit that bill \u2026 but you can save them for Sunday night.
 
Put on a record, butter yourself some toast, and enjoy.
 
1. Graeme Base didn\u2019t even want to be a children\u2019s book author
    
Base specialises in the best kind of children\u2019s books: in Sian Cain\u2019s words, \u201cthe ones adults think children won\u2019t like \u2013 too difficult, too weird, too wordy\u201d.
 
Writing and illustrating kids\u2019 stories was never a path he meant to go down, he tells her \u2013 he would have happily designed, say, record covers. But a talent for drawing and an intricate, esoteric eye set him on a charmed road to the NYT bestseller list.
 
First, there was Animalia, \u201cquite unlike any alphabet book published before or since\u201d. Then, after reading some Agatha Christie on holiday, Base got the idea for his next huge hit, The Eleventh Hour.
 
How long will it take to read: A few minutes.
 
Dive into our best kids\u2019 books poll: Both Animalia and The Eleventh Hour have been chosen by Guardian readers among the 50 best Australian picture books ever published \u2013 you can cast your vote until Wednesday. And don\u2019t miss Lenore Taylor\u2019s moving piece on finally understanding Mem Fox, or Alexis Wright\u2019s tribute to Dick Roughsey.
 
2. The Fukushima towns frozen in time
    
Fifteen years ago, a tsunami \u2013 and the most powerful earthquake in Japan\u2019s recorded history \u2013 caused the world\u2019s worst nuclear disaster since Chornobyl.
 
At a local primary school, \u201cthere are still textbooks lying on the desks, pencil cases are strewn across the floor; empty bento boxes that were never taken home. Along the corridor, shoes line the route the children took when they fled.\u201d
 
Justin McCurry has drawn an evocative picture of a region put on pause. Nature has thrived since \u2013 now only bears, raccoons, and boar are seen on the streets. But what happens if the humans come back? And even if they want to, can they?
 
How long will it take to read: Four or five minutes.
 
3. Bapa\u2019s beans, and other family heirloom recipes
    
\u201cFamily recipes are a form of time travel,\u201d writes Jimi Famurewa. \u201cAn act of cultural preservation that connects us deeply to people we may not have met and places we may not have visited.\u201d
 
Guardian readers have shared the dishes that have joined their families across the generations \u2013 from a Turkish spinaka (spinach and feta pie) to tinned baked beans turned into a delicious Indian curry.
 
***
 
\u201cMy grandparents could make a meal out of anything. Even though there was not much money, there was always a feast, and whoever was there would be included.\u201d \u2013 Sonia, 40, Manchester
 
How long will it take to read: Eight minutes \u2013 much longer if you stop to cook (and eat!) along the way.
 
4. Are You Dead? How a viral Chinese app exposed single people\u2019s deepest, darkest fears
    
The Are You Dead? app released by Moonscape Technologies last year surged in popularity in recent weeks, at one point becoming the most downloaded paid-for app in China, Amy Hawkins reports. It\u2019s since rebranded (to \u201cDemumu\u201d \u2013 a portmanteau of \u201cDeath\u201d and cutesy suffix \u201cMumu\u201d) \u2013 but the controversial bluntness of its original name offers plenty of food for thought.
 
What does it do? Users check in daily by clicking a big green button. If you miss two consecutive days, the app sends an automated alert to your designated emergency contact.
 
Why has it hit such a nerve? The topic of social isolation feels particularly acute in Chinese cities, Hawkins explains, where marriage and birthrates have hit record lows, and many people live alone.
 
And there\u2019s a compounding factor: one analyst she speaks to notes a growing \u201cloneliness economy\u201d. Liberation from traditional family structures may give freedom to many, but can leave a gap in human connection that technology (and companies) are quick to fill.
 
How long will it take to read: Five minutes.
 
5. One hundred years of Miles Davis
    
This year is the centenary of the jazz giant\u2019s birth, and music critic Ammar Kalia asked some of his surviving collaborators, as well as contemporary heavyweights, to analyse what exactly made him so brilliant. 
 
Sonny Rollins: \u201cHe would hear every note each person played, and we all took something different away from his wisdom.\u201d
 
Ambrose Akinmusire: \u201cThe thing I love about Miles is the same thing I love about Dizzy Gillespie or Joni Mitchell or Bj\u00f6rk, which is that they ask themselves daily if they\u2019re the same person they were yesterday.\u201d
 
Bill Evans: \u201cMiles had a way of writing a song or putting a band together that felt like he was playing to just one person.\u201d
 
Terence Blanchard: \u201cMiles didn\u2019t play the trumpet like a trumpet \u2026 he always played the moment, since it\u2019s what was happening at the time in the music that would dictate what he expressed through his horn.\u201d
 
Melissa Aldana: \u201cYou hear one note and you know it\u2019s Miles. You can\u2019t play like that and not be spiritual.\u201d
 
Did you know: 1959\u2019s Kind of Blue is the bestselling jazz album of all time.
 
How long will it take to read: Five minutes.
 
Sign up
 
If you would like to receive these Five Great Reads to your email inbox every weekend, sign up here. And check out out the full list of our local and international newsletters.

                "webTitle": "Crystal Palace leave Mateta out of squad for Forest trip as they weigh up Milan deal",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jan/30/crystal-palace-leave-mateta-out-of-squad-for-forest-trip-as-they-weigh-up-milan-deal",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/football/2026/jan/30/crystal-palace-leave-mateta-out-of-squad-for-forest-trip-as-they-weigh-up-milan-deal",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Crystal Palace leave Mateta out of squad for Forest trip as they weigh up Milan deal",
                    "standfirst": "
  • Serie A club have offered \u00a335m for France strker
  • Palace complete loan move for Villa\u2019s Guessand
",
                    "trailText": "Oliver Glasner has said Jean-Philippe Mateta will not be in Crystal Palace\u2019s squad at Nottingham Forest on Sunday because the striker is \u201cnot at his best\u201d owing to uncertainty over his future",
                    "byline": "Ed Aarons, Will Unwin and Jacob Steinberg",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Oliver Glasner has said Jean-Philippe Mateta will not be in Crystal Palace\u2019s squad to face Nottingham Forest on Sunday because the striker is \u201cnot at his best\u201d, owing to uncertainty over his future.
 
Milan are understood to be hopeful of completing a deal for Mateta, having entered the race to sign him, though they have yet to reach the \u00a340m asking price. The Italian club have offered a deal worth up to \u00a335m for the 28-year-old, who has made no secret of his desire to leave to further his ambitions of a World Cup call-up in the summer.
 
 
 Related: Men\u2019s transfer window January 2026: all deals from Europe\u2019s top five leagues 
 
  
Palace are believed to be considering the offer, having received a \u00a335m bid from Forest last week that they have yet to respond to. They would prefer not to sell to a Premier League rival. Mateta has indicated that his preference is to move to Serie A and has agreed terms with Milan on a three-and-a-half-year deal.
 
Glasner said Mateta would not travel with Palace to Forest, who are interested in the Manchester City goalkeeper Stefan Ortega, but could not say whether Mateta had played his last game for the club.
 
\u201cIt\u2019s nothing to do with the transfers, he is just not in the right place and doesn\u2019t feel in the right place to play,\u201d the manager said. \u201cIt makes no sense. I have to protect the team and that is why he will not travel with us to the game. There\u2019s so much noise and speculation \u2013 you need every single payer at his best, and JP isn\u2019t at his best right now with all the noise that happens. If somebody has some private issues that he can\u2019t really focus on football then it makes no sense to play him because then he can\u2019t help the team or perform on the top level.\u201d
 
On Friday night Palace confirmed the completion of a loan move for Aston Villa\u2019s Ivory Coast forward Evann Guessand, with the option to make it a permanent deal in the summer. But talks with Wolves over J\u00f8rgen Strand Larsen remain on ice, with Palace yet to formalise their verbal agreement to sign the Norway striker for \u00a345m, plus \u00a35m in add-ons.
 
His potential arrival is thought to depend on Mateta leaving but there are believed to be concerns among the Palace hierarchy about paying such a fee, which would smash the club\u2019s record of \u00a335m spent on Brennan Johnson this month.
 
Palace have had two bids for Sidiki Cherif rebuffed by Angers and the 19-year-old striker has informed the French club he would rather join Fenerbahce. Glasner, asked whether he expected any further arrivals before the deadline, with a central defender to replace Marc Gu\u00e9hi also on the agenda, said: \u201cThe club is working almost 24 hours a day. You can imagine it\u2019s not so easy at the end of January but I see the club working really hard to get players in. But to be clear, it can be that JP stays and is still a Palace player on 2 February or it could be that JP has left and we have a new striker at the club.\u201d
 
West Ham are considering a move for Southampton\u2019s Taylor Harwood-Bellis. Nuno Esp\u00edrito Santo wants a defender before the transfer window shuts and has identified Harwood-Bellis, who has one England cap, as an alternative to Chelsea\u2019s Axel Disasi.
 
West Ham have looked at a loan deal for Disasi but Chelsea are trying to find a buyer for the Frenchman, who has not played this season. Harwood-Bellis was relegated with Southampton last season. The Championship club sold Matheus Fernandes to West Ham last summer.
