                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "culture",
                "sectionName": "Culture",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T20:25:34Z",
                "webTitle": "Catherine O\u2019Hara managed to make difficult characters utterly delightful",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026/jan/30/catherine-ohara-comedy-actor-tribute",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/culture/2026/jan/30/catherine-ohara-comedy-actor-tribute",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Catherine O\u2019Hara managed to make difficult characters utterly delightful",
                    "standfirst": "
The death of the 71-year-old actor and comedian leaves behind a long line of unforgettably original comic creations, from Beetlejuice to Schitt\u2019s Creek
  • Catherine O\u2019Hara, actor known for Home Alone and Schitt\u2019s Creek, dies aged 71
",
                    "trailText": "The death of the 71-year-old actor and comedian leaves behind a long line of unforgettably original comic creations, from Beetlejuice to Schitt\u2019s Creek",
                    "byline": "Jesse Hassenger",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
One of the later and less beloved Christopher Guest comedies featuring his troupe of peerless, often SCTV-related improvisers is For Your Consideration, a medium-funny savaging of Hollywood\u2019s feverish awards-season prestige campaigning.
 
 
 Related: Catherine O\u2019Hara, actor known for Home Alone and Schitt\u2019s Creek, dies aged 71 
 
  
The film\u2019s unquestionable highlight is Catherine O\u2019Hara, playing an actor who gets a whisper of awards buzz for a schlocky, still-filming drama called Home for Purim, and slowly loses her mind with the knowledge that she could maybe, possibly be recognized by her peers. O\u2019Hara, known for her distinctively brassy yet malleable trill of her voice and her frequently red hair, peels back her performer\u2019s bravado to expose the frenzied need beneath it. She somehow plays the outsized beneath the regular-sized, as her Marilyn Hack goes from plugging-away workhorse to desperate striver. Unsurprisingly, O\u2019Hara briefly generated awards buzz of her own for playing this part; even less surprisingly, an Oscar nomination was not forthcoming. It couldn\u2019t be; otherwise, it might have marred O\u2019Hara\u2019s masterclass in how certain actors, especially those specializing in comedy, are destined to go under-recognized in their lifetimes.
 
The difference, of course, is that Marilyn Hack is depicted by O\u2019Hara, with tragicomic precision, as a mediocrity. O\u2019Hara, who passed away today at the age of 71, was not. She was exceptional, and within her reputation as a primarily comic actress, she possessed an extraordinary range. She was the best-case scenario of a performer trained in sketch comedy, able to slip into various characters and render them instantly vivid.
    
There are nonetheless signature roles and projects for O\u2019Hara, in television and film. There was SCTV, for which she shared a writing Emmy, and her late-career renaissance brought about by her work as Moira Rose on Schitt\u2019s Creek, for which she won a leading actress in a comedy Emmy that pretty much the entire world agreed was richly deserved. In between those pillars, she was an in-demand character actor and constant TV guest star. She\u2019s particularly indelible to generations of kids for playing the frazzled but ultimately dedicated mom in Home Alone and its sequel, serving as the true emotional heart of the original film. She stole scenes in eventual classics such as After Hours and The Paper, hits like Dick Tracy, bombs like Wyatt Earp, and countless comic and voiceover roles. But the two major film collaborations of her career were with her SCTV pal Guest and Tim Burton.
 
For Guest, O\u2019Hara did flawless teamwork in his mostly mockumentary movies Waiting for Guffman, Best in Show, A Mighty Wind, and For Your Consideration. Guffman and Consideration make for poetic but unsparing bookends; the former ends with O\u2019Hara and her on-screen husband Fred Willard leaving small town Missouri to pursue work as film extras in Los Angeles, while Consideration finds O\u2019Hara\u2019s Marilyn butting up against the limitations of her career, with O\u2019Hara doing a virtuosic bit of fake-plastic-surgery acting. Guest makes wonderful meta-text of O\u2019Hara\u2019s genuine dexterity as a performer; she plays a former folk singer in A Mighty Wind, whose breakup with her long-time partner (Eugene Levy) causes his mental breakdown. She\u2019s also paired with Levy for Best in Show, where she\u2019s also (believably) portrayed as more vivacious than her milquetoast beau. Despite the common ground her characters in the Guest films share, they aren\u2019t just comic archetypes, but distinctive people.
 
Her characters with Burton are equally nuanced, no small feat in such stylized environments. The pair didn\u2019t collaborate as frequently as Burton and Johnny Depp or Danny DeVito, but she was there for one of his biggest breakthroughs, playing artist Delia Deetz, mother to melancholy goth girl Lydia (Winona Ryder), in Beetlejuice, and new caretaker of a house haunted by its sweet-natured former occupants. O\u2019Hara makes Delia somewhat villainous in her garish sculptures and house-wrecking postmodern tastes, as well as her lack of understanding for her daughter; she is also, unquestionably, the heroine of her own story. O\u2019Hara satirizes art-world pretension without sacrificing her innate comic likability. You want to see what this confidently untalented woman gets up to, even as it seems natural for a pair of ghosts to take point on parenting her daughter.
    
She reteamed with Burton for his animation project The Nightmare Before Christmas, where she provided multiple voices, most notably for female lead Sally, a wistful, stitched-together ragdoll in love with Christmas-besotted Halloween planner Jack Skellington. Though Jack\u2019s singing and speaking parts were divided between two performers, O\u2019Hara did her own singing as Sally, and occasionally performed Sally\u2019s Song in concert later in her career. Given the more clipped, brassy tone she was best-known for in comedies, her work as Sally, a soulful wallflower and twisted vine of yearning, is pretty stunning; you\u2019d never guess it was her.
 
Both Burton movies were echoed later in her career: for Frankenweenie, Burton\u2019s stop-motion animated adaptation of his own short film, O\u2019Hara again provided multiple voices, equally adept at playing a caring mom and a character referred to only as \u201cweird girl\u201d. And for his 2024 legacy sequel Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, O\u2019Hara reprised Delia Deetz \u2013 and made her, if anything, more endearing than ever as a still-talent-deficient-but-now-quite-successful artist who loses her husband, subsequently dies in an absurd snake accident, and searches the underworld for her beloved. It\u2019s a perfect turn for O\u2019Hara because she seemed so indefatigable; what other comic actor could be so funny grappling with her own literal mortality and deciding she has her own post-life goal to attain? It didn\u2019t much matter that Burton no longer had the services of her former on-screen partner Jeffrey Jones; O\u2019Hara made Delia as funny as ever and weirdly touching, too.
 
It may be a tough performance to rewatch in the coming days, now that O\u2019Hara is actually gone, far too soon. Then again, maybe not; it\u2019s difficult to watch just about any Catherine O\u2019Hara performance, even the more serious ones, and not feel delighted by her presence. She made big, crazy, sometimes potentially abrasive characters such welcome company.
",

                "id": "sport/2026/jan/30/harry-brook-adds-to-england-woes-by-owning-up-to-false-statement-over-bouncer-incident",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "sport",
                "sectionName": "Sport",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T20:10:17Z",
                "webTitle": "Harry Brook adds to England woes by admitting he lied about nightclub incident",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jan/30/harry-brook-adds-to-england-woes-by-owning-up-to-false-statement-over-bouncer-incident",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/sport/2026/jan/30/harry-brook-adds-to-england-woes-by-owning-up-to-false-statement-over-bouncer-incident",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Harry Brook adds to England woes by admitting he lied about nightclub incident",
                    "standfirst": "
  • White-ball captain claims he was protecting teammates
  • Bethell and Tongue investigated over drinking session
",
                    "trailText": "Harry Brook said he regrets claiming he was out alone in a New Zealand nightclub after reports emerged that Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue are also under investigation",
                    "byline": "Taha Hashim in Colombo",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Harry Brook, the England white-ball captain, has admitted teammates were present on the night he clashed with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand last year.
 
Speaking at the start of England\u2019s tour of Sri Lanka, Brook said that he was on his own when he was punched by a bouncer on the eve of the third one-day international against New Zealand in Wellington.
 
In a statement released on Friday, Brook acknowledged the presence of others that night. It followed reporting from the Telegraph that the Cricket Regulator is investigating the 26-year-old, Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue over their conduct that evening. It was also reported that all three were fined by the England and Wales Cricket Board.
 
 
 Related: Breakdown in cricket relations with Bangladesh rings alarm bells for India\u2019s Olympic bid 
 
  
In the statement, sent to the media after England\u2019s victory against Sri Lanka in the opening Twenty20 international in Pallekele, Brook said: \u201cI accept responsibility for my actions in Wellington and acknowledge that others were present that evening.
 
\u201cI regret my previous comments and my intention was to protect my teammates from being drawn into a situation that arose as a result of my own decisions. I have apologised and will continue to reflect on the matter. This has been a challenging period in my career, but one from which I am learning.
 
\u201cI recognise that I have more to learn regarding the off-field responsibilities that come with leadership and captaincy. I remain committed to developing in this area and to improving both personally and professionally.\u201d
 
Brook was involved in the altercation during his first away series as England\u2019s limited-overs captain and reported the incident midway through the ODI defeat the next day in Wellington. News of the incident did not break until after the Ashes, with the ECB stating that it dealt with the matter \u201cthrough a formal and confidential disciplinary process\u201d.
 
The batter accepted last week that he was fortunate still to be England captain. Brook said: \u201cEven if I had been sacked, I\u2019d have held my hands up and said: \u2018Look, I\u2019ve made the mistake,\u2019 and I\u2019d have been perfectly fine with getting sacked from the job as captain, as long as I was still playing cricket.
 
\u201cI think I\u2019ve got a little bit of work to do to try to regain the trust of the players. I said sorry to them yesterday. I felt like I needed to say sorry for my actions. It\u2019s not acceptable as a player, but as a captain it\u2019s really not acceptable to do what I did in New Zealand. I\u2019ll be the first person to say that. I hold my hands up.\u201d
 
Brook\u2019s U-turn comes as he prepares to lead England at the upcoming T20 World Cup, their campaign beginning next week against Nepal in Mumbai. They began their tour of Sri Lanka with a 2-1 ODI series win in Colombo, Brook hitting a match-winning century in the decider on Tuesday. He finished unbeaten on 16 in the T20 series opener on Friday as England won by 11 runs on DLS.

Brook said: \u201cEven if I had been sacked, I\u2019d have held my hands up and said: \u2018Look, I\u2019ve made the mistake,\u2019 and I\u2019d have been perfectly fine with getting sacked from the job as captain, as long as I was still playing cricket. \u201cI think I\u2019ve got a little bit of work to do to try to regain the trust of the players. I said sorry to them yesterday. I felt like I needed to say sorry for my actions. It\u2019s not acceptable as a player, but as a captain it\u2019s really not acceptable to do what I did in New Zealand. I\u2019ll be the first person to say that. I hold my hands up.\u201d Brook\u2019s U-turn comes as he prepares to lead England at the upcoming T20 World Cup, their campaign beginning next week against Nepal in Mumbai. They began their tour of Sri Lanka with a 2-1 ODI series win in Colombo, Brook hitting a match-winning century in the decider on Tuesday. He finished unbeaten on 16 in the T20 series opener on Friday as England won by 11 runs on DLS.",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-protests-friday-strike",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T20:07:26Z",
                "webTitle": "Anti-ICE protests being held across US as organizers urge national strike",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-protests-friday-strike",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/ice-protests-friday-strike",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Anti-ICE protests being held across US as organizers urge national strike",
                    "standfirst": "
Activists call for Friday \u2018blackout\u2019 in protest against administration\u2019s violent immigration crackdown
",
                    "trailText": "Activists call for Friday \u2018blackout\u2019 in protest against administration\u2019s violent immigration crackdown",
                    "byline": "Fabiola Cineas, Sara Braun, and Rachel Leingang in Minneapolis",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Activists orchestrated a nationwide shutdown on Friday, advocating \u201cno work, no school, no shopping\u201d in a protest against the Trump administration\u2019s sweeping immigration crackdowns.
 
Organizers say Friday\u2019s \u201cblackout\u201d \u2013 or general strike, as some are calling it \u2013 is part of a growing nonviolent movement to combat ICE\u2019s aggressive enforcement tactics, which have come under renewed scrutiny following a series of fatal shootings involving federal agents.
 
Those deaths include Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Keith Porter in Los Angeles and Silverio Villegas Gonz\u00e1lez in Illinois. Friday\u2019s national protest leaders, many of them students at the University of Minnesota, are calling for ICE to leave the city after its nearly month-long operation. They say economic pressure through work stoppages and consumer boycotts is just one way to demand accountability and reform.
 
 
 Related: \u2018ICE Out\u2019 strike and protests: what to know about demonstrations across the US 
 
  
\u201cWe are calling for this strike because we believe what we have been doing in Minnesota should go national,\u201d said Kidus Yeshidagna, president of the Ethiopian Students Union at the University of Minnesota and one of the students organizing the strike.
 
\u201cWe need more people and lawmakers across the country to wake up.\u201d
 
Yeshidagna is part of a coalition of student groups that organized the Minnesota shutdown last Friday, in which thousands of people flooded the streets in sub-zero temperatures and hundreds of businesses shut their doors to demand justice for Good, who was shot by an ICE agent while trying to protect a neighbor. Last weekend, agents killed Pretti, another resident who was observing agents\u2019 activities.
 
The student groups \u2013 including the associations representing Black, Somali, Liberian, Ethiopian and Eritrean students and the graduate labor union \u2013 first gathered on 21 January to plan the calls for local and national strikes. \u201cWe came out in huge numbers despite the cold,\u201d he said, referencing last week\u2019s actions. \u201cWe are now doing it again.\u201d
 
From restaurants and clothing retailers to bookstores and coffee shops, businesses across dozens of cities stayed closed.
 
Protesters in Philadelphia, New York, Boise and Columbus gathered at city halls, courthouses, statehouses and legislative buildings, according to an action tracker. Students at high schools and colleges in Florida, California and other states staged walkouts. In Milwaukee and in Buffalo, Wyoming, people are gathering at parks and on street corners.
 
In Minnesota, where tens of thousands turned out for economic actions and a rally last Friday to protest ICE\u2019s surge in the city, some businesses closed for the day while others stayed open under different models, either donating revenue from the day or providing free coffee and a place for people in the community to rest safely.
 
Bench Pressed, a letter press and retail shop in Minneapolis, stayed open and donated all profits from Friday to people in the community who need help paying rent, which is due this weekend for February. Little Joy Coffee in Northfield, south of Minneapolis, sold a $5 \u201cFuck ICE\u201d honey and cinnamon latte with all proceeds going to mutual aid funds, and has supplies for people to screen-print items with anti-ICE messages and to reach out to their representatives.
 
Modern Times, a cafe in Minneapolis, has indefinitely switched to a free, donation-based model and was closed on Friday to join the general strike. The business said it would be referred to as \u201cPost Modern Times\u201d until the ICE surge is over, refusing to generate taxable income to fund the government that is brutalizing the city.
 
Elliott Payne, the Minneapolis city council president, posted a video after stopping by a local high school walkout, writing: \u201cOur kids are leading the way and it\u2019s our job to stand with them and make a better world possible for them.\u201d
 
Students in Knoxville, Tennessee, walked out of their classes this morning to join an \u201cICE Out\u201d protest, organized by Indivisible Knoxville. In a video originally posted by the Democratic representative Gloria Johnson, students and adults chant and hold signs with messages saying \u201cDefund ICE\u201d and \u201cSkipping Our Lessons to Teach You One\u201d.
 
Sophie Pedigo, a senior at South-Doyle high school, told the Knoxville News Sentinel: \u201cI fully believe in freedom of speech. And what\u2019s happening is so wrong, and I feel like education, the place where you get your education, should not be somewhere that you should be scared of being ripped from your family. That\u2019s just not right. And that\u2019s why I\u2019m here today, because I\u2019m fully against that.\u201d
 
Over 20 Tucson, Arizona, schools closed today, as several staffers participated in the strike.
 
Online, footage spread of high school students in places including San Antonio, Texas, and Salt Lake City, Utah, participating in the walkouts. Hundreds of New York City high school students marched toward a downtown park as a part of the day of action.
 
Volunteers with the People\u2019s Forum, a New York-based non-profit centered on political education and organizing, have been shoveling snow in preparation for the thousands of attendees anticipated to show up at today\u2019s protest in New York City\u2019s Foley Square.
 
\u201cThree weeks ago, no one considered, or even thought of the word \u2018general strike\u2019 as having any relevance in the US context, and now it\u2019s the one thing on everyone\u2019s minds,\u201d said Manolo De Los Santos, executive director of the People\u2019s Forum. \u201cNot just as a figment of imagination, but as a real tool for how people fight back against this fascist regime in Washington.\u201d
 
Santos , who is an immigrant, has been working in the immigrant rights space for \u201cas long as I can remember\u201d. He acknowledged that organizers in Minneapolis have provided a huge source of inspiration over the last few weeks.
 
\u201cWe felt an added sense of responsibility to not leave these brave fighters, these brave people, alone as they face ICE in Minnesota,\u201d he said. Santos also sees today\u2019s protest as preparation for if and when ICE agents activate large-scale operations in more cities across the country.
 
Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC), spoke to the Guardian on his way to attend the New York City ICE protest in Foley Square.
 
\u201cThis [administration] has never been about safety and security, and it\u2019s simply always been about cruelty,\u201d he said.
 
Over the past year, NYIC has provided legal services to those directly impacted by the Trump administration\u2019s immigration crackdowns. The organization represents more than 200 immigrant and refugee groups across the state. \u201cTheir goal is to divide us and scare us into paralysis,\u201d he said. \u201cAnd that\u2019s not going to happen.\u201d
 
Awawdeh hopes that today\u2019s actions will inspire elected officials to use their legislative power to stand up to the Trump administration. \u201cWe\u2019re calling on Congress to ensure that they do not invest one more penny in ICE or border patrol.\u201d
 
The neighbors and family members of Good and Pretti contacted the student organizations to share their support for the protests, Yeshidagna said. Hundreds of organizations, including student groups in other states, unions and major organizing groups, including 50501, have thrown their support behind the action.
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested on charges connected to Minnesota church protest 
 
  
\u201cWe want to obstruct the pillars that are upholding the Trump administration,\u201d Gloriann Sahay, a national coordinator with 50501, said. \u201cBy showing up, we are showing we are more in number and that we are not afraid of this terror being rained down upon us.\u201d
 
Yeshidagna, who grew up in St Paul, said he was in high school and 15 minutes away from where George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. He protested as a student and continues to lead protests now. Since Trump sent ICE officers to Minnesota, he and his peers in the student organizations have watched his friends and family members be targeted.
 
\u201cWe\u2019ve been seeing clear racial profiling in Minnesota,\u201d Yeshidagna said. \u201cThis isn\u2019t just an immigrant issue. This is a human rights issue that is also affecting US citizens.\u201d
 
Friday\u2019s protests coincided with the looming prospect of a government shutdown as Senate Democrats \u2013 and some Republicans \u2013 cobbled together a last-minute deal that funds virtually all government agencies except Homeland Security. Democrats are limiting DHS funding to give them leverage to push for a variety of reform measures, including banning agents from wearing masks and having ICE obtain warrants to make arrests. The House will have to pass the $1.2tn funding package Monday to avoid a prolonged shutdown.

            {
                "id": "football/2026/jan/30/arsenal-terminally-online-premier-league-title-pursuit-is-a-symbol-of-our-times",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "football",
                "sectionName": "Football",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T20:00:37Z",
                "webTitle": "Arsenal\u2019s terminally online Premier League title pursuit is a symbol of our times | Barney Ronay",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jan/30/arsenal-terminally-online-premier-league-title-pursuit-is-a-symbol-of-our-times",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/football/2026/jan/30/arsenal-terminally-online-premier-league-title-pursuit-is-a-symbol-of-our-times",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Arsenal\u2019s terminally online Premier League title pursuit is a symbol of our times",
                    "standfirst": "
A robotic team fuelled by data and scrutinised relentlessly in a climate of angst and rage feels like a digital-age metaphor
",
                    "trailText": "A robotic team running on data and scrutinised relentlessly in a climate of angst and rage feels like a metaphor for the digital age",
                    "byline": "Barney Ronay",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Like most people who have no talent for business ideas, I have a huge number of highly promising business ideas always on the go, ideas that are available for investment from any passing billionaire or Dragons\u2019 Den rainmaker type.
 
Not one of the A-listers, obviously. I\u2019m not insane. Not a Meaden or a Paphitis. But perhaps one of the minor ones, some strangely groomed South African retail magnate called Dork van Frotwangle who looks as if he keeps a bag of human fingers in his freezer and will mysteriously disappear mid-series and never be mentioned again.
 
One key project I\u2019m working up right now is the Temporary Burner Identity. Burner phone. Disposable online backstory. Pre-pixelated features. Can you imagine the joy of being able to go somewhere or do something and not be watched or identified? This is the future of luxury freedom (write that down, Dork).
 
 
 Related: The Arsenal fan psychodrama: Big Defeat Headloss hits hard after United setback | Chris Godfrey 
 
  
Being able to travel to, say, Spain, and nobody knows you\u2019re there. To buy things, have experiences, meet people, and it\u2019s not part of an indelible digital footprint that will echo and rebound and stalk your existence, popping up decades later in those on-screen boxes that want to sell you elite incontinence pants in massive letters while you\u2019re on the train.
 
Or more broadly, just being able to escape. To breathe and get lost in the world, to exist in some anonymous space free from the white noise, the ceaseless robot voices of daily existence. This is human life now ever since The Great Networking of the early 2010s. We are all condemned to live like General Zod in Superman, hurtling through space inside a giant iPad, faces pressed up against the glass in a silent scream.
 
And OK, you won\u2019t be hidden exactly. Just mutable, like you\u2019re striding past the face recognition cameras wearing an endlessly interchangeable Hannibal Lecter-style human face. Like you\u2019ve scissored off a selection of human faces and carry them around in a briefcase and this is actually fine.
 
And OK, OK, yes, it would obviously be used for crime, because every human invention enables crime, its first principle always: what\u2019s the nonce angle here? So perhaps we could build in failsafes. We could monitor you. We could store your movements and data. Just in case. Actually, maybe don\u2019t wear the Temporary Burner Identity at all. That\u2019s probably easier. Buy it. Don\u2019t use it. But we will throw in a mail order powder that gives you a six-pack and makes you magnetically charismatic (disclaimer: powder will not create six-pack or magnetic charisma).
 
This is the real problem. The networked existence. Being seen all the time. It has become inescapable. Nobody planned this properly or thought about what it might do to us. Nobody makes enough allowances for its effects, an advanced version of the Albert Camus idea that everyday life is so absurd that just existing is an act of revolutionary courage, that behind the eyes of every human is a dizzying matrix of pain and confusion. And yes, the algorithm is telling me you\u2019re also thinking about Victor Gy\u00f6keres here.
    
The big question in the current Premier League season is unexpectedly textural. Not so much what tactical shifts are in play, or who is the best goalscorer. But why does it feel like this? Why does an otherwise straightforward set of results feel like an endless doom-scroll of trapped energy and lurking meltdown? The keynote is the basic strangeness of Arsenal, as we enter another staging point in a title race that is simultaneously gripping and tedious, and oddly tender in its contortions.
 
Arsenal will probably win the league from here. They have the points, the squad and the fallible opponents. The only real certainty is that it will be agonisingly intense, the footballing equivalent of a silent scream. Not to mention hugely addictive. I for one am already pining for the game against Leeds on Saturday afternoon, which will be 0-0 at 60 minutes and from there dissolve into repeated clips of Mikel Arteta furiously whirling his arms on the touchline, a Lego-haired avatar of pain, dressed as ever in slickly generic black outdoor clothing, like an elite sniper on a fishing trip.
 
There are some obvious answers as to why it feels like this. The most obvious is that what we are witnessing is a bottling. Simple stuff. A cowardice is taking place. Arsenal have to win the league, or they are basically betas, frauds, cucks, a papier-mache imitation of actual human men.
  
 
 
Watching them try to create or play with fluency is like having your eyes slowly gouged with a blunt teaspoon
 
 
  
The thing is, bottling doesn\u2019t really exist. It\u2019s just a word. It\u2019s outcome-based logic, Deeney\u2019s paradox, the cojones obsession, which confuses being good at football with being morally good and brave and right. Bottling is the absence of analysis.
 
The burden of history has been mentioned, the long wait for a title. But that also feels too vague. These are hugely driven individuals from places such as S\u00e3o Paulo and the Basque Country. Kai Havertz may look like a minor royal cousin with a top-10 world croquet ranking but he has to be hard as nails just to operate in this rarefied air. Gabriel Magalh\u00e3es is not feeling Perry Groves\u2019s breath on his back.
 
But something is clearly being done to them. Arsenal are top, but their leading scorer has five goals. Watching them try to create or play with fluency is like having your eyes slowly gouged with a blunt teaspoon. This is either a phase about to break, or a new way of playing, or a metric of future failure, expected non-goals in the final third of the season.
 
The most interesting explanation is a parable of robotisation. Arsenal\u2019s flaw lies in an overmechanisation of tactics. What we have here is the first post-human football team. This may be halfway to the truth. Arsenal are undeniably laden with data, from use of the StatDNA platform, to talk of an internal AI information bank, millions of data points used to predict not just injury and fatigue but game simulations, where to stand, where to pass, total set piece, mechanised attack patterns. Arsenal do express certain aspects of the modern world. There\u2019s the feeling in his public pronouncements that Arteta is selling some kind of male wellness brand or restating his success vectors for the stakeholders. He even looks in these moments like an AI simulation of Handsome Earnest Football Man.
    
So is this it? Are we looking at a fatal flaw? Is this the hubris of robotisation? It sounds a little bogus. Fear of the future is as old as the future itself. People said this about television in the 1950s. They said steam train travel was impossible because humans would suffocate at such speeds. Artificial intelligence does sound frightening. But it\u2019s not intelligent. It\u2019s not even artificial. Its just a scraping of human thought-goo expressed in lines of code.
 
It is part of the most obvious point of difference, however. Which is: scrutiny. The online life. Being seen, surveilled, constantly interfaced. People often wonder why things are happening the way they are. Answer: it\u2019s always the internet. Populism, rage, polarised stupidity wars. Of course the world has gone off its axis. This is the most profound shift in human consciousness ever enacted, the creation of a global hive-mind, the ability to hear the thoughts, shouts and brain-blurts of every single citizen of Namibia from your bedroom in Brentwood.
 
We are all terminally online now and this Arsenal team is the most extreme expression yet of this experience in sporting form. It comes in part from that internal scrutiny. Arteta is a massive data guy. Everyone at every level is tracked, statted, diced, sliced. How is this going to make you feel, or act, or perform complex movements? Mainly it is external. All fandom is online now, Arsenal\u2019s particularly so, and in a way that feels unusually present. People have been talking about Arsenal bottling the league since September because content must always happen. There is an excess of feeling, micro-reasoning, total analysis, a complete absence of quiet space or places to breathe.
 
This isn\u2019t new but it is more intense from year to year. It is also the most overlooked factor in elite modern sport, the way being observed constantly will of course alter the experience. You can see this creeping into problems on the pitch. Arsenal need to create more, to be more spontaneous, to dance like no one\u2019s watching. Go on. Do it while everyone is watching, while that white noise seeps into every pocket of your existence.
 
How to fix this? Arteta conducted a tension-busting \u201cface-meeting\u201d with his players this week but even this has already become public product, put through the content wringer, mined for meaning. It brings us back to the burner identity. To succeed in the middle of all that heat and light has always been a matter of finding a still space, a bubble of silence. Never more so than now.
 
If Arsenal do fall away this season it will in part be down to this new and entirely pervasive sense of static, a first terminally-online collapse from perhaps the most terminally-online team yet devised.

            {
                "id": "business/2026/jan/30/donald-trump-nominates-kevin-warsh-us-federal-reserve-chair",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "business",
                "sectionName": "Business",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T19:52:20Z",
                "webTitle": "Trump nominates Federal Reserve critic Kevin Warsh as its next chair",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jan/30/donald-trump-nominates-kevin-warsh-us-federal-reserve-chair",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/business/2026/jan/30/donald-trump-nominates-kevin-warsh-us-federal-reserve-chair",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Trump nominates Federal Reserve critic Kevin Warsh as its next chair",
                    "standfirst": "
Pick of former Fed governor to replace Jerome Powell comes as White House seeks to tighten grip on central bank
",
                    "trailText": "Pick of former Fed governor to replace Jerome Powell comes as White House seeks to tighten grip on central bank",
                    "byline": "Lauren Aratani in New York and Tom Knowles",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Donald Trump has announced Kevin Warsh as his nomination for the next chair of the Federal Reserve, selecting a candidate who has been an outspoken critic of the US central bank.
 
The move ends months of speculation about who the president would pick to replace Jerome Powell, as he waged an extraordinary campaign to influence policymaking at the Fed by repeatedly calling for interest rate cuts. Powell\u2019s second term as chair is due to end in May.
 
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said: \u201cI have known Kevin for a long period of time, and have no doubt that he will go down as one of the GREAT Fed Chairmen, maybe the best. On top of everything else, he is \u2018central casting\u2019, and he will never let you down.\u201d
 
 
 Related: What is behind the extraordinary rise in investment into silver and gold? 
 
  
Warsh, 55, a former Federal Reserve governor who has deep ties to Wall Street, had previously interviewed for the job of chair in 2017 when the role went to Powell. Trump\u2019s pick will have to be confirmed by the Senate.
 
Being the chair of the Fed is one of the most powerful roles in the US government, with enormous influence over the world\u2019s largest economy.
 
Stephen Brown, a US economist at Capital Economics, said markets were likely to consider Warsh \u201ca relatively safe choice\u201d and his nomination would alleviate concerns that the president was going to pick \u201ca full-blown Trump stooge\u201d to be the next Fed chair.
 
Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister and former governor of the Bank of England, said in a social media post that Warsh was \u201ca fantastic choice to lead the world\u2019s most important central bank at this crucial time\u201d.
 
The dollar strengthened early on Friday after it was reported that Warsh was expected to be Trump\u2019s choice, and was up 0.5% against a basket of currencies after the nomination. Gold fell by 9.1% to $4,903.60 an ounce. Silver dropped 26.7% to $85.12 an ounce. Wall Street traded slightly lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 down 0.5% in New York.
 
Warsh will still need at least 51 votes in the US Senate to be confirmed. Though Republicans have a 53-47 majority in the chamber, multiple Republican senators spoke in defense of Powell after it emerged that the Fed chair is under federal criminal investigation. One senator, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, said he would block any of Trump\u2019s Fed nominees until the investigation is called off.
 
On Friday, Tillis said that Warsh was \u201ca qualified nominee with a deep understanding of monetary policy\u201d but said that he would still vote against him until Powell\u2019s investigation is resolved.
 
Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat and ranking member of the Senate\u2019s banking committee, said in a statement: \u201cNo Republican purporting to care about Fed independence should agree to move forward with this nomination.\u201d
 
Warsh has warned about inflation risks in the US in the past, but has also echoed Trump\u2019s critique of the Fed for being too slow to cut interest rates. High interest rates can alleviate inflation at the risk of upping unemployment. Rates are currently at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, which most economists at the Fed currently see as neutral to prices and unemployment.
 
Since resigning from the central bank in 2011 over its post-financial crisis stimulus package, Warsh has criticised it publicly on multiple occasions. In April last year, he issued a stinging attack, saying the institution\u2019s central bankers should not be treated as \u201cpampered princes\u201d and it too regularly \u201copines on matters outside its remit\u201d which has led to \u201csystemic errors\u201d in its main role of trying to keep prices stable. 
    
Warsh, a New Yorker who was special assistant for economic policy from 2002 to 2006, served as Fed governor between 2006 and 2011, a period that included the response to the global financial crisis, and was its representative to the G20 group of countries.
 
He is now a lecturer at the Stanford Graduate School of Business and has roles at the courier UPS, the Korean e-commerce company Coupang and the Duquesne Family Office, the investment firm of the billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller.
 
Warsh is married to Jane Lauder, the granddaughter of the cosmetics magnate Est\u00e9e Lauder and daughter of Ronald Lauder, the billionaire who has interests in Greenland and encouraged Trump to attempt to acquire the territory.
 
Other candidates on the shortlist to be Federal Reserve chair had been Kevin Hassett, the national economic council director; Christopher Waller, a Fed governor; and Rick Rieder, an executive at BlackRock.
 
Warsh has been a longtime critic of the ultra-loose monetary policy pursued by the Fed since the financial crisis, including the central bank\u2019s expanded balance sheet. He had previously been seen as a monetary policy hawk, but appears to have aligned himself with the White House\u2019s push for lower borrowing costs.
 
In December, Trump said of Warsh: \u201cHe thinks you have to lower interest rates.\u201d
 
Renaissance Macro Research said in a note that Warsh could have been siding himself with the president to appease him. \u201cWarsh has been a monetary policy hawk his entire career and most importantly, during a time when the labor markets fell out of bed,\u201d it said. \u201cHis dovishness today stems from convenience. The president risks getting duped.\u201d
 
Brown said Warsh\u2019s \u201clong-running hawkish views should help to counteract concerns that he might morph into a full-blown Trump stooge.
 
\u201cThat said, his firm conviction that both AI and the Trump administration\u2019s regulatory push will help to hold down inflation, as well as his longstanding view that the Fed should operate with a much smaller balance sheet, present the risk of some upward pressure on long-term bond yields.\u201d
 
Trump himself had suggested that he was considering whether to install Hassett, a White House official and one of his top economic advisers, as Fed chair.
 
On Friday, Trump wrote on social media: \u201cTheir [sic] was great speculation that highly respected Kevin Hassett was going to be named Chairman of the Fed, and a great Chairman he would have been but, quite honestly, he is doing such an outstanding job working with me and my team at the White House, that I just didn\u2019t want to let him go.\u201d
",

            {
                "id": "us-news/2026/jan/30/alex-pretti-doj-civil-rights-investigation",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "us-news",
                "sectionName": "US news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T19:40:01Z",
                "webTitle": "US DoJ opens federal civil rights investigation into killing of Alex Pretti",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/alex-pretti-doj-civil-rights-investigation",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/us-news/2026/jan/30/alex-pretti-doj-civil-rights-investigation",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "US DoJ opens federal civil rights investigation into killing of Alex Pretti",
                    "standfirst": "
Deputy attorney general makes announcement over fatal shooting in Minneapolis as fierce protests there continue
",
                    "trailText": "Deputy attorney general makes announcement over fatal shooting in Minneapolis as fierce protests there continue",
                    "byline": "Shrai Popat in Minneapolis, Lucy Campbell and Sara Braun in New York",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
The US deputy attorney general announced on Friday that the justice department has opened a federal civil rights investigation into the fatal shooting of the Minneapolis nurse Alex Pretti last Saturday by immigration officers, as fierce protests continued on the streets there.
 \n
\u201cWe\u2019re looking at everything that would shed light on that day,\u201d Todd Blanche, deputy to the attorney general, Pam Bondi, said at a press conference on Friday morning in Washington DC.
 \n
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also said on Friday that the FBI would lead the investigation into the latest killing.
 \n
 \n 
 Related: The federal agents deployed in Trump\u2019s immigration crackdown \u2013 visualized 
 \n
 \n
Pretti, a 37-year-old nurse at the military veterans hospital in Minneapolis and an activist, died while protesting against aggressive immigration raids and protester-control tactics by officers with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), border patrol and other federal agencies.
 \n
He was the third person shot during the surge of immigration enforcement personnel sent to the Twin Cities area of Minneapolis and Saint Paul in Minnesota by the Trump administration as part of its mass deportation agenda, and the second to die after Renee Good was shot dead on 7 January.
 \n
The justice department\u2019s announcement on Friday was a significant development after the Trump administration had earlier indicated a much narrower examination by the DHS.
 \n
Blanche said the new plan was like \u201cany investigation that the Department of Justice and the FBI does every day. It means we\u2019re looking at video, talking to witnesses, trying to understand what happened.\u201d The justice department has not opened such an investigation into Good\u2019s death.
 \n
Protesters have gathered daily across parts of the Twin Cities for weeks. Friday was no exception.
 \n
\u201cThe community is really rallied, and I think it\u2019s important just to stand with them and have more people on the streets,\u201d said Ann Pelsue, 58, who made the three-hour journey from Iron River, Wisconsin, to join demonstrators outside a federal building in a Minneapolis suburb where many people targeted in the immigration raids, as well as protesters and observers who monitor federal enforcement actions, are taken and held.
 \n
Meanwhile, the homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, first disclosed the shift in which agency was leading the investigation into Pretti\u2019s death during a Fox News interview on Thursday evening.
 \n
Noem also conceded that she may have gotten some information wrong in her initial response to Pretti\u2019s shooting, when she held a press conference last Saturday and repeated allegations made by other officials that Pretti had been attacking officers \u2013 a narrative quickly and clearly contradicted by bystander video of him being shot as well as sworn witness testimony.
 \n
\u201cWe were being relayed information from on the ground from CBP agents and officers that were there,\u201d Noem said in Thursday\u2019s TV interview. The Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency includes border patrol, with both alongside ICE under the umbrella of the DHS.
 \n
Noem described to Fox a \u201cvery chaotic\u201d situation, when the host asked whether her responses last Saturday had been \u201cpremature\u201d.
 \n
But the Trump administration had rushed in to blame Pretti. Greg Bovino, then commander of border patrol\u2019s operation who was moved out of Minneapolis days later, said the nurse wanted to \u201cmassacre\u201d federal officers, and numerous officials, including Noem, called Pretti a \u201cdomestic terrorist\u201d. The administration had also quickly mischaracterized the core of what happened when Good was shot, infuriating local leaders and many communities.
 \n
Noem has been facing calls to resign amid widespread and mounting outrage, even among some Republicans. The North Carolina Republican senator Thom Tillis told reporters that Noem\u2019s conduct \u201cshould be disqualifying\u201d.
 \n
Videos of Pretti\u2019s shooting showed that he had his mobile phone in his hand as officers tackled him to the ground after he tried to shield a fellow protester and he did not appear to touch or reach for the gun he had a permit to carry.
 \n
Two other videos emerged this week of an earlier altercation between Pretti and federal immigration officers 11 days before his death.
 \n
The videos from 13 January show Pretti yelling at federal vehicles and at one point appearing to spit before kicking out the taillight of one vehicle. A struggle ensues between Pretti and several officers, during which he is forced to the ground.
 \n \n
Steve Schleicher, a Minneapolis-based attorney representing Pretti\u2019s parents, said the earlier altercation in no way justified officers fatally shooting Pretti more than a week later.
 \n
In a stark post on his Truth Social platform early on Friday morning, Donald Trump suggested that the videos of the earlier incident undercut the narrative that Pretti was a peaceful protester when he was shot.
 \n
\u201cAgitator and, perhaps, insurrectionist, Alex Pretti\u2019s stock has gone way down with the just released video of him screaming and spitting in the face of a very calm and under control ICE officer, and then crazily kicking in a new and very expensive government vehicle, so hard and violent, in fact, that the taillight broke off in pieces,\u201d the US president\u2019s post said. It added: \u201cIt was quite a display of abuse and anger, for all to see, crazed and out of control.\u201d
 \n
Later on Friday, protesters gathered outside the Bishop Henry Whipple building just south of Minneapolis, the federal building and holding center that has become the site of many demonstrations.
 \n
Dozens of people held up placards in Arctic temperatures, reading \u201cICE out now\u201d and \u201cMinnesota strong\u201d while a chorus of whistles blared and cries of \u201cshame\u201d erupted when protesters spotted federal law enforcement enter the facility in their cars on Friday. Supporters set up stands, doling out hand warmers and energy bars to those braving the frigid weather to protest.
 \n
 \n 
 Related: Minneapolis ICE watchers face violence, teargas and arrests. They keep showing up 
 \n
 \n
Yaakov Segal, 23, said he had been demonstrating outside the building \u201cthree or four times a week\u201d since Good\u2019s killing. \u201cI don\u2019t see any sign of slowing down. Minnesota has been showing up ever since they started taking their neighbors,\u201d he said.
 \n
Trump\u2019s \u201cborder czar\u201d, Tom Homan, was sent, over Noem\u2019s head, to Minneapolis to replace Bovino earlier this week.
 \n
\u201cRegardless of who is at the top right now, this is about the fact that you\u2019re not following the rule of law,\u201d said Caleb Dunnewind, 23, another protester, who lives just four blocks away from where Pretti was fatally shot, of federal officials\u2019 conduct.
 \n
Tim Walz, Minnesota governor, and Jacob Frey, mayor of Minneapolis, both Democrats, have voiced public fury over the federal shootings and \u201cinvasion\u201d by federal officials.
 \n
The Associated Press contributed reporting.

                    "bodyText": "The US deputy attorney general announced on Friday that the justice department has opened a federal civil rights investigation into the fatal shooting of the Minneapolis nurse Alex Pretti last Saturday by immigration officers, as fierce protests continued on the streets there. \u201cWe\u2019re looking at everything that would shed light on that day,\u201d Todd Blanche, deputy to the attorney general, Pam Bondi, said at a press conference on Friday morning in Washington DC. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also said on Friday that the FBI would lead the investigation into the latest killing. Pretti, a 37-year-old nurse at the military veterans hospital in Minneapolis and an activist, died while protesting against aggressive immigration raids and protester-control tactics by officers with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), border patrol and other federal agencies. He was the third person shot during the surge of immigration enforcement personnel sent to the Twin Cities area of Minneapolis and Saint Paul in Minnesota by the Trump administration as part of its mass deportation agenda, and the second to die after Renee Good was shot dead on 7 January. The justice department\u2019s announcement on Friday was a significant development after the Trump administration had earlier indicated a much narrower examination by the DHS. Blanche said the new plan was like \u201cany investigation that the Department of Justice and the FBI does every day. It means we\u2019re looking at video, talking to witnesses, trying to understand what happened.\u201d The justice department has not opened such an investigation into Good\u2019s death. Protesters have gathered daily across parts of the Twin Cities for weeks. Friday was no exception. \u201cThe community is really rallied, and I think it\u2019s important just to stand with them and have more people on the streets,\u201d said Ann Pelsue, 58, who made the three-hour journey from Iron River, Wisconsin, to join demonstrators outside a federal building in a Minneapolis suburb where many people targeted in the immigration raids, as well as protesters and observers who monitor federal enforcement actions, are taken and held.                 "id": "law/2026/jan/30/press-freedom-journalist-arrests-ice-don-lemon",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "law",
                "sectionName": "Law",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T19:33:17Z",
                "webTitle": "Press freedom groups denounce arrests of two journalists including Don Lemon after Minnesota anti-ICE protest",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/jan/30/press-freedom-journalist-arrests-ice-don-lemon",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/law/2026/jan/30/press-freedom-journalist-arrests-ice-don-lemon",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Press freedom groups denounce arrests of two journalists including Don Lemon after Minnesota anti-ICE protest",
                    "standfirst": "
Groups say arrests of ex-CNN anchor and Georgia Fort are \u2018extremely alarming\u2019 and an \u2018attack on the first amendment\u2019
",
                    "trailText": "Groups say arrests of ex-CNN anchor and Georgia Fort are \u2018extremely alarming\u2019 and an \u2018attack on the first amendment\u2019",
                    "byline": "Richard Luscombe",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Press freedom groups are warning that the arrests of two independent journalists, including the veteran former CNN anchor Don Lemon, signal a chilling new crackdown on US media by the Trump administration.
 
Lemon was taken into custody on Thursday night by federal agents in Los Angeles, despite a magistrate judge declining to sign off on charges against him a week ago in connection with a protest at a Minnesota church against violent government immigration enforcement actions.
 
Georgia Fort, another reporter who covered the 18 January protest at the Cities church in Saint Paul, posted a live stream of her arrest early on Friday on Facebook.
 
\u201cThe justice department\u2019s arrest of journalists reporting on anti-ICE protests is extremely alarming, especially given that multiple judges refused to approve arrest warrants just last week,\u201d Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said.
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested on charges connected to Minnesota church protest 
 
  
\u201cReporting on protests isn\u2019t a crime \u2013 it\u2019s protected by the first amendment. We are especially concerned about these arrests because they take place against the background of a broader effort by the Trump administration to tighten the vise around press freedom.\u201d
 
Scott Griffen, executive director of the International Press Institute (IPI), echoed a similar fear in a statement that called for the release of Lemon and Fort.
 
\u201cThe arrests of two independent journalists doing their jobs is a shocking and disturbing escalation of the Trump administration\u2019s campaign against the free press in America. This is an unequivocal attack on the first amendment and the American people\u2019s right to know,\u201d he said.
 
\u201cThe outcome of this case will have direct consequences for the future of free media and free information in America. IPI condemns the Trump administration\u2019s attempts to criminalize journalism and calls for the immediate release of both journalists with all charges dropped.\u201d
 
A statement from the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ) said: \u201cThe selective targeting of journalists \u2013 especially, Black and LGBTQIA journalists \u2013 raises urgent concerns about unequal enforcement and retaliatory policing of the press \u2026 and mirrors a broader pattern in which government actors appear quick to criminalize those documenting injustice.\u201d
 
The NABJ\u2019s president, Errin Haines, added: \u201cAs journalists, our first obligation is to bear witness and to inform. When those obligations are met with detention or prosecution instead of protection, we must ask: \u2018What message are we sending about who gets to report and who gets silenced?\u2019\u201d
 
The Reporters\u2019 Committee for Freedom of the Press said it was an \u201cunprecedented\u201d use of federal law by the justice department that amounted to overreach.
 
\u201cHistorically, the limited number of cases that have been brought against a journalist documenting a protest on private property have been handled as trespass cases at the state level. Those charges are almost always dropped, or if the cases go to trial, the journalists typically prevail,\u201d Gabe Rottman, the group\u2019s vice-president of policy, said.
 
Jenna Ruddock, advocacy director of Free Press Action, said the arrests were part of Trump\u2019s \u201call-out assault on Minnesota communities\u201d, and an attempt to silence coverage of it.
 
\u201cWhile journalists and civilians continue to heroically document conditions on the ground in the face of escalating violence from federal agents, the Trump administration is using every weapon at its disposal to shut down efforts to document, report and dissent,\u201d she said.
 
\u201cThese latest arrests are just the latest in a long line of first amendment violations by the administration. Too often, corporate media have readily capitulated to the administration\u2019s demands. Independent journalists, on the other hand, are continuing to lead by example with their critical reporting under increasingly unsafe conditions \u2013 indeed, with targets on their backs.\u201d
 
Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation program director at PEN America, said: \u201cThe fact that a federal magistrate judge and a federal appeals court already rejected the evidence against Lemon makes his arrest all the more troubling, putting on full display the continued misuse of government power to deflect accountability and intimidate a free press.\u201d
 
Democratic politicians joined the condemnation of the journalists\u2019 arrests. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, told the chamber: \u201cThe arrest is a dark message to journalists everywhere: if you dare criticize this administration, watch your back. That is not democracy. That is a police state and that is pure authoritarian bile. Democracy will suffer if the government chokes our civil liberties.\u201d
 
Hakeem Jeffries, leader of House Democrats, said there was \u201czero basis\u201d for Lemon\u2019s arrest, which he called \u201ca disgraceful affront to the first amendment and a corrupt weaponization of the criminal justice system\u201d.
 
In a statement, Jeffries said: \u201cDon [Lemon] is the most recent target of the ongoing attacks by Donald Trump and his sycophants on those who challenge the administration and refuse to bend the knee to their extremism.
 
\u201cThe illegitimate extremists in the Trump administration will all be held accountable for their crimes against the constitution. America will not be intimidated.\u201d

That is not democracy. That is a police state and that is pure authoritarian bile. Democracy will suffer if the government chokes our civil liberties.\u201d Hakeem Jeffries, leader of House Democrats, said there was \u201czero basis\u201d for Lemon\u2019s arrest, which he called \u201ca disgraceful affront to the first amendment and a corrupt weaponization of the criminal justice system\u201d. In a statement, Jeffries said: \u201cDon [Lemon] is the most recent target of the ongoing attacks by Donald Trump and his sycophants on those who challenge the administration and refuse to bend the knee to their extremism. \u201cThe illegitimate extremists in the Trump administration will all be held accountable for their crimes against the constitution. America will not be intimidated.\u201d",

                "id": "sport/2026/jan/30/chess-nodirbek-abdusattorov-narrowly-ahead-as-wijk-aan-zee-reaches-final-weekend",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "sport",
                "sectionName": "Sport",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T19:32:26Z",
                "webTitle": "Chess: Uzbek pair share narrow half-point lead as Wijk aan Zee reaches final weekend",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jan/30/chess-nodirbek-abdusattorov-narrowly-ahead-as-wijk-aan-zee-reaches-final-weekend",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/sport/2026/jan/30/chess-nodirbek-abdusattorov-narrowly-ahead-as-wijk-aan-zee-reaches-final-weekend",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Chess: Uzbek pair share narrow half-point lead as Wijk aan Zee reaches final weekend",
                    "standfirst": "
Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Javokhir Sindarov lead the 14-man field, but their closest rivals are all only half a point behind with two rounds to go
",
                    "trailText": "Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Javokhir Sindarov lead the 14-man field, but their closest rivals are all only half a point behind with two rounds to go",
                    "byline": "Leonard Barden",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Uzbekistan\u2019s Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Javokhir Sindarov are just half a point ahead of their closest three rivals as the \u201cchess Wimbledon\u201d at Tata Steel Wijk aan Zee heads into its final two rounds this weekend. Abdusattorov was the clear leader, but he has drawn three and lost one of his last four games.
 
Leading scores after 11 of the 13 rounds are Abdusattorov and Sindarov 7, Matthias Bl\u00fcbaum (Germany), Jorden van Foreest (Netherlands) and Hans Niemann (US) 6.5, Vincent Keymer (Germany) 6, Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus (Turkey), Gukesh Dommaraju (India), Vladimir Fedoseev (Slovenia) and Anish Giri (Netherlands) 5.5.
    
Erdogmus, 14, has already set multiple age records. He is the best 12-, 13- and 14-year-old in chess history. He is the youngest ever 2600-rated player, and is now closing in on the 2700 mark, where he would beat the previous records set by China\u2019s Wei Yi at 15 years nine months and Magnus Carlsen at 16 years four months.
 
He has a wealthy sponsor, and is coached by the elite GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. His playing style is a well-organised mix of strategy and tactics, and he has already played the \u201cTurkish Immortal\u201d game at the 2025 Fide Grand Swiss. Erdogmus looks increasingly like a player who will dominate world chess in the 2030s.
 
On Wednesday, for a brief moment, it could have been even better. In his game with Gukesh, Erdogmus missed a beautiful hidden win at move 28 which would have taken him into a share of the tournament lead and also made him the youngest ever to defeat a reigning world champion.
 
Erdogmus has his own characteristic stance when seated at the board, which the commentator Simon Williams called his \u201cdeath sway\u201d. Long ago in the mid-20th century, the English master and author Gerald Abrahams had a similar action, but he swayed from side to side in a Talmudic shuckling movement that was irreverently nicknamed the \u201crunaway rocking horse\u201d.
 
As for Gukesh, he has become a player of ups and downs. The most crushing down was against Abdusattorov.
    
Gukesh blundered fatally by 36\u2026Rg5?? allowing 37 Qxf6+ and 38 Qxg5+, winning a rook with check. The decisive moment was caught on video, as the grief-stricken Indian buried his head in his hands and could not bear to look at the board.
 
Two days on, after also losing his next game then winning in fine style in round eight, Gukesh took a more philosophical view. He said: \u201cI cannot explain what happened. These kinds of blunders are easier to handle than something you can explain. So this just happens. Shit happens!\u201d
 
The worst ever blunder by a reigning world champion was probably when Vladimir Kramnik allowed checkmate in one by the computer Deep Fritz in their 2006 match, played during the few years when humans and chess engines were of approximately equal strength.
 
After 11 of the 13 rounds in the Challengers, whose winner qualifies for the 2027 Masters, four players have broken clear of the field: Andy Woodward (US) leads with 8.5, followed by Aylin Suleymanli (Azerbaijan) and Vasyl Ivanchuk (Ukraine) 8, and Marc\u2019Andria Maurizzi (France) 7.5. The youngest competitor, Argentina\u2019s Faustino Oro, aged 12, has 6.
 
Wijk aan Zee continues daily at 1pm GMT. The 13th and final round, including any required playoff for first prize, will be on Sunday. Games can be followed live and free on lichess, chess.com, and the official site, where the commentators are England\u2019s GM Simon Williams and IM Jovanka Houska.
 
4009: 1 Rxg7+! Kxg7 2 Nh5+ Kh6 3 Qxf6+ Kxh5 4 g4+! Kxg4 5 Rd4+ Kh5 6 Rh4 mate.
",

            {
                "id": "cities/2026/jan/30/a-place-of-two-halves-how-margates-art-led-renewal-has-left-it-splintered",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "cities",
                "sectionName": "Cities",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T19:14:28Z",
                "webTitle": "\u2018A place of two halves\u2019: how Margate\u2019s art-led renewal has left town \u2018splintered\u2019",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2026/jan/30/a-place-of-two-halves-how-margates-art-led-renewal-has-left-it-splintered",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/cities/2026/jan/30/a-place-of-two-halves-how-margates-art-led-renewal-has-left-it-splintered",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "\u2018A place of two halves\u2019: how Margate\u2019s art-led renewal has left town \u2018splintered\u2019",
                    "standfirst": "
Madonna labelled it \u2018heaven\u2019 on a recent visit, but the cost of living in the seaside resort is hitting many residents hard 
",
                    "trailText": "Madonna labelled it \u2018heaven\u2019 on a recent visit, but the cost of living in the seaside resort is hitting many residents hard",
                    "byline": "Rachel Hall",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Not many chefs working in small, family-run restaurants expect global megastars to turn up for dinner and to design them a menu from scratch.
 
But that\u2019s what happened to Simona Di Dio last weekend, when she cooked dishes inspired by her Italian grandmother\u2019s recipes for Madonna, who sat on the single wooden dining table in Di Dio\u2019s cosy, candlelit Italian restaurant in Margate\u2019s old town.
 
\u201cIt was really informal and really lovely, and relaxed. It was really special and she was really nice,\u201d said Di Dio.
 
She said it was \u201cmind-blowing\u201d to realise she had cooked her richly flavoured bean and kale stew and unusual Neapolitan beef shin pasta for one of the world\u2019s most famous musicians, though she acknowledged: \u201cMargate is always full of opportunities.\u201d 
 
Di Dio moved with her partner, Harry Ryder, to Margate a decade ago, priced out of London and Canterbury, and Di Dio said she spotted there was \u201calready a buzz\u201d in the town back then, but the pair have been astonished to witness its changing fortunes.
    
As well as raving about her visit to Di Dio\u2019s Cantina Caruso restaurant during a visit organised by the Turner prize-winning artist Tracey Emin, Madonna enthused about Margate on Instagram, describing the town as \u201cheaven\u201d and \u201cenergised by creativity\u201d.
 
While Di Dio and Ryder recognised Madonna\u2019s depiction of Margate as filled with artists, musicians and performers \u2013 vocations shared by many of their staff members \u2013 they felt that it was important not to idealise the town, which has a sharp social and economic divide.
 
 
 Related: \u2018My idea of heaven\u2019: Madonna sings praises of artists\u2019 paradise Margate 
 
  
Noting that the town has some of the most deprived postcodes in the UK, Ryder said: \u201cIt\u2019s not all rosy. She didn\u2019t see it all, she saw the art scene. Obviously there is a lot more to it.\u201d
 
But he added that although the influx of wealthier people and \u201cDFLs\u201d (Down From Londons) has been much maligned, lots of newer arrivals do want to contribute to the area.
 
Among the projects aiming to bridge the divide between Margate\u2019s \u201ctwo towns\u201d is the Perfect Place to Grow project, a cafe situated on the site of Tracey Emin\u2019s TKE Studios which trains local 18 to 24-year-olds who are struggling to access sustainable employment.
 
David Wilson, a chef and support worker who runs the kitchen, said: \u201cYoung people who try to engage with the Jobcentre and employment services locally are given very uninspiring options and we try to do the opposite of that.\u201d
 
Margate\u2019s strong brand has given trainees the opportunity to work with celebrity chefs such as Jos\u00e9 Pizarro and Nathan Outlaw, he said.
    
Many local people have mixed feelings about Margate\u2019s growing appeal to the rich and famous. Dan Thompson, an artist who has lived in the town for 20 years, moved in to what used to be one of the town\u2019s \u201croughest streets\u201d, but has been unable to keep up with prices rising as high-end galleries have moved in, and is now homeless and living with friends.
 
He said this experience was shared by others in his cohort of DIY experimental artists who moved in in the early 2000s \u2013 with many having since relocated to Dover in search of cheaper rents.
    
But he acknowledged that there have been \u201cmassive spillover benefits\u201d from the town\u2019s recent gentrification for some \u2013 for example, local tradesmen have profited from the increased demand for their services.
 
He is curating an exhibition that opens next week called Lost Margate, which looks at the way different waves of arrivals have rewritten Margate\u2019s story.
    
\u201cFor 300 years, it has only existed to take money from Londoners, so has always reinvented itself,\u201d he said. \u201cPeople absolutely love this place, and every generation that comes in falls in love with it for a slightly different reason.\u201d
 
Connor Sansby, a poet who has lived in Margate his whole life, is contributing a work to the exhibition, which uses the seaside town\u2019s waves as a metaphor for gentrification, in which new arrivals erase that which existed before.
 
 
 Related: Labour MPs call for action to tackle deprivation in coastal \u2018sea wall\u2019 seats 
 
  
\u201cMargate has become a place of two halves. It\u2019s two places occupying the same space,\u201d he said, noting that the new art world has \u201csplintered\u201d from local creatives.
 
\u201cThey\u2019re not interacting with the Margate native population, so they don\u2019t understand some of the issues,\u201d he said, citing the battle over a Greggs takeaway opening as a symbol for the disconnection between people who need affordable food options and those who do not.
 
Despite this, Sansby agreed with Madonna\u2019s assessment: \u201cIt does occasionally feel like an absolute dream. There\u2019s a culture and a community of people who\u2019ve been here the whole time, and we are all fantastic.\u201d
 
Margate\u2019s shabby high street is often seen as exemplifying the town that is being left behind amid the boutiques, restaurants and art galleries opening up in its old town.
 
Leo Kilburn-Long, who works in the McDonald\u2019s on the street, said he appreciated how Margate\u2019s changing fortunes have led to \u201cnew stuff popping up recently\u201d to reverse the high street\u2019s decline.
    
But he viewed gentrification as a double-edged sword: \u201cCost of living down here is ridiculous, you have to spend an arm and a leg to even afford a little room in somebody\u2019s gaff,\u201d he said. \u201cMargate is a great place to go visit, but to stay down here is so expensive.\u201d
 
Amy Holbourne, who works on the high street, hoped that Madonna\u2019s enthusiastic post may \u201chelp bring a lot of business to the town\u201d.
 
But she said believed that rising housing prices had resulted in growing homelessness and drug addiction.
    
Her niece, who has three children, has been on a social housing waiting list for three years and has been living with her grandfather. \u201cThere\u2019s just no housing round here,\u201d she said. \u201cThe council need to really sort it out.\u201d
 
Asked if she too would describe Margate as \u201cheaven\u201d, she said: \u201cI live here, I wouldn\u2019t describe it as that \u2026 but it\u2019s improving.\u201d

                    "bodyText": "Not many chefs working in small, family-run restaurants expect global megastars to turn up for dinner and to design them a menu from scratch. But that\u2019s what happened to Simona Di Dio last weekend, when she cooked dishes inspired by her Italian grandmother\u2019s recipes for Madonna, who sat on the single wooden dining table in Di Dio\u2019s cosy, candlelit Italian restaurant in Margate\u2019s old town. \u201cIt was really informal and really lovely, and relaxed. It was really special and she was really nice,\u201d said Di Dio. She said it was \u201cmind-blowing\u201d to realise she had cooked her richly flavoured bean and kale stew and unusual Neapolitan beef shin pasta for one of the world\u2019s most famous musicians, though she acknowledged: \u201cMargate is always full of opportunities.\u201d Di Dio moved with her partner, Harry Ryder, to Margate a decade ago, priced out of London and Canterbury, and Di Dio said she spotted there was \u201calready a buzz\u201d in the town back then, but the pair have been astonished to witness its changing fortunes. As well as raving about her visit to Di Dio\u2019s Cantina Caruso restaurant during a visit organised by the Turner prize-winning artist Tracey Emin, Madonna enthused about Margate on Instagram, describing the town as \u201cheaven\u201d and \u201cenergised by creativity\u201d. While Di Dio and Ryder recognised Madonna\u2019s depiction of Margate as filled with artists, musicians and performers \u2013 vocations shared by many of their staff members \u2013 they felt that it was important not to idealise the town, which has a sharp social and economic divide. Noting that the town has some of the most deprived postcodes in the UK, Ryder said: \u201cIt\u2019s not all rosy. She didn\u2019t see it all, she saw the art scene.                 "id": "politics/2026/jan/30/jeffrey-esptein-sent-money-peter-mandelson-husband-after-prison-release-emails-reveal",
                "type": "article",
