                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Attorney general defends missing Congress deadline \u2013 as it happened",
                    "standfirst": "
We\u2019re closing this blog. Please follow us for all the latest Epstein updates here: 
  • Epstein files updates: DoJ releases more than 3m new files as Todd Blanche says it \u2018did not protect\u2019 Trump
  • US justice department releases more than 3 million new pages of Epstein files
",
                    "trailText": "Todd Blanche says \u2018we didn\u2019t protect anybody\u2019 in the files as he announces release of 3m more documents",
                    "byline": "Lucy Campbell (now); Fran Lawther, Chris Stein and Sarah Haque (earlier)",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
 
 6.11pm GMT 
   
The day so far
  
  
Deputy US attorney general Todd Blanche announced the latest \u2013 and final \u2013 release of the justice department\u2019s files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, including 3m pages, 180,000 images and 2,000 videos.
 
Blanche insisted that no men, including Donald Trump, were protected in the release of the files, and that the White House \u201chad no oversight\u201d over the DoJ\u2019s review. Blanche explained what material had not been included, and that every woman\u2019s face had been redacted. Epstein\u2019s victims had been thorough \u201cunspeakable pain\u201d, Blanche said, adding that he shared frustration \u201cwith the entire process\u201d. He also defended the DoJ\u2019s missing its congressionally set deadline (which expired in December), comparing the amount of material to \u201ctwo Eiffel towers of pages\u201d and citing a need to protect victims.
 
We\u2019re launching a separate live blog on the Epstein files now, which you can continue to follow here.
 
Also today:
 
     
  • Don Lemon, the former CNN anchor, was arrested late last night on charges that he violated federal law during a protest at a church in Minnesota earlier this month. His arrest sparked outrage from former colleagues, first amendment advocates and members of Congress. \u201cThis is outrageous and cannot stand. The First Amendment is under attack in America!\u201d Lemon\u2019s former CNN colleague Jim Acosta wrote in a post on X. Read our report here.
    •  
  • Iran said it\u2019s ready to negotiate with the US, but only if talks are not under duress and do not extend to Iran\u2019s missile programme, as diplomats scramble to head off the threat of a regional conflict. More here.
    •  
  • The US Senate is scrambling to find agreement on a government funding package as a partial shutdown looms at midnight, after the killings of two US citizens by federal agents in Minneapolis upended spending talks and has given Democrats rare leverage over Trump\u2019s mass deportation campaign. The Senate\u2019s top Democrat, Chuck Schumer, has outlined a series of reforms to federal agents he wanted codified in the DHS\u2019s funding measure, including the requirement that officers wear body cameras, abide by a code of conduct and cease wearing masks and conducting \u201croving patrols\u201d aimed at people they suspect of being illegally in the US. More on that here.
    •  
  • And Trump announced Kevin Warsh as his nomination for the next chair of the Federal Reserve, selecting a candidate who has been an outspoken critic of the US central bank and ending months of speculation about who the president would pick to replace Jerome Powell. Trump has waged an extraordinary campaign to influence policymaking at the Fed by repeatedly calling for interest rate cuts. Powell\u2019s second term as chair is due to end in May. More here.
    •  
 
   
Updated at 6.15pm GMT
  
 
 
 5.57pm GMT 
    
  
Also in the files is Ghislaine Maxwell\u2019s US naturalization certificate, which lists her home address at Little St James Island, one of Epstein\u2019s two private islands in the US Virgin Islands. 
 
   
 
 
 5.45pm GMT 
    
  
Update: Trump did not say anything about the files. If he says anything as the day progresses, we\u2019ll have it here.
 
   
 
 
 5.21pm GMT 
    
  
Meanwhile, Donald Trump has been speaking from the Oval Office after signing an executive order aimed at launching an IndyCar race in Washington DC this summer.
 
He\u2019s taking questions from reporters now, if he says anything about the Epstein files I\u2019ll let you know here.
   
   
 
 
 5.19pm GMT 
    
  
Among the files released by the US justice department today is a copy of Ghislaine Maxwell\u2019s police booking intake form from July 2020.
 
It includes a picture of Maxwell in what looks like a prison orange jumpsuit, along with personal details including her full name and a redacted address in Bradford, New Hampshire.
   
   
Updated at 5.23pm GMT
  
 
 
 5.13pm GMT 
   
White House 'had no oversight' over review of files released today, Blanche says
  
  
Blanche also told reporters earlier that the White House \u201chad nothing to do\u201d with the DoJ\u2019s review of the files it released today.
 
Asked if he had updated the White House about today\u2019s announcement, Blanche replied:
 
 
They had nothing to do with this review. They had no oversight over this review. They did not tell this department how to do our review, what to look for, what to redact, what to not redact.
 
 
Blanche added that the White House knew he was holding today\u2019s news conference and that the DoJ was releasing the files, but \u201cthere\u2019s no oversight by the White House into the process that we\u2019ve undertaken over the past 60 days\u201d.
   
   
Updated at 5.35pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.49pm GMT 
    
  
Here\u2019s a quick rundown of what Blanche said is not in the release:
 
     
  • files that contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims\u2019 personal and medical files, and any similar files that, if disclosed, would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy
    •  
  • any depiction of child sexual abuse material or child abuse images
    •  
  • anything that would jeopardize an active federal investigation
    •  
  • anything that depicts or contains images of death, physical abuse or injury
    •  
  • files covered by various privileges, including deliberative process privilege, work product privilege, and attorney client privilege
    •  
 
\u201cAlthough the act allows for withholding for items necessary to keep secret in the interest of national security or foreign policy, no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis,\u201d Blanche added.
 
   
Updated at 4.54pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.45pm GMT 
    
  
The justice department\u2019s Epstein Library now includes an age verification, asking users if they\u2019re over 18.
 
Blanche earlier told reporters that some of the content being released includes pornography, with redactions.
 
   
 
 
 4.42pm GMT 
   
Blanche defends DoJ missing congressionally set deadline on release of files
  
  
Blanche says he won\u2019t be commenting on criticism the DoJ has faced on its handling of the release of the files and defends its missing the congressionally set deadline.
 
 
People can criticise all they want, my point was to make plain that when it comes to what we\u2019ve been doing the past two months and why, we weren\u2019t able to complete the review of over six million pages.
 
You\u2019re talking about two Eiffel Towers of pages in 30 days in a way that made sure we complied with the act.
 
 
He says the department was \u201cobviously\u201d not defying the 30-day deadline set by Congress (a reminder, that expired in December), but was complying with the need to protect victims.
 
   
Updated at 4.45pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.36pm GMT 
    
  
Blanche tells reporters:
 
 
There\u2019s this built in assumption that somehow there\u2019s this hidden tranche of information of men that we know about that we\u2019re covering up or that we\u2019re choosing not to prosecute. That is not the case.
 
I don\u2019t know whether there are men out there that abused these women. If we learn about information and evidence that that allows us to prosecute them, you better believe we will. But I don\u2019t think that the public or you all are going to uncover men within the Epstein files that abuse women.
 
 
   
Updated at 5.10pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.34pm GMT 
   
DoJ 'did not protect' Trump when reviewing Epstein files, Blanche insists
  
  
Blanche insists that no men, including Trump, were protected in the release of the Epstein files.
 
 
I can assure that we complied with the statute, we complied with the act. We did not protect President Trump. We didn\u2019t protect or not protect anybody, I think there\u2019s a hunger or a thirst for information that I do not think will be satisfied by the review of these documents. There\u2019s nothing I can do about that.
 
 
Trump\u2019s direction to the DoJ was to be \u201ctransparent\u201d and \u201cthat\u2019s exactly what we did\u201d, Blanche says.
 
   
Updated at 4.39pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.30pm GMT 
   
Epstein's victims have gone through 'unspeakable pain', says Blanche
  
  
Asked about survivors that have \u201cexpressed frustration\u201d at the DoJ\u2019s process for releasing the files, Blanche responds: \u201cSame here.\u201d
 
 
If there\u2019s frustration with quote, the entire process, same here.
 
 
\u201cThe victims of Epstein have gone through unspeakable pain,\u201d he adds. He says that he hopes that the release of the files has been able to \u201cbring closure\u201d to the victims.
 
   
Updated at 5.01pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.26pm GMT 
    
  
The deputy attorney general also said that no further files were due to be released. 
 
Todd Blanche told reporters: \u201cToday\u2019s release marks the end of a very comprehensive document identification and review process to ensure transparency to the American people and compliance with the act.\u201d 
 
   
 
 
 4.25pm GMT 
    
  
Blanche declined to comment on the arrest of former CNN anchor Don Lemon last night.
 
 
Do I have a \u2018reaction\u2019 to it? I don\u2019t know what that means. Are you looking for me to do, jump up and down? No I don\u2019t have a reaction to it, I don\u2019t know that the charges are unsealed yet. So, no. I\u2019m not going to comment on that.
 
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested on charges connected to Minnesota church protest 
 
 
   
Updated at 4.26pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.25pm GMT 
    
  
Todd Blanche addressed mistakes made during the first release of Epstein files in December. People examining the files at the time discovered that some of the file redaction can be undone with Photoshop techniques, or by simply highlighting text to paste into a word processing file.
 
On Friday, Blanche said: \u201cMistakes are inevitable. We, of course, want to immediately correct any redaction errors that our team may have made. And so the department has established an email and inbox for victims to reach us directly to correct redactions and any concerns when appropriate.\u201d
 
   
 
 
 4.16pm GMT 
    
  
The justice department faced criticism for not releasing all the Epstein files as required by law.
 
After missing a 19 December deadline set by Congress to release all of the files, the justice department said it tasked hundreds of lawyers with reviewing the records to determine what needs to be redacted, or blacked out, to protect the identities of victims of sexual abuse.
 
The number of documents subject to review has ballooned to 5.2 million, including duplicates, the department said.
 
On Friday, Blanche rejected any accusations that the DoJ was not taking child exploitation or trafficking seriously enough.
 
He said:
 
 
Just last year, the FBI located located over 2,700 victims of child exploitation. The Department of Justice found and terminated 3.8 million dark web pedophile accounts.
 
In August, we charged 11 defendants for extensive sex trafficking in Los Angeles of illegal immigrants and underage women. Last month, we charged five men who were engaged in a sadistic extortion extortion network of deranged young men abusing women.
 
Over the past, several months last summer and into the fall, we executed Operation Restore Justice, rescuing 205 child victims and arresting 293 offenders. I point this out because I take umbrage at the suggestion, which is totally false, that the attorney general or this department does not take child exploitation or sex trafficking seriously, or that we somehow do not want to protect victims. We do.
 
 
   
Updated at 4.23pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.13pm GMT 
   
Every woman's image has been redacted in latest release, Blanche says
  
  
During his press conference on Friday morning, Todd Blanche addressed redactions made by the justice department.
 
 
We redacted every woman depicted in any image or video, with the exception of Miss [Ghislaine] Maxwell. We did not redact images of any man unless it was impossible to redact the woman without also redacting the man.
 
To this end, though, and to ensure transparency, if any member of Congress wishes to review any portions of the responsive production in any unredacted form, they are welcome to make arrangements with the department to do so.
 
 
   
Updated at 5.02pm GMT
  
 
 
 4.11pm GMT 
    
  
The files, posted to the DoJ website, include some of the several million pages of records that officials said were withheld from an initial release of documents in December.
 
They were disclosed under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which was enacted after months of public and political pressure on the Trump administration.
 
   
 
 
 4.10pm GMT 
   
DoJ releasing 3m more Epstein files
  
  
The justice department is releasing more than 3m pages from its Jeffrey Epstein files, deputy attorney general Todd Blanche announced this morning. 
 
Blanche said they include 2,000 videos and 180,000 images related to Epstein. 
 
Blanche added that the images included lots of commercial pornography and images seized from Epstein\u2019s devices.
 
We\u2019ll bring you more on this as we get it.
 
   
 
 
 4.05pm GMT 
   
DoJ releases more Epstein files today
  
  
Blanche announces that the DoJ is releasing more documents tied to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
 
   
Updated at 4.07pm GMT
  
 
 
 3.54pm GMT 
   
Deputy AG holds press conference on Epstein files
  
  
Deputy attorney general Todd Blanche has said he will hold a news conference at 11am ET at the Department of Justice.
 
NBC News hears from two senior administration officials this will be related to the Epstein files. We\u2019ll bring you all the latest once that gets under way.
 
   
Updated at 4.08pm GMT
  
 
 
 3.32pm GMT 
   
Noem concedes she may have got her response to Pretti shooting wrong
  
  
Kristi Noem has conceded that she may have got some information wrong in her initial response to the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents.
 
\u201cWe were being relayed information from on the ground from CBP agents and officers that were there,\u201d Noem said in a Fox News interview with Sean Hannity last night, describing a \u201cvery chaotic\u201d situation when the host asked if her responses had been \u201cpremature\u201d. \u201cWe were using the best information we had at the time,\u201d she said.
 
The DHS secretary has been facing calls to resign amid widespread and mounting outrage, even among some Republicans, over her response to the killing of Pretti during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis last weekend. 
 
Shortly after his killing, Noem claimed without any evidence that Pretti was a \u201cdomestic terrorist\u201d that had been \u201cbrandishing a gun\u201d at officers \u2013 a narrative directly contradicted by video footage of the incident.
 
 
 Related: Pressure mounts on Kristi Noem as Republicans join calls for her to go 
 
  
Noem dodged questions from Hannity about why she believed the term \u201cdomestic terrorist\u201d to describe Pretti and Renee Good, also killed by a federal officer earlier this month, was appropriate. 
 
\u201cWell, Sean, we\u2019re continuing to gather information, and the FBI leading this investigation is important to make sure that we talk about both these situations appropriately,\u201d she replied.
 
Asked about Democrats (and notably not the aforementioned Republicans) calling for her to go, Noem dismissed the \u201cradicals\u201d calling for her firing.
 
 
These radicals are attacking me, but I\u2019m just doing my job. I\u2019m following the law, enforcing the laws like President Trump promised he would do, to keep people safe in this country.
 
   
   
 
 
 3.04pm GMT 
    
  
The arrest of former CNN anchor Don Lemon has sparked outrage from former colleagues, first amendment advocates and members of Congress.
 
\u201cThis is outrageous and cannot stand. The First Amendment is under attack in America!\u201d Lemon\u2019s former CNN colleague Jim Acosta wrote in a post on X.
 
Seth Stern, director of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called Lemon\u2019s arrest \u201ca naked attack on freedom of the press\u201d.
 
\u201cLemon\u2019s arrest under a bogus legal theory is a clear warning shot aimed at other journalists,\u201d he said in a statement to the Guardian. \u201cThe unmistakable message is that journalists must tread cautiously because the government is looking for any way to target them.\u201d
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested on charges connected to Minnesota church protest 
 
 
   
 
 
 3.00pm GMT 
    
  
After weeks of federal insurgency, Minnesota fought back, and it seems Donald Trump has lost faith in the people running his ICE operation in the state. So where does this leave Trump\u2019s \u2018ICE patriots\u2019? How do Republicans unite over immigration policies that kill Americans? And where does it leave the far-right agitators in Trump\u2019s cabinet?
 
In the latest edition of our Politics Weekly America podcast, Jonathan Freedland speaks to George Conway, a founding member of the Lincoln Project, who is running for Congress, about what happens next. 
 
Have a listen here:
 
 
 Related: Is Trump\u2019s ICE dream over? \u2013 podcast 
 
 
   
Updated at 3.01pm GMT
  
 
 
 2.48pm GMT 
   
Independent journalist among those arrested for Minnesota church protest
  
  
Among those arrested by federal agents for a protest earlier this month at a Minnesota church is Georgia Fort, an independent journalist who was covering the demonstration.
 
\u201cAgents are at my door right now. They\u2019re saying that they were able to go before a grand jury sometime, I guess, in the last 24 hours, and that they have a warrant for my arrest,\u201d Fort said in a video posted to Facebook, apparently shortly before she was taken into custody.
 
She continued:
 
 
This is all stemming from the fact that I filmed a protest. As a member of the media, we are supposed to have our constitutional right of the freedom to film, to be a member of the press. I don\u2019t feel like I have my first amendment right as a member of the press, because now federal agents are at my door, arresting me for filming the church protest a few weeks ago.
 
 
Fort concluded with: \u201cI\u2019m going to have to hop off here and surrender to agents. As a member of the press, I filmed the church protest a few weeks ago, and now I\u2019m being arrested for that.\u201d
 
   
 
 
 2.24pm GMT 
   
Top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries blasts arrest of Don Lemon
  
  
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat House minority leader, has issued a statement on X defending Don Lemon following his arrest by federal agents earlier today:
 
 
Don Lemon is an accomplished journalist whose urgent work is protected by the First Amendment. 
 
There is zero basis to arrest him and he should be freed immediately. 
 
The Trump Justice Department is illegitimate and these extremists will all be held accountable for their crimes against the Constitution.
 
 
The arrest could become a topic of investigation for House Democrats, if they win back control of the chamber in the November midterm elections, which would give them the power to issue subpoenas.
 
   
 
 
 2.14pm GMT 
   
Attorney general Bondi announces arrest of Don Lemon, three others over church protest
  
  
The US attorney general, Pam Bondi, has confirmed the arrests of former CNN anchor Don Lemon along with three other people for the protest earlier this month at a Saint Paul, Minnesota, church.
 
Here\u2019s what Bondi wrote on X:
 
 
At my direction, early this morning federal agents arrested Don Lemon, Trahern Jeen Crews, Georgia Fort, and Jamael Lydell Lundy, in connection with the coordinated attack on Cities Church in St Paul, Minnesota.
 
 
More details soon \u2026
 
   
Updated at 2.20pm GMT
  
 
 
 2.06pm GMT 
    
  
Here\u2019s everything we know about the arrest of former CNN anchor Don Lemon, from the Guardian\u2019s Sam Levine, Jeremy Barr and Anna Betts:
 
Don Lemon, the former CNN anchor, was arrested late Thursday on charges that he violated federal law during a protest at a church in Minnesota earlier this month, according to his lawyer.
 
Abbe Lowell, a lawyer for Lemon, said that Lemon was \u201ctaken into custody by federal agents last night in Los Angeles, where he was covering the Grammy awards\u201d.
 
\u201cDon has been a journalist for 30 years, and his constitutionally protected work in Minneapolis was no different than what he has always done,\u201d Lowell said. \u201cThe first amendment exists to protect journalists whose role it is to shine light on the truth and hold those in power accountable.\u201d
 
\u201cInstead of investigating the federal agents who killed two peaceful Minnesota protesters, the Trump justice department is devoting its time, attention and resources to this arrest, and that is the real indictment of wrongdoing in this case,\u201d Lowell added. \u201cThis unprecedented attack on the first amendment and transparent attempt to distract attention from the many crises facing this administration will not stand. Don will fight these charges vigorously and thoroughly in court.\u201d
 
The New York Times and CBS News also both reported the arrest on Friday morning. It is understood that Lemon remains in custody as of Friday. The Guardian has contacted the Department of Justice for comment.
 
\u201cThis is outrageous and cannot stand. The First Amendment is under attack in America!\u201d Lemon\u2019s former CNN colleague Jim Acosta wrote in a post on X.
 
 
 Related: Ex-CNN anchor Don Lemon arrested on charges connected to Minnesota church protest 
 
 
   
 
 
 1.42pm GMT 
    
  
Don Lemon\u2019s arrest comes as the justice department pursues charges against protesters who disrupted a service at the Cities church in Saint Paul, Minnesota, earlier this month.
    
The protesters believed that the church\u2019s pastor was a field director for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose agents have swarmed the Twin Cities in recent weeks in an aggressive immigration enforcement campaign that has resulted in the deaths of two US citizens.
 
However, the government\u2019s prosecutions have faced roadblocks in the form of federal judges who have refused to approve charges against those allegedly involved in disrupting the service \u2013 including Lemon, at least prior to today.
 
Here\u2019s more about that:
 
 
 Related: Appeals court rejects DoJ push to charge more people over Minnesota church protest 
 
 
   
Updated at 1.47pm GMT
  
 
 
 1.19pm GMT 
   
Federal agents arrest former CNN anchor Don Lemon
  
  
Don Lemon, a former CNN anchor, was arrested by federal agents in Los Angeles, his lawyer said on Friday, days after a magistrate judge refused to approve charges against him for documenting a protest at a church in Minnesota.
 
\u201cDon Lemon was taken into custody by federal agents last night in Los Angeles, where he was covering the Grammy awards. Don has been a journalist for 30 years, and his constitutionally protected work in Minneapolis was no different than what he has always done,\u201d his attorney Abbe Lowell said in a statement.
 
He continued:
 
 
Instead of investigating the federal agents who killed two peaceful Minnesota protesters, the Trump Justice Department is devoting its time, attention and resources to this arrest, and that is the real indictment of wrongdoing in this case. This unprecedented attack on the First Amendment and transparent attempt to distract attention from the many crises facing this administration will not stand. Don will fight these charges vigorously and thoroughly in court.
 
 
Here\u2019s more about the justice department\u2019s previous effort against him:
 
 
 Related: Judge declines to sign off on charges against former CNN anchor Don Lemon 
 
 
   
Updated at 1.37pm GMT
  
 
 
 1.02pm GMT 
    
  
Writing on his Truth Social platform about the appointment of Kevin Warsh as chair of Federal Reserve, Donald Trump said:
 
 
I have known Kevin for a long period of time, and have no doubt that he will go down as one of the GREAT Fed Chairmen, maybe the best. On top of everything else, he is \u2018central casting,\u2019 and he will never let you down. Congratulations Kevin!
 
 
Warsh won out over Trump loyalist Kevin Hassett. The president posted on Truth Social that:
 
 
Their [sic] was great speculation that highly respected Kevin Hassett was going to be named Chairman of the Fed, and a great Chairman he would have been but, quite honestly, he is doing such an outstanding job working with me and my team at the White House, that I just didn\u2019t want to let him go. Kevin is indescribably good so, as the expression goes, \u2018if you can\u2019t do better, don\u2019t try to fix it!\u2019 Thank you Kevin for doing such a great job!
 
 
   
Updated at 1.36pm GMT
  
 
 
 12.50pm GMT 
   
Trump to Iran: end nuclear ambitions and stop killing protesters or face US military
  
  
Donald Trump has warned Iran it must end its nuclear programme and stop killing protesters if the large US armada of warships deployed in the Middle East are not to be used.
 
Trump was speaking at the premiere of the documentary Melania as the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, landed in Turkey to discuss whether there was a basis for a deal with the US.
 
The US president said protesters were being killed in their thousands, but that he had stopped Iran from carrying out executions.
 
Trump\u2019s own administration has come under renewed scrutiny after US immigration officers killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Keith Porter in Los Angeles, and Silverio Villegas Gonz\u00e1lez in Illinois. ICE observers have reportedly faced violence, teargas and arrests.
 
Iran is prepared for the resumption of talks with the United States, but they should be fair and not include Iran\u2019s defence capabilities, Iran\u2019s chief diplomat said on Friday.
 
\u201cIf negotiations are fair and equitable, Iran is ready to participate in such talks,\u201d foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said in a press conference with his Turkish counterpart in Istanbul.
 
Araqchi said no talks between Tehran and Washington were currently arranged.
 
   
 
 
 12.35pm GMT 
   
Trump nominates Kevin Warsh as US Federal Reserve chair
  
  
Donald Trump has nominated the former Federal Reserve governor Kevin Warsh as its next chair amid an extraordinary attempt by the president to tighten his grip on the US central bank and flout its longstanding independence.
 
Trump told reporters on Thursday that he planned to announce his choice for chair of the Federal Reserve on Friday morning, hinting that \u201ca lot of people think that this is somebody that could have been there a few years ago\u201d. He then announced early Friday, as teased, and it was indeed Warsh.
 
If confirmed by the Senate, Warsh will replace Jerome Powell, who Trump first appointed in 2018, but later infuriated the US president by defying his repeated calls for lower interest rates.
 
In December, Trump said of Warsh: \u201cHe thinks you have to lower interest rates.\u201d
 
Read more:
 
 
 Related: Donald Trump nominates Kevin Warsh as chair of Federal Reserve 
 
 
   
 
 
 12.22pm GMT 
   
Opening Summary
  
  
Activists have called for a nationwide shutdown on Friday, advocating \u201cno work, no school, no shopping\u201d in a protest against the Trump administration\u2019s sweeping immigration crackdowns.
 
Organisers say Friday\u2019s \u201cblackout\u201d \u2013 or general strike, as some are calling it \u2013 is part of a growing non-violent movement to combat ICE\u2019s aggressive enforcement tactics, which have come under renewed scrutiny after a series of fatal shootings involving federal agents.
 
\u201cWe are calling for this strike because we believe what we have been doing in Minnesota should go national,\u201d said Kidus Yeshidagna, president of the Ethiopian Students Union at the University of Minnesota and one of the students organising the strike.
 
\u201cWe need more people and lawmakers across the country to wake up.\u201d
 
 
 Related: Anti-ICE protests to be held across US as organizers urge national strike 
 
  
In other updates:
 
     
  • The Democrats and the White House reached a deal to avoid a government shutdown, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer\u2019s office confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. The deal will advance a package of spending bills, while separating a Department of Homeland Security spending bill from the package. The agreement will include funding for DHS for two weeks at current levels, while Democrats continue negotiating further guardrails on immigration agents in light of the recent fatal shootings in Minneapolis.
    •  
  • Donald Trump sued the US Treasury and Internal Revenue Service for $10bn (about \u00a37.9bn) over an unauthorized disclosure of his tax returns during his first term, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday evening. Thursday\u2019s lawsuit puts Trump in the unusual position of suing government agencies that are part of the executive branch, which he leads. Trump famously broke precedent by not releasing his tax returns while running for, and then attaining, the presidency.
    •  
  • Trump\u2019s \u201cborder czar\u201d Tom Homan held a news conference in Minneapolis today, where he said \u2018no agency is perfect\u2019 but crucially did not mention the fatal shootings of US citizens by immigration agents there this month. During Thursday\u2019s press conference, Tom Homan noted that the administration has \u201crecognised that certain improvements could and should be made\u201d in the ongoing immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota, but didn\u2019t specify what those looked like or when they would be implemented. The border czar also refused to comment on the newly published video footage of Alex Pretti earlier this month, which appears to show officers grabbing Pretti and bringing him to the ground during intense protests that have gripped Minneapolis. \u201cWe\u2019ll let the investigation play out and let it go where it goes,\u201d Homan added.
    •  
  • Trump signed an executive order on Thursday laying the groundwork to slap tariffs on goods from countries that provide oil to Cuba, the White House said. The order, which ratchets up Trump\u2019s pressure to topple the Communist government, declares a national emergency and establishes a process for the US secretaries of state and commerce to assess tariffs against countries that sell or otherwise provide oil to the island nation. The White House has yet to specify tariff rates for violating its new policy of blocking Cuba from buying oil.
    •  
 
 
 Related: Trump threatens tariffs on goods from countries that sell oil to Cuba

Also in the files is Ghislaine Maxwell\u2019s US naturalization certificate, which lists her home address at Little St James Island, one of Epstein\u2019s two private islands in the US Virgin Islands. Blanche added that the White House knew he was holding today\u2019s news conference and that the DoJ was releasing the files, but \u201cthere\u2019s no oversight by the White House into the process that we\u2019ve undertaken over the past 60 days\u201d. Here\u2019s a quick rundown of what Blanche said is not in the release: files that contain personally identifiable information of victims or victims\u2019 personal and medical files, and any similar files that, if disclosed, would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy any depiction of child sexual abuse material or child abuse images anything that would jeopardize an active federal investigation anything that depicts or contains images of death, physical abuse or injury files covered by various privileges, including deliberative process privilege, work product privilege, and attorney client privilege \u201cAlthough the act allows for withholding for items necessary to keep secret in the interest of national security or foreign policy, no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis,\u201d Blanche added. He says the department was \u201cobviously\u201d not defying the 30-day deadline set by Congress (a reminder, that expired in December), but was complying with the need to protect victims. Todd Blanche addressed mistakes made during the first release of Epstein files in December. People examining the files at the time discovered that some of the file redaction can be undone with Photoshop techniques, or by simply highlighting text to paste into a word processing file. The order, which ratchets up Trump\u2019s pressure to topple the Communist government, declares a national emergency and establishes a process for the US secretaries of state and commerce to assess tariffs against countries that sell or otherwise provide oil to the island nation. The White House has yet to specify tariff rates for violating its new policy of blocking Cuba from buying oil.",

                "id": "world/2026/jan/30/mexico-sheinbaum-trump-tariffs-cuba-oil-crisis",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "world",
                "sectionName": "World news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T18:08:10Z",
                "webTitle": "Mexico president says Trump tariffs on Cuba\u2019s oil suppliers could trigger humanitarian crisis",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/30/mexico-sheinbaum-trump-tariffs-cuba-oil-crisis",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/world/2026/jan/30/mexico-sheinbaum-trump-tariffs-cuba-oil-crisis",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Mexico president says Trump tariffs on Cuba\u2019s oil suppliers could trigger humanitarian crisis",
                    "standfirst": "
Island country only has oil enough to last 15-20 days, and 12-hour blackouts have become commonplace
",
                    "trailText": "Island country only has oil enough to last 15-20 days, and 12-hour blackouts have become commonplace",
                    "byline": "Thomas Graham in Tijuana and Ruaridh Nicoll in Havana",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Mexico\u2019s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has warned that Donald Trump\u2019s move to slap new tariffs on countries sending oil to Cuba could trigger a humanitarian crisis on the island, which is already suffering from chronic fuel shortages and regular blackouts.
 
The US president signed an executive order on Thursday declaring a national emergency and laying the groundwork for such tariffs, ratcheting up the pressure to topple the communist government in Havana.
 
A White House statement cited the Cuban government\u2019s alleged ties to Russia, Hamas and Hezbollah to explain the new tariffs. While the statement did not name Mexico, Sheinbaum\u2019s government has been the top supplier of oil to the island since 2025, surpassing Russia and Venezuela.
 
 
 Related: Trump threatens tariffs on goods from countries that sell oil to Cuba 
 
  
Sheinbaum said on Friday that her government would seek more information about the tariffs from the US state department, while looking for alternative ways to provide humanitarian aid to the Cuban people.
 
\u201cWe will seek a way, without putting Mexico at risk, of course, but always seeking solidarity with the Cuban people,\u201d she told reporters.
 
The new tariff policy comes as Cuba struggles with increasingly severe blackouts. Sheinbaum said the tariffs could \u201cdirectly affect hospitals, food supplies and other basic services for the Cuban people\u201d.
 
Cuba\u2019s president, Miguel D\u00edaz-Canel Berm\u00fadez, said in a post on X that Trump sought to \u201csuffocate\u201d the island\u2019s economy and that the tariffs revealed the \u201cfascist, criminal, and genocidal nature of a clique that has hijacked the interests of the American people for purely personal gain\u201d.
    
Cuba\u2019s situation has become even more precarious since the US captured and transported Nicol\u00e1s Maduro, a key ally of the government in Havana, from Venezuela at the start of the year.
 
A week later, Trump wrote in a Truth Social post: \u201cTHERE WILL BE NO MORE OIL OR MONEY GOING TO CUBA \u2013 ZERO!\u201d
 
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported an estimate that Cuba only has enough oil to last 15 to 20 days at current levels of demand and domestic production, and could soon face sharp rationing.
 
Sheinbaum\u2019s comments came after a week of increasing threats from Washington. US officials briefed that gunboats could be deployed off Cuba, and said efforts were under way to find Cuban ministers prepared to collaborate with the US.
 
Speaking on Wednesday, Mike Hammer, the US charg\u00e9 d\u2019affaires in Havana, said: \u201cThe Cubans have complained for years about a \u2018blockade\u2019, but now there is going to be a real blockade.\u201d
 
The issue of oil shipments to Cuba is a fraught one for Sheinbaum, who is striving to show the Trump administration that Mexico is a partner on trade and security without alienating the left wing of her party, Morena.
 
The Trump administration has recently repeated its threats of unilateral military strikes on drug-trafficking cartels in Mexico, just as the two countries begin to renegotiate the trillion-dollar USMCA North American free trade agreement.
 
In Havana, 12-hour daily blackouts have become commonplace. Many Cuban families are struggling to cook food, finding it hard to get hold of gas canisters, and are resorting to cooking over charcoal.
 
But Jorge Pi\u00f1on, an expert on Cuba\u2019s energy at the University of Texas, said the situation has the potential to grow even more severe.
 
\u201cIf we do not see any crude oil or fuel deliveries within the next six to eight weeks, then the government will have a major crisis on their hands,\u201d he said.
",

                    "firstPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T18:08:10Z",

                "webTitle": "\u2018Isolation isn\u2019t the way forward\u2019: readers on their unusual living arrangements",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/2026/jan/30/alternative-living-arrangements",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/wellness/2026/jan/30/alternative-living-arrangements",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "\u2018Isolation isn\u2019t the way forward\u2019: readers on their unusual living arrangements",
                    "standfirst": "
We spoke with five people from Atlanta to rural Germany and the UK whose households range from grandparents to three couples who own a farmhouse
",
                    "trailText": "We spoke with five people from Atlanta to rural Germany and the UK whose households include friends and grandparents",
                    "byline": "Nicola Slawson and Jane Clinton",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
\u2018How many grandparents can say they get to hold their grandchild every day?\u2019
 
In Atlanta, Carolyn Martinez, 65, lives in a household spanning four generations \u2013 and a lifelong friendship. Her 90-year-old mother, who has lived with her for more than 40 years due to various disabilities, shares the house with Martinez, 65, her adult daughter, aged 25, and her granddaughter, aged three months. \u201cMy mum has lived with me literally all my adult life,\u201d she says. \u201cShe just wasn\u2019t able to live by herself.\u201d
 
The household also includes Martinez\u2019s best friend of more than three decades, who originally moved in \u201cfor a few months\u201d after a divorce. That was 25 years ago. \u201cI could not have raised my daughter as a single mother without her,\u201d Martinez says. When her friend, now aged 79, was diagnosed with breast cancer a few years after moving in, the arrangement became permanent. \u201cThere was no point in her leaving,\u201d she says. \u201cBy then she was an integral part of our household.\u201d Her friend is now \u201cT\u00eda\u201d (auntie in Spanish) to her children and grandchildren, a role Martinez says reflects how deeply friendship can function as family.
 
Earlier this year, Martinez\u2019s daughter moved back home when she became pregnant, adding another generation to the household. \u201cHow many grandparents can say they get to hold their grandchild every day?\u201d she says. \u201cIt\u2019s a blessing.\u201d While the house can be busy and hectic, it\u2019s also \u201ca lot of fun\u201d and Martinez says having multiple adults around makes life easier emotionally and practically. \u201cThere\u2019s always someone to say: are you OK? Is there something you need?\u201d she says. \u201cYou don\u2019t have that if you live alone.\u201d
 
Martinez has always lived this way and can\u2019t imagine doing otherwise. \u201cIt can be harder work \u2013 or maybe just different work,\u201d she says, particularly when living with friends rather than relatives. But she believes the benefits outweigh the challenges. \u201cIt keeps me young and it keeps me connected,\u201d she says. \u201cLiving like this keeps us all on a more even keel than any one of us would be alone.\u201d
 
\u2018The real thing that\u2019s held us together is how we party\u2019
 
In rural Germany, Tracey Kelliher, a 48-year-old Irish musician who has lived in Berlin for 17 years, is part of a group of three couples who bought an old farmhouse together despite barely knowing one another. The idea of communal living had been something she had long imagined for the future, but the coronavirus pandemic accelerated the decision. \u201cWe really followed our gut,\u201d she says. \u201cI\u2019m a calculated risk-taker \u2013 not a lunatic \u2013 but this just felt right.\u201d What began as a practical choice, driven by affordability and a desire not to do it alone, quickly became something deeper.
 
Before committing, however, Kelliher and her girlfriend, Wallis, had serious reservations. \u201cWe had a bit of a panic moment,\u201d she says. \u201cMy way of dealing with it was: I need more information. I basically needed to see into the future.\u201d It was only after a group conversation, where others acknowledged the scale of the leap, that she felt able to move forward. \u201cThey said: this is scary. It\u2019s a scary decision,\u201d she says. \u201cAnd even if it doesn\u2019t work out, everything\u2019s going to be OK. That was all we needed to hear.\u201d
 
When they first got the keys, the house had no heating and no running water. \u201cWe\u2019d be wearing ski suits indoors,\u201d Kelliher says. \u201cYou could tell the temperature by how much you could see your breath.\u201d The group spent their early months chopping wood, tending fires and collecting water together \u2013 conditions she describes as unexpectedly bonding. \u201cEven that was kind of team building,\u201d she says. \u201cYou become a family really quickly when you\u2019re living like that.\u201d Although she had initially imagined needing strict private space, she found herself loving the intimacy. \u201cThe communal way of living was a gift I never knew I wanted.\u201d
 
What surprised her most, however, was how the group really cemented their bond. She assumed it would be through the renovation or shared artistic interests. \u201cBut actually the real thing that\u2019s held us together is how we party,\u201d she says. Evenings around the fire became central to their life together. \u201cWe sing together \u2013 we didn\u2019t know that beforehand. It turns out we can all sing. We\u2019re doing four-part harmonies, dancing around the fire, with a guitar or music on.\u201d She describes it as the \u201cglue\u201d that turned a practical arrangement into a family. \u201cThat\u2019s what solidified us.\u201d
 
Friends and family, particularly those back in Ireland, were concerned when they heard the idea, she says, often focusing on what might go wrong \u2013 even though many admitted they longed for the same thing. \u201cAlmost everybody wants it,\u201d Kelliher says. \u201cPeople know isolation isn\u2019t the way forward.\u201d
 
The group, who all maintain homes in Berlin and split their time between the city and the farm, put significant effort into making the arrangement work on paper as well as emotionally. Unable to secure a group mortgage, they set up a company and drew up contracts covering everything from inheritance to what would happen if couples broke up. \u201cFor me, that\u2019s perfect,\u201d Kelliher says. \u201cIt means I don\u2019t ever have to think about it. It\u2019s done.\u201d Over time, formal meetings gave way to more organic decision-making, underpinned by trust. \u201cWhat makes it work is that we put other people before ourselves,\u201d she says. \u201cThere\u2019s no malice \u2013 if something comes up, you just say it.\u201d
 
Now, four years on, the renovation is nearing completion, with separate living spaces and shared communal areas. Their biggest concern, Kelliher says, is not conflict but distance. \u201cOur worry is that we might end up spending less time together \u2013 and none of us want that.\u201d
 
\u2018My son has grown up seeing that friends can be like family\u2019
 
In Bristol in the UK, Natalie Bennett lives with her 10-year-old son Ruben and his father, Aaron, her longtime friend with whom she has never been in a romantic relationship. When Bennett fell pregnant unexpectedly, they decided to do things differently and moved in together despite only being friends. \u201cI didn\u2019t want all the parenting to fall on my shoulders as a single parent. I wanted to see if we could do things differently and parent as friends,\u201d Bennett says. After initially living together for two years, they separated households for several years before moving back in together when Aaron\u2019s flatmate decided to move out, and he realised it was going to be difficult to rent alone with a child.
 
Living together again, she says, has made day-to-day life easier and less isolating. They split bills and childcare, share cooking and bedtimes and even co-own their home, even though their finances remain separate. \u201cIt\u2019s not that different from parenting as a couple,\u201d she says. \u201cWe get the benefits of that without being in a romantic relationship.\u201d The arrangement has also meant her son no longer moves between two homes and they all get to see more of each other.
 
Their household is also shaped by friendship. Bennett\u2019s close friend Alex \u2013 who previously lived with her son and his father \u2013 also lives with them two nights a week, helping with childcare and cooking. His support is invaluable, Bennett says, describing it as the village everyone talks about needing when you first have a child. \u201cMy son\u2019s grown up seeing that friends can be like family.\u201d
 
Bennett, who is doing a PhD on single parents with important non-romantic relationships, believes these kinds of platonic relationships are often undervalued, particularly when it comes to raising children.
 
Bennett says the biggest challenge has been navigating social expectations. \u201cPeople assume you\u2019re meant to be hostile if you co-parent or that romance is the only real intimacy,\u201d she says. But living this way has changed how she thinks about family and support. \u201cI think people would be less lonely if they felt able to expect more from their friendships.\u201d
 
\u2018We kept noticing little ways to help each other out\u2019
 
Sara Anastazia, 47, and her friend, Mia, moved in with their respective children when both women were going through a divorce.
 
\u201cWe began sharing a beautiful, big, five-bedroom home in 2023,\u201d says Sara, who is a community strategist and lives in Philadelphia. \u201cIt was a temporary six-month let while the owner was abroad. At the time, my kids were 14 and 16, and Mia\u2019s were 12 and five. It was incredibly helpful to live with another mom. We kept noticing little ways to help each other out and support each other, like with the laundry, getting ready for school, food shopping, chores and sharing meals. Our costs went down tremendously, and we both like to cook, so we would enjoy meals together.\u201d
 
She says they agreed to some very loose ground rules, but they \u201ctrusted each other\u201d and it worked out.
 
When the owner of the house returned, Sara and Mia, who is a cook and culinary educator, and their families moved out. \u201cWe went our separate ways for about a year, but we were still in touch,\u201d says Sara. \u201cThen in August of 2025, we lucked out and found an upstairs-downstairs rental.\u201d
 
Sara now lives in the two-bedroom downstairs with her son, 19, who stays two or three times a week. Her other son, 16, joins them for dinner from Sunday through to Thursday. Mia lives in the four-bedroom accommodation upstairs with her children, who are 14 and seven. \u201cWe share meals together one to two nights a week,\u201d she says. \u201cOur kids know each other a lot better now, and we all made cookies together at Christmas. We share the yard, and this spring we\u2019re looking forward to gardening. Coffee and tea mornings together are my joy. We also hold regular work sessions and have worked together hosting events.\u201d They keep costs down by sharing the internet and car insurance.
 
Sara and Mia feel very strongly about inspiring other women who may be going through divorce or a relationship break-up.
 
\u201cIt is very important to both of us that we can support women in our local community who are trying to navigate difficult situations,\u201d she says, with them letting women stay when they have the room.
 
\u201cThat is a priority for us. We really want to inspire other women who are trying to extricate themselves [from a relationship] and show the creative ways to do this.\u201d
 
She says of their living arrangement: \u201cI highly recommend this strategy for anyone exiting a relationship.\u201d
 
\u2018I can\u2019t imagine a better place to raise a child\u2019
 
A conversation Peter Reimer had as an undergraduate with one of their favourite professors about housing cooperatives spurred them to investigate this living arrangement when they moved to Chicago.
 
\u201cI found one, was interviewed and got a spot,\u201d says Peter, 31, a data analyst. \u201cI have been living in this co-op since 2018, but have moved houses within it. When I moved in, I put down a one-month security deposit and a membership charge of around $35.\u201d
 
Peter met their partner in 2018 at a co-op dinner. They are married and now have a two-year-old with another child on the way. They live in a 22-person house. For the first year and a half of their child\u2019s life, they had just one room, but now they rent a second room and hope to rent another in the future, though they will have to wait until someone moves out before one becomes available.
 
\u201cAs membership turns over, we can rent more rooms without moving, so it\u2019s a lot less hassle,\u201d says Peter, who adds that the support network of the house has been hugely helpful as they bring up their child.
 
\u201cMy partner works remotely as a therapist, and sometimes she needs exclusive access to the room,\u201d they say. \u201cWe are doing some co-parenting with some of our housemates, so we always had somewhere for the kid to nap when my partner was working.\u201d
 
Their rent gets them a room in the co-op and access to the common spaces. Depending on the size of the room, Peter says you can expect to pay between $500 and $800 a month, which is cheaper than the going rate for studios and one-bedroom apartments in Chicago.
 
\u201cAt the co-op you have a room, access to a large kitchen, a big dining room, common spaces, a bike room and a big yard, but they\u2019re not just yours \u2013 you\u2019re sharing them with other people,\u201d they say.
 
Rent includes the water bill and maintenance of the house. The housemates pay for electricity, heating, internet, their food, a rainy-day fund and an education fund, and the cost for all these is between $200 and $240 a month, depending on means.
 
In Peter\u2019s house, there is one room with an en-suite bathroom, and the remaining 21 people share six bathrooms. Everyone in the house is expected to do chores, including cooking and cleaning, totalling about five and a half hours a week.
 
\u201cI can\u2019t imagine a better place to raise a child,\u201d says Peter. \u201cIt\u2019s cheap, the common spaces are way bigger than I could afford living on my own, and I love living with people. The community, solidarity and mutual aid within the house are unparalleled. The only price is more time on meetings and figuring out living compromises, but it\u2019s a small price to pay.\u201d

                "id": "film/2026/jan/30/melania-review-trump-film-is-a-gilded-trash-remake-of-the-zone-of-interest",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "film",
                "sectionName": "Film",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T18:07:16Z",
                "webTitle": "Melania review \u2013 Trump film is a gilded trash remake of The Zone of Interest ",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/jan/30/melania-review-trump-film-is-a-gilded-trash-remake-of-the-zone-of-interest",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/film/2026/jan/30/melania-review-trump-film-is-a-gilded-trash-remake-of-the-zone-of-interest",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Melania review \u2013 Trump film is a gilded trash remake of The Zone of Interest ",
                    "standfirst": "
Dispiriting, deadly and unrevealing \u2013 there is a decent documentary to be made about the former model from Slovenia, but this one is unredeemable
\u2022 One adult for the 9.40am in Sittingbourne: a front row seat for Melania\u2019s ominous UK opening
\u2022 Eggs, hats and unfettered ambition: what we learned about Melania Trump from her documentary
",
                    "trailText": "Dispiriting, deadly and unrevealing \u2013 there is a decent documentary to be made about the former model from Slovenia, but this one is unredeemable",
                    "byline": "Xan Brooks",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
My audience with Melania is booked for Friday lunchtime at a retail park on the outskirts of Bristol, inside a large cinema which appears to have been swept and emptied in readiness. When Brett Ratner\u2019s contentious, Amazon-backed documentary previewed at the White House last weekend, the guestlist included Mike Tyson, Queen Rania of Jordan and the president himself. Today it\u2019s just me in the room and Melania on the screen. It makes for a more intimate and exclusive affair.
 
 
 Related: One adult for the 9.40am in Sittingbourne: a front row seat for Melania\u2019s ominous UK opening 
 
  
This mood of cosy conviviality extends all the way through the opening credits; at which point the chill descends and the novocaine kicks in, as the film\u2019s star and executive producer proceeds to guide us \u2013 with agonising glacial slowness \u2013 through the preparations for her husband\u2019s second presidential inauguration. She glides from the fashion fitting to the table setting, and from the \u201ccandlelit dinner\u201d to the \u201cstarlight ball\u201d, with a face like a fist and a voice of sheet metal. \u201cCandlelight and black tie and my creative vision,\u201d she says, as though listing the ingredients in a cauldron. \u201cAs first lady, children will always remain my priority,\u201d she coos, and you can almost picture her coaxing them into her little gingerbread house.
 
No doubt there is a great documentary to be made about Melania Knauss, the ambitious model from out of Slovenia who married a New York real-estate mogul and then found herself cast in the role of a latter-day Eva Braun, but the horrific Melania emphatically isn\u2019t it. It\u2019s one of those rare, unicorn films that doesn\u2019t have a single redeeming quality. I\u2019m not even sure it qualifies as a documentary, exactly, so much as an elaborate piece of designer taxidermy, horribly overpriced and ice-cold to the touch and proffered like a medieval tribute to placate the greedy king on his throne.
          
And so it goes on. Melania moves through the action like a listless automaton, talking constantly but saying nothing, squired from Mar-a-Lago to Trump Tower to her final destination, the White House. What drama there is chiefly hinges on her concern that her white blouse is too loose at the neck and needs to be cut and then tightened, much to the consternation of the fitters. Melania misses her mother, she says, but she loves Michael Jackson and Barron and possibly her husband as well, although Trump himself is mostly a background presence here, shuffling in at intervals to brag about his election win and complain that his inauguration clashes with the televised college football playoffs. \u201cThey probably did it on purpose,\u201d he says.
 
 
 Related: Eggs, hats and unfettered ambition: what we learned about Melania Trump from her documentary 
 
  
It\u2019s dispiriting, it\u2019s deadly and it\u2019s spectacularly unrevealing. Ratner\u2019s film plays like a gilded trash remake of Jonathan Glazer\u2019s The Zone of Interest in which a button-eyed Cinderella points at gold baubles and designer dresses, cunningly distracting us while her husband and his cronies prepare to dismantle the Constitution and asset-strip the federal government. \u201cWhite and gold \u2013 that\u2019s so you,\u201d purrs one of her lickspittles as she busies herself with the colour-scheme for the ball and the incoming first lady allows that yes indeed, this is true.
 
It\u2019s no spoiler to reveal that phew, thank heavens, Trump\u2019s second inauguration goes swimmingly well in the end. This despite the unfortunate clash with the college football game. This despite the infuriating looseness of the first lady\u2019s white blouse. The preparations are exhausting but the euphoria of the moment sees her through, all the way to the starlight ball where she briefly boogies along to the Village People\u2019s YMCA. \u201cBeing awake for 22-hours felt like nothing,\u201d she gushes, which is nice to hear and good for her. But the fun\u2019s not infectious and the guests are a nightmare, and two hours of Melania feels like pure, endless hell.
 
\u2022 Melania is out now
",

                "id": "world/2026/jan/30/israel-military-gaza-death-toll-broadly-accurate",
                "type": "article",
                "sectionId": "world",
                "sectionName": "World news",
                "webPublicationDate": "2026-01-30T18:06:47Z",
                "webTitle": "Israel accepts health authorities\u2019 Gaza death toll is broadly accurate, saying 70,000 have died",
                "webUrl": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/30/israel-military-gaza-death-toll-broadly-accurate",
                "apiUrl": "https://content.guardianapis.com/world/2026/jan/30/israel-military-gaza-death-toll-broadly-accurate",
                "fields": {
                    "headline": "Israel accepts health authorities\u2019 Gaza death toll is broadly accurate, saying 70,000 have died",
                    "standfirst": "
Israeli military\u2019s U-turn in accepting official figures comes after years of attacking data as \u2018Hamas propaganda\u2019
",
                    "trailText": "Israeli military\u2019s U-turn in accepting official figures comes after years of attacking data as \u2018Hamas propaganda\u2019",
                    "byline": "Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem",
                    "main": "",
                    "body": "
Israel\u2019s military has accepted the death toll compiled by health authorities in Gaza is broadly accurate, marking a U-turn after years of official attacks on the data.
 
A senior security official briefed Israeli journalists, saying about 70,000 Palestinians had been killed by Israeli attacks on the territory since October 2023, excluding those missing.
 
It is the first time Israel has publicly estimated the toll from the war in Gaza. Previously the government and military had only provided figures for militants Israel claimed to have killed.
 
Gaza health authorities said the direct toll from Israeli attacks had exceeded 71,660 people, with at least 10,000 presumed buried in the rubble of bombed buildings.
 
For more than two years, Israeli officials and media had attacked the Palestinian figures as \u201cHamas propaganda\u201d and dismissed them as \u201cnot accurate\u201d.
 
The abrupt shift in stance raises broader questions about Israel\u2019s defence of its campaign in Gaza. A UN commission, rights groups and scholars have accused Israel of committing genocide in the territory.
    
\u201cWhat other accusations could turn out to be true?\u201d the Israeli newspaper Haaretz said after the briefing. \u201cThe Israeli public must ask itself what this belated recognition indicates about the army and the government\u2019s credibility regarding Israel\u2019s conduct in Gaza.\u201d
 
It is also likely to intensify scrutiny of civilian casualties in Gaza. The Israeli military previously claimed to have killed 22,000 militants in Gaza, suggesting that, by its own count, more than two-thirds of the 70,000 dead were non-combatants.
 
That figure is significantly below the 83% civilian toll indicated by a classified Israeli military database, but well above the 50% casualty rate previously claimed by Israel\u2019s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
 
Israel was still reviewing how many of the dead were civilians, the Times of Israel said, but believed the overall toll compiled by Gaza health authorities was \u201clargely accurate\u201d.
 
A military spokesperson declined to confirm or deny the figure given at the briefing, saying only that \u201cthe details published do not reflect official IDF data\u201d. 
 
The Palestinian database does not provide a breakdown of fighters and non-combatants. It does identify most of the dead by name, date of birth and Israeli-issued identity numbers.
    
Israeli attacks on Gaza health authorities ignored a long track record of reliable record-keeping. During past wars in Gaza the final toll recognised by Israel and observers including the UN was broadly in line with Palestinian data.
 
There was little coverage or discussion of the death toll in Israeli media. Most major outlets attended the briefing, but with the exception of Haaretz, initially ignored the new figure.
 
Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper quoted the figure in a report focused on diplomatic manoeuvring between the US, Qatar and Israel. The report quoted an official, saying: \u201cOur estimate is that roughly 70,000 Gazans were killed in the war, not including missing persons.\u201d
 
The paper\u2019s online outlet, Ynet, later published a short piece on the toll late on Thursday evening. It was not a headline on television news shows.
 
The Israeli military also said it would open the key Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt on Sunday, for the first time since Israeli forces seized control of the border area nearly two years ago, in May 2024.
 
Palestinians who left Gaza could now apply to return for the first time since the war began, a spokesperson said. A European Union force would supervise the crossing, but Israel would retain full control of everyone who entered and left, the spokesperson said.
 
Reopening Rafah has been presented as a central part of US efforts to push Donald Trump\u2019s ceasefire plan for the territory firmly into a second stage. It will only be open to pedestrians, so will not ease shortages of food and shelter aid, medicine and other basic humanitarian goods in Gaza.
",
